$FIRY Q3 2026 earnings: Firy pays off its debt, while ad sales pass gaming

Firy, the gaming and advertising group formerly named Skillz, is now mostly an ad business and has paid off all its debt. Third-quarter revenue rose 14% to $31 million because chief executive Andrew Paradise said the RZR advertising unit grew 141% and passed half of total sales. Together with steep marketing cuts, that narrowed the operating loss excluding legal bills and one-offs to $1 million.

• Revenue: $𝟑𝟏.𝟑𝐌 (+14% from a year ago)
• RZR advertising revenue: +𝟏𝟒𝟏% (passed 50% of total revenue)
• Skillz paying monthly users: 𝟏𝟎𝟗𝐊 (-30% from a year ago)
• Total debt (after October payoff): $𝟎 (down from $128M at year-end)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because Firy removed its biggest financial threat after the quarter ended. Selling its stake in Exit Games for $55 million in October allowed finance chief Alex Walsh to pay off the last $50 million of maturing debt and keep about $76 million in cash by our math. One caution: the original Skillz gaming platform lost paying users for a fourth straight quarter, and Firy still has not collected any of its $730 million legal award from Papaya Gaming.

The question now is whether RZR's advertising profits can cover corporate overhead and fund the business before top partner games leave Skillz in early 2027. Either RZR's growth carries Firy to positive cash flow next year as promised, or shrinking gaming fees and unpaid ad bills keep the group burning cash. Fourth-quarter cash flow and Skillz user counts will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐖𝐚𝐥𝐥
Firy carried $127.6 million of debt at the start of the year, due in December 2026, which threatened its cash buffer. In the third quarter, the company paid off $80 million of those notes, leaving $49.5 million on the balance sheet at the end of September.

After the quarter closed in October, finance chief Alex Walsh said Firy "received $55 million from the sale of our Exit Games stake and redeemed the remaining $49.7 million of our senior secured notes". Chief executive Andrew Paradise confirmed "and we are now debt free". By our math, the sale and payoff leave the company with about $76 million in cash and eliminate ~$8 million in yearly interest payments.

What to watch: year-end cash on the fourth-quarter balance sheet. Holding cash near $70 million would show that removing interest payments and selling the stake solved the funding squeeze for good.

🟢🟢 𝐑𝐙𝐑 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
Firy runs two main businesses alongside its Beamable tools: Skillz, its original mobile gaming contest platform, and RZR, its advertising technology unit that helps mobile apps find users. Paradise said RZR revenue grew 141% from a year ago and "for the first time made up the majority of quarterly revenue". He added that "Roughly two-thirds of each new revenue dollar converted to Adjusted EBITDA".

The press release does not print the segment table, but the user metrics let us check the split. Multiplying 109,000 paying Skillz users by $45.20 in monthly revenue per payer over three months equals $14.8 million. By our math, that leaves about $16.6 million for RZR, up from $10.3 million last quarter and right on track to nearly double for the full year.

What to watch: the exact RZR revenue and profit table in the third-quarter filing. A segment profit margin above 25% would confirm the two-thirds conversion rate that Paradise described.

🟢 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧
Firy has spent years losing money because player incentives and legal bills swamped its gaming revenue. This quarter, the company cut sales and marketing — advertising and cash bonuses given to players — from 63.4% of revenue a year ago to 39.3%, a drop of 24.1 percentage points.

General and administrative costs, which pay for staff and lawyers, also fell by 2.7 percentage points to 61.1% of revenue. Because of those cuts and RZR's growth, the operating loss shrank by 26.9 percentage points to 32.5% of revenue. Excluding one-offs and $5.0 million of legal bills, the Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $1.2 million, or 3.8% of sales.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA excluding legal costs. Crossing into positive territory would mark Firy's first profitable quarter on that measure since its turnaround began.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐳 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Paradise said Firy is seeing rapid progress in its move from turnaround to growth, and total revenue rose 14% from a year ago. Yet all of that expansion came from advertising, while the original Skillz contest platform lost users again.

• Paying monthly active users: 109,000, down 7% from last quarter and down 30% from a year ago
• Total monthly active users: 343,000, down 44% from a year ago
• Gross marketplace volume (total contest entry fees): $125.5 million, down 10% from a year ago
• Average monthly revenue per paying user: $45.20, down 23% from $58.90 a year ago

By our math, Skillz revenue derived from paying users fell to about $14.8 million from $20.8 million in the second quarter. Some of the drop from last quarter reflects a one-time $3.7 million tax reserve benefit in the spring, but the steady loss of 8,000 paying players this quarter shows the gaming turnaround has not taken hold.

What to watch: fourth-quarter paying users and Skillz segment revenue. Three months ago management promised sequential revenue growth for Skillz in the fourth quarter, so another drop would break that commitment.

🔴 𝐏𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐚 𝐉𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭
Firy holds a $730 million court judgment against rival Papaya Gaming for false advertising, which bulls view as a windfall that dwarfs the business itself. In October, Paradise said the U. S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware "ordered Papaya Gaming not to move cash out of its U. S. bank accounts". He also noted that an expert hired by Papaya valued its equity at $1.29 billion.

Despite the favorable court order, Firy has collected zero cash from Papaya so far, while spending $21.5 million on lawsuits over the first nine months of 2026. Papaya is fighting enforcement through insolvency proceedings in Israel and Chapter 15 bankruptcy protection in Delaware, so any payout could take years or settle for a fraction of the award.

What to watch: court disclosures on how much cash actually sits inside the frozen U. S. bank accounts. A small balance would leave Firy dependent on Israeli courts to collect its award.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing operational and accounting questions were not addressed in the third-quarter earnings release.

• Tether Studios game departure: top games Solitaire Cube and 21 Blitz are set to leave in early 2027; the quarterly filing will show how much revenue still comes from two partner studios.
• Internal accounting controls: the release still lists unresolved material weaknesses in financial reporting that Firy aims to fix before the end of 2026.
• Indirect tax reserves: past quarters included multi-million-dollar revenue swings from tax reserve releases; the filing's footnote will show if any reserve changes affected Q3 sales.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟒.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Uncollected customer bills rose 69% from $14.4 million at the end of 2025, growing much faster than total revenue. Because RZR sells advertising on credit while Skillz collects player deposits upfront, RZR's growth tied up $10.6 million of cash over the first nine months of the year.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑, 𝐛𝐲 𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐡): -$𝟏𝟒.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Firy burned $35.9 million of cash in operations over the first nine months of 2026, down from $56.2 million in the same period last year. Subtracting the first half leaves $14.3 million of third-quarter cash burn by our math, driven by $5.0 million in legal bills and higher customer receivables.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟔.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The share count rose 8.5% from 15.3 million a year ago and 3.3% from last quarter. Firy did not buy back any stock during the first nine months of 2026, so employee stock grants steadily increased the number of shares.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰: 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 (> $𝟎)  ⇄ reversing
🠆 unchanged from Modest positive (> $0)
Unchanged. Walsh repeated that the group expects "modest positive operating cash flow in 2027". Reaching that goal from a nine-month cash burn of $35.9 million requires legal bills to fall and RZR customers to pay their invoices faster, helped by saving about $8 million a year in debt interest.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐳 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝟐𝟑%?
Average monthly revenue per paying user dropped from $59.10 in Q2 to $45.20 in Q3, even though contest entry fees per payer stayed steady at $384.80. Did Firy lower its cut of contest fees, or did a tax reserve release inflate Q2?

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐏𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐚'𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐳𝐞𝐧 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬?
The Delaware court ordered Papaya Gaming not to move cash out of its U. S. bank accounts. Knowing whether those accounts hold a few million dollars or a large share of the $730 million judgment tells investors if near-term recovery is realistic.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐳 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐐𝟑 𝐭𝐨 𝐐𝟒?
Three months ago, management projected that Skillz revenue would grow sequentially in the fourth quarter. With paying users down to 109,000 in Q3 and major partner games leaving in early 2027, does that fourth-quarter target still stand?

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐛 𝟔𝟗% 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫?
Accounts receivable rose by $9.9 million in nine months, eating up cash even as RZR profits grew. How long are advertising customers taking to pay, and how much of that balance comes from Firy's two largest ad buyers?

FULL RELEASE: 

NEW YORK, NY — The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) held its 2026 City Convention on Saturday, bringing together members from across the five boroughs to debate the organization's political direction, establish priorities, and determine its strategy for the years ahead.
Over the course of the convention, delegates debated and voted on resolutions addressing electoral strategy, organizational capacity, labor organizing, and the future of the democratic socialist movement in New York City.

Among the most significant outcomes, delegates approved “Run AOC 2028 to Win a Democratic Socialist President,” a resolution calling on the organization to build toward electing Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as the country's first democratic socialist president in 2028.

Delegates also approved resolutions addressing the organization's electoral and organizational infrastructure, including:

One Big Election: Aligns internal chapter leadership elections (including chapterwide leadership positions, branch leadership, and working group leadership) to take place between November and December.
Paying Full-Time Leadership to Organize a Socialist Agenda Through Mayoral and Electoral Coordination: Formalizes NYC-DSA’s two co-chairs as paid positions in the chapter bylaws.
Organize with Public Housing Residents and Workers For Better Conditions & an End to “Democracy For Some”: Affirms NYC-DSA’s commitment to social housing and prioritizes efforts to demand $1 billion for public housing across New York State during the next legislative session, while charting a path toward deeper federal-level investment in public housing for all.
From Brooklyn to Buffalo: Building DSA Electoral Power Statewide: Commits the chapter to building the necessary relationships and infrastructure with other New York DSA chapters to contest statewide and/or national races such as Governor, Senator, and President.
NYC-DSA for a $30 Minimum Wage ($30 by '30): Establishes a campaign fighting for a $30/hour minimum wage in New York City by 2030.
NYC-DSA and a Mass Labor-Left Movement: Sets an expanded strategy for the chapter’s labor organizing, including commitments to develop and win pro-labor legislation, and recruit labor candidates to run for office in 2028.
Building Socialism Requires Tackling Amazon: Commits the chapter to joining, building, and leading a citywide coalition to challenge Amazon’s power in New York City and to support rank-and-file organizing by Amazon workers.
Organize Our Base: Black and Latinx Membership Drive: Establishes a Black and Latinx membership drive to recruit and retain more members of color, with a goal of welcoming 400 new Black and Latinx members by April 2027.
Affirm NYC-DSA’s Commitment to Equity: A Task Force to Promote Equitable Organizing Culture: Establishes a new task force to improve internal systems, including responsibilities such as conducting a chapterwide assessment and developing a mandatory anti-oppression training program for chapter leaders.
Build Community Safety Through Prevention, Not Policing: Establishes a multi-year campaign to end racist and classist policing and invest in community alternatives and build on Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s proposed Department of Community Safety.

The Mind-Boggling Story of the The Remdesivir Cartel and the Gilead Team Inside the NIH Hospital COVID Protocols

You can’t make this sh!t up. With endnotes.

On 28 September 2026, Sen. Ron Johnson filled a room in the Russell Senate Office Building with twenty-one people and let them talk for four hours about what happened inside American hospitals during COVID.[1, 2] Nurses. A trauma surgeon. A lawyer who represents 212 families in 40 states. A physician who sits in the Oklahoma Senate. Johnson’s office says it holds 583 testimonies from 46 states. Twenty-one people spoke.[2]Senator Ron Johnson@SenRonJohnsonWatch the entire roundtable here⬇️Senator Ron Johnson @SenRonJohnsonCOVID-19 Hospital Protocols: Real Stories from Real People5:40 PM · Oct 1, 2026 · 4.52K Views7 Replies · 41 Reposts · 85 LikesJohnson’s office describes what they said: remdesivir and ventilation “forced on patients as the only viable options,” ivermectin and monoclonal antibodies denied “even when rigid hospital protocols were failing,” families kept from dying relatives, and “callous comments by doctors and nurses to unvaccinated patients and their families.” These are people who watched what happened at the bedside, and several of them paid for saying so. They are owed more than four hours in a Senate office building.[2]📷A nurse who watched the roundtable wrote a post that Wall Street Apes circulated: “It was handed to us from the top down. Every hospital got the same treatment guidelines, guidelines that said in writing, not a mandate, but every hospital followed this like it was the law.”[3] She added the payment rules, the lockouts, the staff mandate and a legal shield that runs to 2029. “If you didn’t follow it, you were out.”She was right about almost all of it. We checked each claim against the Federal Register, the Congressional Record, CMS manuals, court files, lobbying disclosures and the drug company’s own filings. Then we asked the question underneath hers: who wrote these rules?Different hands wrote each layer: an NIH panel, HHS’s preparedness office, Congress and the Medicare agency, the Medicare agency again, the HHS Secretary, and each hospital’s own administration. The hospitals acted as if all of them did.
Six layers
The treatment guidelines. Written by a panel at the National Institutes of Health.[4]
The drug. The Department of Health and Human Services signed a deal with Gilead Sciences that governed who got remdesivir from July through September 2020 and recorded its price.[5]
The money. Congress wrote a 20 percent Medicare bonus on the payment for each COVID inpatient stay. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) added a second payment for stays that used remdesivir.[6, 7]
The visitors and the staff mandate. CMS wrote the nursing-home visitor ban and the staff vaccine mandate.[8, 9]
The legal shield. HHS declared COVID countermeasures immune from suit, and has extended the declaration to 31 December 2029.[10, 11]
The hospital’s own daily orders. This is the layer a nurse actually touches. A surgeon at the hospital that treated the first American COVID patient swears under penalty of perjury that his chief medical officer sent staff “weekly to daily directives” relaying CDC and CMS requirements for more than a year.[12]The NIH panel says its guidelines “should not be considered mandates.”[4] CMS’s own explainer for the 20 percent bonus says it is “not intended to grant rights or impose obligations.”[13] Hospitals followed the guidelines and the payment rules as if they were law. The surgeon, Dr. James P. Miller, swears that at Everett “it was understood that you would lose your job and/or license if you did not maintain compliance,” and that he was taught at a CMS-compliance conference that non-compliance “meant certain financial destruction and bankruptcy for that hospital or medical group.”[12]📷The rest of this article follows the layers one at a time, then the people who sat around the table when they were written.
The panel that wrote the treatment protocolThe panel began in March 2020 at the request of the White House Coronavirus Task Force, passed through the HHS Secretary to NIH. Anthony Fauci’s institute, NIAID, “initiated the formation” of it. The first guidelines went up on 21 April 2020.[4] Three co-chairs ran it: Roy Gulick of Weill Cornell, Cliff Lane of NIAID and Henry Masur of the NIH Clinical Center.[14, 15] Over four years it voted 438 times.[16]It never published how a single member voted. It never published a rule requiring a member to sit out a vote on a product made by a company that paid them. The only conflict-of-interest procedure on record is that the co-chairs reviewed disclosures twice a year “to determine suitability for membership,” and that panel leadership used them to decide whether a member should take part.[14, 4, 16]The disclosure tables show why that matters. In April 2020 eleven panel members listed a financial relationship with a drug company. Nine of the eleven listed Gilead, the maker of remdesivir: Aberg, Adimora, Baker, Bedimo, Daar, Gandhi, Glidden, Naggie and Tebas. Gulick, Lane and Masur each wrote “None.”[14, 17]Lane wrote “None” while serving as the last-named author of ACTT-1, the NIAID-sponsored trial whose results carried the panel’s remdesivir recommendation. The trial paper says Gilead employees took part in protocol discussions and weekly calls, and that NIAID “ultimately made all decisions.”[18] NIAID’s statisticians proposed changing the trial’s main measure to time to recovery on 22 March 2020, after about 7 percent of patients had enrolled; the amendment is dated 1 April. FDA’s reviewer called the change reasonable.[19] The Government Accountability Office found federal agencies spent about $162 million on remdesivir research through 2020 and ended up with no patent rights; Gilead held them.[20]
Eight weeks that decided the drugThe sequence is the story, so here it is in order.
18 March 2020. Fauci’s diary: HHS Secretary Alex Azar “said that he could approve HC and Remdesivir now with the powers that he has... I took a deep breath and said that this was wrong and should not be done.”[21]
21 April. The panel’s first guidelines find “insufficient clinical data to recommend either for or against” remdesivir.[14]
28 April. Gilead’s Merdad Parsey asks Fauci to hold the trial announcement “so that they can formulate a statement and policy to not allow an unfavorable or too favorable response of the Stock Market.” Fauci writes that he told him no way, and that Parsey backed off.[22]
29 April. NIAID announces the results. An email that morning says FDA “[has] written (and cleared with Gilead) a new sentence” for the NIH press release. Gilead’s own statement reached Fauci “before markets open this morning.”[23] At the White House that day Fauci says remdesivir “will be the standard of care,” in the same remarks calling the 31 percent improvement something that “doesn’t seem like a knock-out.”[24]
1 May. FDA issues the emergency authorization on “topline data,” with distribution “controlled by the United States (U.S.) Government.”[25] Gilead’s chief executive stands in the Oval Office with the President.[26]
12 May. The panel flips from “insufficient clinical data” to recommending remdesivir for severe disease, “on the basis of preliminary clinical trial data.” That is thirteen days after “standard of care.”[27]Five months later the largest remdesivir trial reported. WHO’s Solidarity study followed 11,330 hospitalized patients and found 301 deaths among 2,743 on remdesivir against 303 among 2,708 on standard care, with no reduction in ventilator use or hospital stay.[28] That was 15 October. FDA approved remdesivir a week later on the strength of NIAID’s trial; the review does not discuss Solidarity.[29, 30] On 2 November a Medicare payment that names remdesivir began paying.[7] On 20 November WHO’s guideline panel, reporting no conflict of interest among its members, conditionally recommended against remdesivir for hospitalized patients.[31] The NIH panel’s guideline cited Solidarity for the first time on 11 February 2021.[27]NIAID’s own trial found patients recovered in a median of 10 days on remdesivir against 15 on placebo. Deaths by day 29 were 11.4 percent against 15.2 percent, a difference too small to count statistically.[18] Solidarity, the French DisCoVeRy trial of 857 patients and the 2023 Cochrane review all found little or no effect on deaths in hospitalized patients.[28, 32, 33] Gilead’s Veklury sales were $2.8 billion in 2020, $5.6 billion in 2021 and $3.9 billion in 2022.[34, 35, 36]
The dealThe agreement that governed who got remdesivir from July through September 2020 is a three-party memorandum dated 27 June 2020, between HHS, Gilead and the drug distributor AmerisourceBergen. HHS did not buy the drug. Hospitals paid. HHS’s Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response, Robert Kadlec, signed for the government.[5]The terms read like a franchise agreement. Gilead would “use commercially reasonable efforts” to supply about 501,900 treatment courses for July through September. “ASPR will set allocation quantities,” and Gilead and the distributor “shall have no responsibility or discretion” over which hospitals got the drug. The price was $520 a vial, about $3,250 a course. If Gilead could not sell August or September allocated stock by 31 October, even after offering it to foreign governments, “HHS agrees to indemnify Gilead ... for the losses associated with the Excess Product at $390 per vial,” up to 145,000 courses, a ceiling of about $353 million. And the memorandum states that the PREP Act’s immunity and pre-emption protections “extend to the participation of Gilead and Distributor in this MOU.”[5]Under HHS’s plan the preparedness office set each state’s share and state health departments chose the hospitals.[37] New Jersey’s memo of 26 June 2020, written for the donated stock a day before the memorandum, shows how one state ran it: report twice a week, and “Failure to report data may negatively affect qualification for future allocations.” It left the prescribing call to “the attending physician of record.”[38]Seven weeks before Kadlec signed, six Democratic senators wrote that they were “concerned by recent reports” that he had “failed to disclose” to the Senate and the Office of Government Ethics that he co-founded a company in 2012 and consulted for Emergent BioSolutions, which had received more than $733 million from his office.[39] Emergent paid his consulting firm $120,000 a year from 2012 to 2015. Emergent’s executive chairman confirmed the $360,000 total under oath on 19 May 2021.[40] The stockpile moved from CDC to Kadlec’s office in 2018. The Washington Post reported that moving it was part of Emergent’s 2017 corporate strategy.[41, 39]On 11 February 2020, Fauci’s diary shows Kadlec offering Japan remdesivir under compassionate use for Diamond Princess passengers, before any trial had reported.[42] The memorandum wrote the Secretary’s PREP Act immunity into the deal.
The bonusSection 3710 of the CARES Act, signed 27 March 2020, orders Medicare to raise the payment weight of any hospital stay for “an individual diagnosed with COVID-19” by 20 percent.[6] That is the bonus the nurse described. It was 15 percent when it first appeared.On 19 March the Senate Republican leadership’s bill, S. 3548, carried a 15 percent add-on. The Finance Committee’s own summary of it says 15.[43, 44] The American Hospital Association told its members that same day to ask their lawmakers for “a Medicare add-on payment equal to 25% of the diagnosis-related group.”[45] On Friday 20 March the association’s advisory still described 15. By Sunday 22 March, as the Republicans released a revised bill, its advisory described 20.[46] A House Ways and Means summary dated 23 March, describing the Senate text as of Sunday 22 March, said the add-on “is more generous than earlier drafts: 20 percent, as compared to 15 percent in the first draft.”[47]Nobody has said who changed the number. The hospital lobbies were loud in those days. On 20 March the Federation of American Hospitals raised its funding request to $225 billion. On 21 March the association’s executive vice president told Modern Healthcare he expected the Senate’s opening offer to be “massaged and improved.”[48] Politico called the $100 billion hospital fund that followed “a major win for hospital lobbies” and wrote that “provider lobbyists in the past several days moved the needle considerably on funding talks.”[49] The Federation’s chief executive said of the finished bill: “It provides what we asked for.”[50]The second payment came in November. CMS’s rule for the new COVID-19 treatments add-on pays part of a stay’s extra cost on stays that used a listed product, a ceiling of roughly $19,500 a case at the rule’s own example threshold of about $30,000. The rule lists two products: convalescent plasma and remdesivir. CMS said the purpose was to avoid “financial disincentives for hospitals to provide new COVID-19 treatments.”[7, 51] Ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine were not on the list.The relief fund dwarfed both. HHS said in August 2021 it was “distributing $178 billion to hospitals and healthcare providers.” The Government Accountability Office found providers kept $135 billion, about $84 billion of it to hospital-based systems. The first $30 billion went out by each provider’s share of Medicare fee-for-service payments, not by COVID cases.[52, 53, 54]The $40,000 ventilator figure in the nurse’s post matches a Kaiser Family Foundation study of 2017 Medicare claims ($40,218) that excluded the 20 percent bonus; it is not a CMS estimate. The $24,000 figure matches no Medicare figure in that study.[55] The real average, from the HHS inspector general’s audit of $2.7 billion in COVID claims for September to November 2020, was about $16,300 a claim.[56] Nurses say they were told to code patients as COVID for the money. The inspector general audited that question on a sample of 149 of 166,107 claims and found 146 correct and three wrong. The sample covered three months of Medicare fee-for-service claims. The claims at the hospitals named in Johnson’s testimonies have not been pulled.
The lobby inside the billing systemThe American Hospital Association told its members to ask for the bonus, tracked it through its member advisories, and then went to CMS to defend it. On 6 April it asked CMS to extend the 20 percent to long-term care hospitals.[57] In August CMS announced that for admissions from 1 September it would require a positive COVID test on the record to keep the money, and said it would recoup the payment if none was there.[58] The association wrote to CMS Administrator Seema Verma on 26 August: “we urge CMS to allow provider documentation to suffice if the test result is unavailable.” Its reasoning: “The U07.1 diagnosis code therefore remains sufficient for identifying COVID-19 cases for the DRG add-on policy.”[59]The association does not only lobby the billing system. It chairs and staffs part of it. It owns the copyright on the UB-04 billing manual, which the National Uniform Billing Committee calls “the only official source of UB Data.” AHA staff chair that committee and hold its secretariat, and the committee told hospitals how to flag COVID claims on 23 March 2020, four days before the law was signed.[60] The association is one of four “Cooperating Parties” that approve the ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines, which federal law makes mandatory and which say, of COVID, that “the provider’s documentation that the individual has COVID-19 is sufficient” to assign the code the bonus is keyed to.[61, 62] The association spent $19.5 million lobbying in 2020, its own filings show.[63]The Federation of American Hospitals’ first-quarter filing says it “advocated in support of lifting sequester, increasing DRG payments.”[64]Now the file. The Senate Finance Committee’s own 19 March summary of the add-on carries the author tag “Baker, Brett (Finance).”[44] The Finance Republicans’ health staff in those years included a Brett Baker: Senior Advisor, Health Policy under Chuck Grassley in 2018, and Deputy Health Policy Director under Mike Crapo by February 2021.[65] In April 2022 a Brett Baker is a registered lobbyist for the American Hospital Association at The Nickles Group, the firm that was already the association’s outside lobbyist in 2020. His form lists Senate Finance Committee jobs under Crapo, Grassley and Hatch, “Deputy Health Policy Director; Health Policy Dir.; Senior Policy Advsr; Policy Advisor,” and a House Ways and Means professional-staff post as his government experience.[66] That is a revolving door: a senior Finance Republican health aide through February 2021 is the hospital lobby’s man in 2022.
What reached the bedsideJames Miller was a trauma and acute-care surgeon who also worked in critical care at Providence Regional Medical Center Everett in Washington State, the hospital that treated the first American COVID patient.[67] He signed a 72-paragraph declaration under penalty of perjury on 31 May 2024. It names the hospital officials who, he swears, carried the federal requirements to the staff.[12]In late February or early March 2020, he swears, Stephen Campbell, chief medical officer of the Providence Medical Group, informed him that “the CDC had sent us a powerful antiviral.” Miller says the drug was “understood to be remdesivir, which was given to the hospital as compassionate use directly from the CDC,” and swears Campbell’s representations about its effectiveness were “inaccurate.”[12] The New England Journal of Medicine’s report on the first U.S. case confirms that doctors at Providence “pursued compassionate use” of remdesivir for him.[67]
“The Chief Medical Officer, Jay Cook, would send out weekly to daily directives to the staff and physicians providing updates of the CDC and CMS requirements ... throughout the entire COVID crisis (over one year). ... it was understood that you would lose your job and/or license if you did not maintain compliance with the unscientific and constantly shifting federal health requirements.” Dr. James Miller, sworn declaration, 2024.[12]Miller swears that masking, ventilator use, protective equipment, staff vaccination, distancing and the shutdown of elective surgery “were all determined by the federal health agencies and forced upon the staff and patients by the hospital administrators.” He swears that after the directives began, “the hospital’s unanticipated mortality in indexed trauma surgery patients increased by more than 100% (doubled),” and that “the administration was confronted with this data and made no changes.”[12] He swears he found Medicare fraud by several providers in March 2020, “with the approval of the Chief Medical Officer of the hospital,” reported it to authorities, and that administrators then tried to fabricate grounds to fire him and go after his license. He swears the default on death certificates assigned to him was COVID, and that the hospital’s COVID numbers turned downward on or about 17 March 2020 while leadership went on publishing inflated counts and collecting federal aid.[12] After he resigned in January 2022, he swears, four requests for a fair hearing on a “microaggression” investigation that cleared him were denied by Cook, the chief of surgery and two committee https://t.co/UDonViyg1z Miller’s account those directives carried the CDC and CMS requirements to the hospital’s staff. No copy is public. Washington’s public records law covers state and local agencies, not a private hospital system like Providence, and state law shields hospital peer-review files.[68, 69, 70] The copies sit in Providence’s system and in the inboxes of the physicians who received them. A Senate committee’s letter to Providence is the tool that gets them.Other doctors fought the protocols at their own cost. Paul Marik, a critical-care physician in Norfolk, Virginia, sued Sentara Healthcare on 9 November 2021 over its ban on ivermectin and other drugs in his protocol. He swore that he believed about half the patients admitted to his ICU had received or were getting remdesivir, and that he does not prescribe it and stops it. The injunction hearing was on 18 November, the date on a letter suspending his privileges for 14 days that Marik found on 20 November. The judge denied the injunction on 23 November. Sentara’s own guidelines listed remdesivir starting criteria drawn from the NIAID trial and did not require the drug.[71]
What the evidence said, and what the protocols didEarly in 2020 the profession’s own guideline told doctors to watch patients on high-flow oxygen and “early intubation in a controlled setting if worsening occurs.”[72] Reported deaths among ventilated COVID patients averaged 45 percent across 69 studies and 57,420 patients.[73] At Northwell in New York, by 4 April 2020, 24.5 percent of 1,151 ventilated patients had died and 72.2 percent were still in hospital; the claim that 88 percent died divides 282 by the 320 whose outcome was known.[74]One steroid worked. Britain’s RECOVERY trial, funded in part by the Wellcome Trust and the Gates Foundation, showed dexamethasone helped patients on oxygen or ventilators, and NIH recommended it for ventilated patients and for patients on supplemental oxygen on 25 June 2020.[75, 76] The panel recommended against hydroxychloroquine in June 2020 and against ivermectin in August 2020 outside a trial. In February 2021 it moved ivermectin to “insufficient evidence ... to recommend either for or against.”[77, 78, 79] The payment rule named neither drug.
Visitors, mandates and the shieldOn 13 March 2020 CMS told nursing homes to “restrict visitation of all visitors and non-essential health care personnel, except for certain compassionate care situations, such as an end-of-life situation.” David R. Wright signed it.[8] CMS’s later visitation memo, QSO-20-39-NH, revised on 8 May 2023 as the emergency ended, says “Visitation is allowed for all residents at all times.”[80] The nurse’s post called the policy “the same green light to lock families out”; the first federal visitation memo was this one.[3]On 5 November 2021 CMS required 15 types of Medicare- and Medicaid-certified providers, hospitals and nursing homes among them, to ensure their staff were vaccinated. CMS Administrator Chiquita Brooks-LaSure approved the rule and HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra signed it.[9] Two federal courts blocked it in late November. On 13 January 2022 the Supreme Court stayed both injunctions, five to four, with Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Barrett dissenting.[81] CMS withdrew it in June 2023.[82]The legal shield is older than both. Azar signed the PREP Act declaration on 10 March 2020, putting into effect the Act’s rule that, “subject to other provisions,” a covered person “shall be immune from suit and liability under federal and state law with respect to all claims for loss caused by, arising out of, relating to, or resulting from the administration to or use by an individual of a covered countermeasure,” except for claims of “willful misconduct.”[10] HHS has amended it twelve times. The twelfth, signed by Becerra in December 2024, runs it to 31 December 2029.[11] Injured patients go to a federal compensation program; only willful-misconduct claims can reach court. As of 1 July 2026 it had received 14,146 COVID claims, decided 7,584, found 112 eligible and paid 62.[83]

KYIV BRIDGES HIT, MAJOR ATTACK REPORTED ON KERCH BRIDGE, TANKER ALERTS IN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ

World Conflict Live 24/7 | End-of-day report | Monday, November 16, 2026
Good evening. Here’s where today’s major stories stand through 9:55 p.m. Eastern.

UKRAINE AND RUSSIA

A late-day report described a large ballistic missile attack against Ukraine. Kyiv Mayor Klitschko said Russian strikes hit the city’s Northern and Southern bridges. A separate report named Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Zircon hypersonic missiles in a Kyiv bridge strike.

In Dnipro, regional officials said a drone struck a roadway Monday morning, setting cars on fire. 1 person was killed. The initial report put the number of injured at 10, all of whom were hospitalized. 2 men, ages 26 and 47, were in serious condition. Officials later raised the injury count to 13. The day’s attacks also damaged apartment buildings and vehicles.

Separate strikes hit energy facilities in the Dnipro region. Ukrainian energy company DTEK said the entire city lost power. Crews began restoring electricity to water and heating systems and other essential facilities first.

A strike also set fire to the Oleina sunflower oil plant in Dnipro. Its U.S. owner, Bunge, confirmed the strike, said no employees were injured and temporarily suspended operations at the plant.

In Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, crews ended a two-week search in Komyshuvakha. The confirmed death toll from the November 2 airstrike stood at 72. The strike hit a school where residents had come to collect humanitarian aid. Those killed included rescuers, police, medical staff, utility workers and school staff. One was a teacher who gave online lessons from the shelter to children who had evacuated.

4 people remain missing and 4 are still hospitalized. Ukraine’s Interior Ministry said Russian forces struck the search site 9 times during the operation, injuring 3 police officers and 4 rescuers.

At the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea, the Kremlin initially reported an overnight Ukrainian drone strike. Road traffic was briefly halted while trains continued to run. The Kremlin described the damage as minor, and no injuries were reported.

Russian occupation authorities in Crimea later confirmed a new overnight strike. Further reports said a span was gone and that more than 15 strikes had been observed at the bridge.

A report received at 9:55 p.m. Eastern described a large-scale Ukrainian missile and drone attack on the Kerch Bridge as ongoing. It said at least 10 cruise missiles and 25 drones had struck the bridge.

Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down a record 2,049 Ukrainian drones in 24 hours and intercepted 4 long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 7 guided bombs. Later, early reports put a new wave of Ukrainian drones over Russia at more than 400, an unverified figure.

As Moscow came under heavy drone attack, Mayor Sobyanin said 142 drones had been shot down. All of the capital’s airports were reported closed at the time.

In southern Russia, the Rostov regional governor said an overnight Ukrainian drone attack started fires at 4 industrial sites in Azov. 3 men were injured and hospitalized. ASTRA reviewed footage and located one fire near 2 oil depots.

Another report said Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky oil refinery, hitting its AT-4, AT-5 and AT-6 oil processing units and a gasoline production complex. The refinery can process about 6.6 million tons of oil a year.

In Salavat, Bashkortostan, local residents reported a Ukrainian attack and a fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex.

BLACK SEA RESCUE AND SHIPPING ALERTS

Off Bulgaria, a rescue operation was launched after the crew of the Somali-flagged cargo ship BETUL 8 reported it was sinking about 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra. Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry said the ship was carrying wheat from Romania to Egypt with 12 people aboard. Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey dispatched 4 ships, and Bulgarian aircraft joined the search.

Bulgarian broadcaster bTV reported that the crew took to life rafts. Their condition and the cause of the emergency remained unclear.

Romania deployed 2 Navy bomb disposal teams after a French Atlantique 2 patrol aircraft spotted 2 drones drifting off the Romanian coast on November 15. One team was checking drone parts for explosives from a Coast Guard vessel about 45 nautical miles east of Mangalia. A second team was aboard a minesweeper heading toward Sfântu Gheorghe. That drone was first spotted about 53 nautical miles east of Chituc. The French crew was flying a NATO deterrence mission from Romania. The drones’ origin remains unclear.

Romania also advised ships to route around an area off the Danube Delta after drones struck 3 commercial vessels near the Sulina Canal late Saturday. Officials said 2 ships were hit in Romanian territorial waters. No casualties were reported. The Defense Ministry warned of airborne and floating objects approaching from the north. Transit remains permitted under advisory No. 172/2026, which took effect November 15 and applies until further notice.

STRAIT OF HORMUZ

UK Maritime Trade Operations issued Warning 207-26 after an unidentified projectile struck a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz at 12:58 a.m. Eastern, sparking an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, and no casualties were reported. The extent of the damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. Authorities were investigating, and UKMTO advised ships to proceed with caution and report suspicious activity.

In another UKMTO notice, a third party reported an attack that disabled a tanker and started an engine-room fire 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. UKMTO listed the report time as 2:00 p.m. Eastern. The crew was reported safe. The extent of the damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. UKMTO urged caution while authorities investigated.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed 2 more oil tankers caught fire after striking mines on the southern route through the strait. It put the number of tanker fires since Sunday at 6. Its statement gave no vessel names or crew details.

In a separate claim relayed by @Osint613, Iran’s regular navy reported a 4th tanker fire in 24 hours. It said a tanker suffered severe damage after hitting a mine east of the strait and claimed the vessel had switched off its navigation systems in waters Iran calls restricted.

Separately, @hey_itsmyturn reported a blast in the strait. The location and cause remained unclear.

Diplomatic talks continued as Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, left Islamabad for Muscat on Monday evening after meeting Pakistani officials. Those officials said they were awaiting Washington’s response to Iran’s proposal to reopen the strait.

Iranian Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia said it would stay closed until the U.S. accepts Iran’s terms and warned of a stronger response to renewed attacks. He previously claimed Iran controls the strait and could retaliate beyond the region.

IRAN AND U.S. MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed it captured a U.S. MQM-170 drone intact south of Qeshm Island on Monday morning. It said an electronic warfare unit took control of the drone’s guidance system and landed it. The Guards claimed it had been monitoring air defense and electronic warfare systems. They described it as the unit’s 4th capture of that model and the 8th intact drone their forces have captured near the strait.

In a separate claim, the Guards said they shot down a U.S. Army MQ-1C Gray Eagle over Qeshm Island. Iranian state broadcaster IRIB aired footage it said showed the interception.

In southwestern Iran, @hey_itsmyturn reported 2 missile launches from Haftkal in Khuzestan Province. The first was reported at 8:01 a.m. Eastern, or 4:31 p.m. local time. Its destination remained unconfirmed. The second was reported at 3:18 p.m. Eastern.

The same account reported anti-aircraft fire along the road from Andimeshk to Ahvaz, intense air defense activity in Ramhormoz and jet activity over western Tehran. What prompted the activity in Ramhormoz remained unclear, as did the aircraft’s identity and the reason for the activity over Tehran. A report attributed to Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency said air defenses were activated in Isfahan.

Iran is also facing pressure on its natural gas supply ahead of winter. i24NEWS reported that Israel’s security cabinet was told Sunday that shortages could leave Iranian families struggling to heat their homes and add pressure to the economy. Reuters cited Iran’s national gas company as saying wartime damage to 4 processing plants had worsened the shortage. Whether it will trigger protests remains unclear.

U.S. Central Command confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, CVN 71, is operating in its area of responsibility. i24NEWS reported that its arrival brings the number of U.S. aircraft carriers operating in the Middle East to 3 and that about 53,000 U.S. troops are stationed in the region.

The U.S. Army is seeking 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers to replace converted shipping containers used as troop shelters. The plan calls for 10 in Israel, 5 in Saudi Arabia and 2 in Lebanon. The bunkers would offer better protection from indirect fire, including blasts from nearby missile and drone strikes. The Army wants each task order completed within 45 calendar days of award and expects to give contractors 3 days to submit quotes once a formal request is issued.

The Pentagon has recorded 23 U.S. service member deaths in operations tied to the Iran war, attributing 11 to enemy fire and classifying 12 as nonhostile.

In Washington, CNN cited 7 U.S. officials as saying new intelligence suggests Iran is exploring possible attacks on senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C. The options reportedly include a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. CNN said the intelligence identified specific locations and potential targets, prompting U.S. contingency planning. Officials remain divided over whether Iran has the ability or intent to act.

The White House said it is monitoring potential threats and that “at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Iran’s U.N. mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations.

ELSEWHERE IN THE MIDDLE EAST

Israel’s military said it struck a weapons shipment bound for Hezbollah overnight near Janta, in eastern Lebanon’s Beqaa Valley close to Syria. The IDF said the shipment had crossed from Syria into Lebanon and that the area had been used before to move weapons to Hezbollah. Lebanese media described it as the first Israeli airstrike in the area in several months. Lebanon’s National News Agency reported no injuries.

In southern Lebanon, @Osint613 cited Lebanese reports of an Israeli strike on Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh area.

In Beirut, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz urged Hezbollah to hand over its weapons voluntarily, saying, “No country can have two armies.” He met Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to discuss what follows the U.N. peacekeeping mission. Its mandate expires December 31, with withdrawal scheduled through 2027. Waltz said Washington expects U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which helped end the 2006 war, to stay in force with some amendments.

In Gaza, the IDF said it demolished a 300-meter tunnel in an Israeli-controlled area near the Yellow Line. It said its Harel Brigade found the tunnel during an ongoing operation against Hamas tunnels and other infrastructure.

In Saudi Arabia, a statement attributed to the Saudi-led coalition said air defenses intercepted and destroyed 2 Houthi drones in the Makkah and Riyadh regions.

In Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, an explosion was reported in Erbil Governorate Monday morning. Separately, Reuters cited 2 security sources as saying sirens sounded at the Khor Mor gas field after a drone flew over the facility.

Iraq and Jordan also banned Telegram on Monday, citing national security concerns, extremist content, cybercrime and other illegal activity.

UNITED STATES

U.S. airlines continued to recover from Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Around 8:00 a.m. Eastern, FlightAware showed 18,531 cancellations and 28,560 delays since Friday, for a total of 47,091 disruptions from multiple causes. Reuters later reported that U.S. air travel had largely returned to normal after more than 18,000 cancellations and nearly 28,000 delays over 3 days.

United Airlines experienced a fresh systemwide IT and operational problem that held up departures Monday. The airline later said it had resolved the issue.

In the Bronx, 2 police officers and a civilian were reportedly shot. Early reports said the suspect was barricaded and the victims’ conditions were unclear. A later update said the suspect was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and all 3 victims were expected to survive.

New York City announced it was disbanding the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group and setting up a civilian Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the civilian team will be unarmed, have no arrest powers and work with demonstrators and police to ease tensions.

In the interim, 30 uniformed officers will handle dialogue and de-escalation. A separate NYPD patrol unit will support crowd management and make arrests as needed. The reforms also ban tear gas, long guns and kettling, a tactic that confines protesters to a limited area.

In Columbia, Missouri, about 40 to 50 employees evacuated the Kraft Heinz plant on Waco Road after a bomb threat around 5:30 p.m. Central on Sunday. Police and bomb-detection dogs searched the building and found no explosives. Workers were allowed back inside around 10:00 p.m. Central. Police reported no injuries. The investigation remained open Monday, with no suspects in custody. Local station 93.9 The Eagle reported it is the only plant in North America that makes Oscar Mayer hot dogs.

Chase customers reported trouble signing in and viewing balances or transactions. Downdetector logged more than 2,000 reports about Chase by 11:04 a.m. Eastern, and Plaid confirmed a disruption to its Chase connections.

Trackers also recorded reports involving Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One and TD Bank. One tracker showed 59 U.S. Bank reports and 113 Capital One reports in separate hourly snapshots. TD Bank users also reported trouble signing in and using the app. The extent of the problems at those 5 banks remained unclear.

In Michigan, veterans and gun owners called for a boycott of Fenix Ammunition following remarks by its owner, Justin Nazaroff. The report said he questioned veterans’ benefits and tax breaks, compared the risks of military service to logging, fishing and roofing, and accused troops of fighting for defense contractors. It described derogatory remarks about veterans and Gold Star widows and inflammatory comments about U.S. troops, race and Jewish people.

The same report said Nazaroff posted what was described as a Nazi salute and threatened to shoot military recruiters if they came to his home to force him into a war involving Israel. Critics pointed to pandemic loans received by his own company, some of which were forgiven. Fenix sells ammunition to customers who include military veterans and has sought business from police departments.

Thanks for following along today. Have a good night, and we’ll see what tomorrow brings.

🏛️ BABY BOOMERS: THE NEXT BAD GUY —
Who Holds the Deed, Who Owes the Bill, Who Pays 🏠
🧭 THE RECKONING ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 20 OF 20
You Paid Into Social Security. Where Did the Money Go? | Natalie Brunell... https://t.co/aJHrzyDMeP via @YouTube 

Donna retired in May 2019, at 58. She thought about selling her Denver house and moving somewhere smaller, until she looked at the market. "If I sold my house, I wouldn't be able to replace it," she said.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PART THREE — WHO PAYS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE WOMAN IN THE AVERAGES

She told her story to Yellow Scene, in a January 2026 piece by Ty Flores. On paper, Donna is a boomer homeowner, part of the generation said to own the country. In practice, she is boxed in. The same article reported that a 9.7 percent rise in Medicare premiums consumed roughly a third of 2026's cost-of-living increase, which averaged about $56 a month.

Nineteen posts tested the talking point she supposedly embodies. This one says what held up, what cannot be proven, and what could fix it.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE PEOPLE IN THIS SERIES

Cinda Gillilan is paying rent in Silver City and doing the math on 2032. The Websters say they cannot pay the taxes on the house they built. Henry Ruhl got a bill for his wife's care weeks after he buried her. Gene Lokken's family paid about $12,000 a month after his insurer decided 19 days was enough. Butch Lewis opened a letter and did not live to see the rescue that carries his name.

Across the table, Jay Washington has three degrees and a coin-flip chance of out-earning his parents, and Brittany Gilroy cannot find a starter home with a down payment in the bank. The talking point describes the average boomer. The bill lands on the median one, and on the young renter beside her.

◆ ◆ ◆

EVIDENCE WE CANNOT PROVE

Some claims cannot be settled by the record. They are listed so silence is not mistaken for proof.

❌ Whether anyone planned to make the boomers the next bad guy. Post 18 documented the blame from several directions, but framing is not proof of coordination.

❌ Whether noncitizen voting changed any 2026 result. State audits find dozens or hundreds per state, and federal claims of hundreds of thousands are unproven.

❌ Whether anyone is building a system to control Americans through their money. Post 17 shows who profits from each swipe and who is shut out when the rails stop. It found no evidence of a plan.

One more is political.

❌ Whether the border wave or the pandemic spending was meant to keep a party in power. Posts 7 and 14 document the policies and costs; the motive is not in the record.

❌ What decades of weight-loss drug use will do to Medicare's budget or patients' health.

Three more questions are argued on the record, and none is settled.

⚖️ Whether the SEC's 2004 rule caused the 2008 collapse. Critics say yes, and the SEC's own trading director said it undid no leverage limits.

⚖️ How much DOGE actually saved. GAO could not verify most of what it reviewed, and no one has published a full accounting.

⚖️ Whether corporate greed and corruption drove the young's decline. The record shows growth flowing unequally, insurers overpaid by MedPAC's estimate, and nine in ten 2026 voters calling corruption a major factor. Proving motive is beyond it.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE READER'S VERDICT

✅ ESTABLISHED
▸ Boomer households hold more housing wealth and net worth than any other generation.

▸ Debt held by the public hit 100 percent of the economy in fiscal 2026, the highest at a fiscal year-end since 1946, on a $2.0 trillion deficit.

▸ The 2008 crisis was officially found avoidable. The banks repaid their rescue, and by ProPublica's count one Wall Street executive went to jail.

▸ The retirement trust fund runs out in late 2032, triggering a 22 percent cut, and the surplus the boomers paid in was lent to the Treasury and spent.

▸ Poverty among Americans 65 and older is the highest of any age group under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts housing and medical costs.

▸ Medicare Advantage is paid about $76 billion more than traditional Medicare would cost in 2026 by MedPAC's estimate, which insurers dispute.

▸ Net interest, $1.142 trillion in fiscal 2026, passed Medicare and the military.

▸ Both parties wrote the bill: Republican tax cuts a Democratic president mostly made permanent, Clinton-signed deregulation, a party-line Democratic rescue law, and Social Security fixes abandoned under Bush and Obama.

▸ Absolute mobility fell from about 90 percent for children born in 1940 to about 50 percent for those born in the 1980s.

📊 STRONG EVIDENCE
▸ Americans 65 and older head about one owner-occupied home in three, per Census figures republished by the home builders.

▸ Investors own about 18 percent of single-family homes under the broadest definition, mostly small owners, per BatchData.

▸ Tax cuts account for a larger share of the debt's rise since 2001 than the 2008 and COVID rescues combined, per the Peterson Foundation.

▸ The top tenth of households hold about four-fifths of government and municipal bonds held directly, per the Fed.

⚖️ DISPUTED
▸ Whether the generational gap is mainly about age or mainly about a broken ladder. The mobility research favors the second.

❌ NOT ESTABLISHED
▸ That boomers own all, or most, of America's homes.

▸ That migrant spending is a major cause of the federal deficit.

▸ That the Pentagon's untrackable $2.3 trillion, or the Social Security surplus, was stolen.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE ROAD BACK

▸ MERGE THE TRUST FUNDS. Combining the retirement and disability funds would move the cliff from late 2032 to 2034 and shrink the automatic cut from 22 percent to 17. It needs Congress and does not close the gap.

▸ RAISE OR LIFT THE PAYROLL TAX CAP. Earnings above $184,500 are untaxed for Social Security in 2026. Seniors' groups favor this route, as did 68 percent of Americans asked by Pew in 2023 about taxing high earners for Social Security and Medicare.

▸ FIX THE OVERPAYMENT. CBO's menu shows that cutting Medicare Advantage benchmarks by 10 percent would save about $615 billion over a decade, and the Republican-led Joint Economic Committee found the overpayment raises Part B premiums for seniors in both kinds of Medicare.

▸ FUND THE BASICS. The FAA says it needs $30 billion more to replace failing equipment. The White House offered about $4 billion.

▸ KEEP CASH WORKING. The Payment Choice Act, with sponsors from both parties, would require businesses to take cash up to $500; it sits in committee.

▸ SHARE THE GROWTH. Chetty's team found that spreading growth as broadly as in the 1940s would reverse more than two-thirds of the mobility decline.

◆ ◆ ◆

EPILOGUE

In a 1983 film, a drug lord stands up in a restaurant and tells the diners they need people like him, so they can point their fingers and say there goes the bad guy.

Every era needs one, and this one has been offered the boomers. After twenty posts, most of the numbers point elsewhere: books the Pentagon still cannot balance, wars on a credit card, a crash its own investigators called avoidable, rescues and tax cuts from both parties, a pandemic that closed Main Street while the giants grew, insurers paid more to cover the old, and growth that stopped reaching the bottom half of every generation. Above both parties sits the money: federal lobbying hit a record $4.4 billion in 2024, and the industries in this series give to both sides.

The boomers are not innocent of the bill. As a generation, they had history's best timing, they collect more than they paid in, and their programs are the budget's largest. But the boomers most likely to pay are not the ones in the averages. They are renters on a single check, and owners like Donna in Denver, holding a house she cannot replace, each facing a check that shrinks in 2032.

Cinda Gillilan named the year, and it is six years away. Whoever holds power then will decide who gets handed the bill, and whether the country says goodnight to a bad guy or to the fiction that it needed one.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📜 SOURCE METHODOLOGY
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Census figures appear only as republished by outside groups, chiefly the National Association of Home Builders.

Primary sources include the Federal Reserve's surveys and accounts; Treasury and CBO budget data; GAO reports on TARP, DOGE and insurance; the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission; SEC, FBI and FinCEN records; MedPAC; the Joint Economic Committee; the 2026 Trustees report; NERC and EIA; and peer-reviewed research in JAMA, Science and the Review of Financial Studies.

Company estimates are labeled; advocates are quoted for positions, not proof.

Age groups are under 40, 40 to 61, and 62 and older. Election results follow AP calls and exit polls.

Mr. Boulos, the people of Sudan have heard enough appeals for humanitarian access. What they desperately need is for powerful governments to confront the machinery that keeps their suffering alive.

And since you are discussing Sudan from Abu Dhabi, there is a question that deserves an answer.

How can Washington demand an end to drone attacks while leaving the networks that finance, equip, and sustain Sudan’s armed factions at the center of an unresolved international controversy?

In January 2025, your own Treasury Department identified UAE-based Capital Tap Holding as a supplier of money and weapons to the Rapid Support Forces.

In September 2026, UN investigators documented transnational networks involving individuals and entities operating in the UAE that facilitated military support and the recruitment of foreign fighters.

The UAE denies supporting the RSF. These allegations therefore demand credible, independent investigation and effective enforcement.

Washington has imposed sanctions, including against networks supporting both sides. Those measures matter. But Sudanese families are entitled to ask what has actually changed in the flow of weapons, financing, and military technology.

A humanitarian truce without serious efforts to interrupt the supply chains sustaining the war risks becoming little more than a temporary silence between successive massacres.

The Jeddah process offers an established diplomatic framework. What it needs is enforceable commitments, credible monitoring, and consequences for those who continue enabling atrocities.

Mr. Boulos, you speak of protecting aid workers from deadly drones.

Then follow the drones.

Follow the money.

Follow the procurement networks.

And demand accountability wherever the evidence leads, regardless of whose territory, companies, or political relationships are involved.

The children of El Fasher cannot survive on diplomatic statements. They deserve protection from the weapons that kill them, and justice for the crimes already committed.

Peace will not be measured by the number of meetings held in Abu Dhabi, but by the number of Sudanese lives those meetings help save.

Rant if anyone cares to read:

C.J. Stroud has slowly but surely, and politely, been asserting himself more this season when it comes to having a voice in the Texans offensive scheme, game plans and play calling.

And while I think that's a GOOD thing, I also think it speaks to some much larger issues with how this organization has handled its franchise quarterback.

A few thoughts:

1. Stroud is increasingly speaking up about what he wants offensively.

We've seen it in his public comments about wanting to be more aggressive, pointing to concepts they've already shown they can execute successfully, and now most recently discussing the need to expand the playbook and route tree to have better answers against certain blitz looks.

We were told Stroud would have more command and control of the offense this season, but how much does he actually have? Is he unable to check into better plays against these looks? Or are the answers they've installed simply not good enough?

Hard to know without being in those meetings, but the results speak for themselves. This offense has repeatedly struggled to adjust when defenses present something different than what was anticipated. Are they not valuing any in-game feedback?

2. Why did it take desperation to start leaning into Stroud's strengths?

Stroud has a very high football IQ IMO and I think his time at Ohio State played a big part in that.

I do give Nick Caley credit for seemingly being more receptive to his input than Bobby Slowik appeared to be.

But it also feels like much of the increased willingness to lean into Stroud has come out of desperation following the 0-4 and 2-5 starts rather than a genuine commitment to building the offense around his abilities from the beginning.

Why does it feel like your 25-year-old quarterback has to continually push for aggressiveness, adjustments and concepts that should already be part of the offensive plan?

3. This raises bigger questions about the organization's entire approach to Stroud.

How much input did Stroud actually have in the hiring of Caley to begin with?

DeMeco Ryans and Nick Caserio spent the offseason publicly declaring Stroud was their guy, while also repeatedly challenging and criticizing him. Yet the reported contract negotiations, including what appeared to be a low initial offer and an unwillingness to accept his counter, painted a somewhat different picture.

And then there's the offensive philosophy itself.

If Stroud is your franchise quarterback, why does it continually feel like the organization is trying to fit him into its preferred offensive identity, with all these New England connections and philosophies, rather than building around what HE does best?

We've seen the blueprint for success when they spread things out, play aggressively and give Stroud answers. Yet they have continually reverted right back to the same issues.

4. And now the damage is already done.

The reluctance to fully trust Stroud and build around his strengths until they were practically forced to has helped put them in this position.

Now they're 3-6, the defense has regressed into the bottom half of the league, and the deficiencies in their coaching, offensive philosophy and roster construction are being exposed.

Meanwhile, the quarterback they chose not to extend is arguably the biggest reason they're even competitive.

And the biggest irony? Stroud's play, despite everything around him, has only strengthened his negotiating position. They could now be looking at a significantly larger contract than what they would've gotten a deal done for this offseason.

And I guess that's ultimately where all of this comes together for me.

If you truly believed in C.J. Stroud as your franchise quarterback the way you've publicly said you do, wouldn't your actions have reflected that?

For one, you would've made a much stronger effort to get him paid and secure his future here before the season.

And two, you would've made sure he had a meaningful voice in choosing the offensive coordinator who would be responsible for his development, and been far more willing, and quicker, to let him help shape the offense around what he does best.

Instead, at least from the outside looking in, it feels like the organization wanted Stroud to fit its vision rather than allowing Stroud to help define that vision.

And only when things started falling apart did they seemingly begin giving him more of that influence.

Now they're sitting at 3-6, with a number of organizational issues being exposed, and a quarterback whose value has only increased despite the circumstances around him.

That's what frustrates me more than anything. It's not just about the losses or the contract. It's the apparent disconnect between how highly this organization says it values Stroud and how much trust they've actually been willing to place in him.

And so much of the mess they're in right now feels self-inflicted.

text:
THE TOP 10 REASONS AI DATA CENTER FINANCING SHOULD MAKE INVESTORS NERVOUS

With apologies to David Letterman.

AI has a demand story. It also has a financing story. And the financing story deserves a closer look.

Let’s look at the numbers.

10. CoreWeave has $47.5 billion in debt.

That’s reported debt principal as of September 30, 2026. This isn’t a startup borrowing a little money to buy servers.

9. Add the leases.

CoreWeave has another $19.3 billion in recognized lease liabilities.

Debt plus recognized lease liabilities: approximately $66.9 billion.

8. There’s another $47.4 billion waiting in the wings.

These are estimated future lease payments on agreements already signed but not yet commenced.

Add them together and you get approximately $114.3 billion in debt and lease-related commitments.

Not all of that is current debt. But somebody eventually has to pay for it.

7. Free cash flow is running in the wrong direction.

For the first nine months of 2026:

Operating cash flow: $5.64 billion.

Capital expenditures: $23.56 billion.

Simplified free cash flow: negative $17.92 billion.

That’s an enormous funding requirement.

6. Interest isn’t cheap.

CoreWeave recorded $1.75 billion in interest expense over nine months.

Its Q3 interest expense was $769 million, compared with $207 million in operating income.

That’s a ratio worth watching.

5. 2027 is approaching quickly.

CoreWeave has approximately $10.97 billion of debt principal maturing in 2027.

Refinancing is easy when credit markets are open. It’s a different conversation when lenders get nervous.

4. The good news is the backlog.

CoreWeave reports $132.3 billion in remaining performance obligations.

That’s substantial contracted demand.

But backlog isn’t cash, and contractual obligations aren’t all unconditional guarantees of payment.

3. Welcome to financial engineering.

Meta’s Louisiana data center project with Blue Owl illustrates the structure.

Reported project financing: $27 billion.

Meta owns 20%. Blue Owl owns 80%.

Meta has a reported $28 billion lease-related guarantee over 20 years, but has not guaranteed repayment of the project bonds.

The distinction between guaranteeing a lease and guaranteeing the debt matters.

2. Enter the insurance companies.

Ares Management reported approximately $690.6 billion in assets under management in Q3 2026.

Ares has warned about complex transactions that can make project debt appear nearly as secure as the corporate credit supporting it, even when the actual repayment guarantees are weaker.

Insurance capital is enormous. But it isn’t unlimited, and it isn’t risk-free.

1. The question nobody should ignore: WHO ACTUALLY TAKES THE LOSS?

If AI demand disappoints, GPU prices fall, equipment becomes obsolete, customers renegotiate contracts or refinancing markets freeze, who absorbs the losses?

The technology company?

The project company?

The private credit lender?

The insurance company?

Or ultimately the policyholder?

That’s the question buried underneath the AI infrastructure boom.

My point isn’t that AI demand is fake.

The demand may be real. The revenue may be real. The technology may be transformative.

But the financing structures deserve the same scrutiny as the technology.

Investors need to examine debt, leases, guarantees, cash flow, maturities and off-balance-sheet commitments.

A $132 billion backlog sounds impressive.

A $114 billion financing commitment deserves equal attention.

In finance, the story is interesting. The evidence is what matters.

7/7 🏁 FINAL POST — BASALT v0.4.1 BENCHMARK CONCLUSIONS

This is the second and final additional post in our thread about testing the dense Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4 model on an RTX 5090 Laptop with 24GB VRAM.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🐢 4. WHAT HAPPENS BEYOND VRAM CAPACITY?

At 256K, the entire KV cache no longer fits in GPU memory.

We used --kv-resident to move part of the KV cache into system RAM.

Results:

📦 Plain decoding — 4.7 tok/s

⚡ DFlash 2 — 5.1 tok/s

DFlash 2 acceleration dropped from 3.2× at 131K to just 1.09× at 256K.

The reason is the bandwidth limitation between system RAM and the GPU.

Our laptop supports PCIe 5.0 x16, but the actual negotiated connection runs at PCIe 4.0 x8 — 16 GT/s per lane.

Measured CPU→GPU bandwidth: 14.4 GB/s.

Once KV-cache transfers become the main bottleneck, speculative decoding offers almost no advantage.

This does not mean the model is incapable of processing 256K tokens.

It means the performance of this particular configuration is primarily limited by data transfer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 5. LONG-CONTEXT RETRIEVAL ACCURACY

We embedded five control records into long documents and attempted to retrieve them.

The initial instruction was:

“Find and list all control records.”

Result: 0/5.

However, we discovered a methodological issue in the follow-up request, so this result cannot be considered a reliable measurement of the model’s ability to independently identify every record.

We then performed targeted retrieval tests, asking for each control record by its exact identifier.

Results:

✅ 131K context — 5/5 correct.

✅ 256K context — 5/5 correct.

Even at 256K, with part of the KV cache residing in system RAM, the model correctly retrieved all five requested values.

This distinction is important.

Technically accepting a long context, retrieving a specific fact by a known identifier, and independently identifying all relevant facts are different capabilities.

We confirmed successful targeted retrieval, but we have not established reliable free-form discovery of every relevant fact.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 6. FINAL BENCHMARK RESULTS

On the RTX 5090 Laptop 24GB, running Basalt v0.4.1 with the dense Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4 model:

🏆 Maximum generation speed on an individual task: 194.3 tok/s

⚡ Maximum speed during an individual response quarter: 264.3 tok/s

🚀 Standard chat: up to 121 tok/s

✅ Maximum fully GPU-resident context:

• Without DFlash — 203,776 positions
• With DFlash 2 — 140,288 positions

📦 With an actual input prompt of 197,886 tokens, plain decoding maintained 23.5 tok/s.

🐢 At 256K, with partial KV-cache offloading to RAM, generation speed dropped to approximately 5 tok/s.

Plain decoding remained remarkably stable throughout each continuous response.

DFlash 2 behaved differently: generation speed could vary significantly within a single response, sometimes increasing substantially after the first quarter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 7. THE MAIN TAKEAWAY

The theoretical memory footprint of a KV cache is not the same as the maximum context an inference engine can actually allocate in VRAM.

And even a powerful GPU cannot guarantee high performance when data must constantly move across a relatively slow interconnect.

This is why benchmarking the entire system matters more than looking at isolated GPU specifications.

Real engine. Real model. Real hardware. Real workloads.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

sentdefender: Retired U.S. Navy Admiral Philip Davidson, whose 2021 testimony gave rise to the “Davidson Window” for China achieving the required capability in order to invade Taiwan by 2027, said on a podcast released Friday that he hopes he was wrong, according to TWZ. “If I’m wrong, that means the things we recommended from Indo-Pacific Command...have been effective. And there hasn’t been war.”

Davidson credited changes since 2021, including U.S. missile and Marine deployments along the First Island Chain, Japan doubling its defense spending to 2% of GDP, Taiwan extending conscription to a year, and the AUKUS security partnership among Australia, the UK and the U.S. 

“I would like to see the $14 billion in committed to Taiwan move over there in the next few months or a year,” Davidson said. A roughly $14 billion package, largely PAC-3 and NASAMS air defense missiles, cleared Congress’s informal review in January but has not received President Trump’s sign off and has been on hold since his summit with Chinese President Xi in May, according to the AP. 

Separately, Taiwan has a backlog of almost $30 billion in previously approved arms awaiting delivery, according to George Mason University’s Taiwan Security Monitor. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said in May that arms sales to Taiwan were paused to ensure the U.S. has the munitions it needs for Iran operations.

text:
At the seventh U.S.-China Hong Kong Forum on November 16, 2026, Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng called for stronger bilateral ties, economic cooperation, and people-to-people exchanges.

At the forum, themed “Tomorrow Will Be Better Than Today,” Ambassador Xie called 2026 a landmark year for China-U.S. relations, citing state visits by Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump within six months.

Xie outlined three key priorities for advancing bilateral relations: adhering to the strategic guidance of both countries’ leaders, expanding mutually beneficial cooperation, and strengthening connections between the Chinese and American peoples.

He emphasized the importance of translating the vision agreed upon by the two presidents in Beijing into action: building a constructive and strategically stable China-U.S. relationship. He added that subsequent discussions in Washington further reinforced this shared vision, guided by the principles of “respect, fairness and reciprocity.”

The ambassador called on both countries to broaden cooperation, manage their differences constructively, and explore ways for major powers to coexist peacefully, in the interests of their citizens and global stability.

Highlighting China’s innovation-driven, high-quality development and continued commitment to opening up, Xie said these efforts offer significant opportunities for practical cooperation between the two economies.

Citing figures from the U.S.-China Business Council, he noted that 92 percent of surveyed American companies reported making profits in China last year, while 95 percent considered their operations in the country important to maintaining global competitiveness.

He also encouraged Hong Kong to leverage its unique advantages as a “super connector” and “super value-adder” to further strengthen economic and commercial ties between China and the United States.

On people-to-people engagement, Xie highlighted President Xi’s longstanding commitment to fostering exchanges between the two countries. 

He pointed to the “50,000 in Five Years” initiative, which exceeded its target of bringing young Americans to China for study and exchange programs two and a half years ahead of schedule.

He also championed a new initiative to welcome 100,000 young Americans to China over the next five years.

He commended the China-United States Exchange Foundation for promoting cross-sector dialogue and organizing youth initiatives, including “A Shared Voyage: China-U.S. Youth Friendship Program”.

The China-United States Exchange Foundation and the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries co-hosted the seventh U.S.-China Hong Kong Forum in Hong Kong.

More than 300 delegates attended, including former dignitaries and representatives from China, the United States, and other countries in strategic, business, and think-tank roles.
