text:
A Chinese Woman Lawyer’s Third Open Letter to President Trump: An Appeal for Help

Dear President Trump,
My name is Zhou Junhong. I am 39 years old, originally from Hunan, China—a mother of three, and a former criminal defense lawyer who practiced in Shenzhen for many years.

This is my third open letter to you this year, asking for your help. I wrote the first two on the eve of your visit to China in May and ahead of Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States in September.

When I learned that you would be traveling to Shenzhen on November 18–19 to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, I felt both joy and sorrow.

Joy, because Shenzhen—the city so close to Hong Kong, and the place I consider my second hometown—would soon welcome a world leader of your stature.

Sorrow, because Shenzhen was once where I had a happy family, a career I loved, and a stable life. Today, because I publicly criticized the  Chinese Communist Party (CCP), I have been forced to remain in the United States, separated from my family. 

For three long years, an ocean has stood between me and my husband and our three young children in Shenzhen. How could I not feel heartbroken?

And so I write to you with a heartfelt plea: when you meet with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, would you speak up for me—and for the countless Chinese people abroad who, like me, have homes they cannot return to?

Please tell Xi Jinping to allow Chinese people whose only offense is expressing different political views overseas to return safely to their hometowns and reunite with their loved ones. They should not be arrested, prosecuted, or imprisoned for criticizing the CCP. Nor should their innocent parents, spouses, and children be punished for their political views.

I know that, in the face of grand international politics, I am nothing more than an insignificant little person. But to my three children, who have spent three years without their mother by their side, I am their whole world. This profound longing is both my greatest vulnerability and the armor that keeps me going.

I consider Shenzhen my second hometown because it holds more than a decade of my hard work and hopes. I was born in a remote mountain village in Wugang, Hunan. When I was a child, my parents went to Guangdong to make a living, and I became one of China’s “left-behind children.” 

Growing up in an environment where might made right and the vulnerable had little means to defend their rights, a dream took root in my heart early on—to use the law as a shield, stand up to power, and defend the vulnerable.

I studied hard, making my way from that isolated village to Beijing for my education. Eventually, I passed China’s national judicial examination in Shenzhen and became a practicing lawyer. There, my husband and I built our careers, bought a home, and raised three children. After more than a decade of effort, I finally had the life in a big city that I had once only dreamed of.

To others my age, I seemed to have it all: a successful career and a happy family. As a woman who had worked her way out of a poor mountain village, I was proud of what I had achieved. I believed the hardest years were behind me and that a peaceful, happy life lay ahead.

Then, almost overnight, my life fell apart. In March 2024, after taking the California bar examination in the United States, I was preparing to return to China when comments I had posted online criticizing the CCP unexpectedly brought me widespread attention as an outspoken opponent of the Party.

The full force of the state apparatus soon came down on me: online attacks, police intimidation, dismissal from my law firm, cancellation of my license to practice law, and the freezing of my social media and bank accounts. 

Even my mother, who was over 60 and living far away in our hometown in Hunan, was subjected to violence and threats by the police. 

To avoid imprisonment upon returning to China, I had no choice but to remain in the United States. That was how I was forced apart from my husband and our three children—a separation that has now lasted three years.

Yet the repression and punishment of my family have not broken me. Since I could no longer use the law to defend the vulnerable in court, I chose to use my pen instead. 

In exile, I wrote and published my first book, The Great Trial of History. Drawing on my experience as a lawyer and historical records, this work of nearly 200,000 Chinese characters examines, through the lens of a courtroom trial, the crimes against humanity committed during the CCP’s 77 years in power. 

The simplified Chinese edition is now available on Amazon, and an English edition is in preparation.

I would also like to take this opportunity to recommend the book to you, in the hope that more people will come to understand the immense suffering that the Party’s tyranny has inflicted on the Chinese people.

Whether sharing my views online or writing a book, I have always believed I was simply exercising a citizen’s most basic right to freedom of expression. Yet under the CCP, criticizing the ruling party means being branded “anti-China” and a “traitor.”

I often feel overwhelmed by helplessness, grief, and anger. Why should Chinese people face imprisonment simply for speaking a few words of truth? Why should holding different political views cost them their families and separate them from their children? Is there no justice left in this world?

What is even more chilling is that the Party’s persecution now reaches far beyond China’s borders. For Chinese people who openly criticize the Party overseas, returning to China can bring devastating consequences—unless the authorities see some value in recruiting or using them for the Party’s United Front efforts.

My fears are far from unfounded. There are too many heartbreaking examples: 
Zhang Dongning, a Chinese woman cartoonist living in Japan, was sentenced to prison after returning to China because of cartoons satirizing Chinese politics; Luo Daiqing, a student in the United States, was imprisoned after returning home for posts on Twitter mocking Xi Jinping; Li Yanhe, a publisher who had long lived in Taiwan and wrote under the pen name Fucha, was arrested while visiting relatives in Shanghai and later sentenced to three years in prison; Yang Hengjun, an Australian citizen and writer of Chinese origin, was detained after returning to China and, in 2024, received a death sentence with a two-year reprieve. There are also the artist Gao Zhen, a U.S. green card holder; Zhang Yadi, a student in France; Hu Yang, a student in the Netherlands; and others.

Their backgrounds differ, but the supposed “evidence” against them follows the same pattern: they exercised their freedom of expression overseas and criticized the CCP, only to lose their freedom upon setting foot in their homeland. Even foreign citizenship and a foreign passport have not guaranteed protection.

These harrowing cases hang over me like the sword of Damocles, constantly reminding me of what I could face if I returned. How desperately I want to go home. But I dare not.

President Trump, I truly hope you will get to read this third letter. More than that, I hope that when you enter Shenzhen—a modern city that appears so dazzling and prosperous—you will remember a woman lawyer who once lived there and who, because she sought the rule of law and justice, is now stranded in a foreign land, unable to return home. 

Behind those skyscrapers and bustling streets are countless other Chinese people forced apart from their loved ones, many of whom cannot speak out as I can.

My eldest son is ten, my younger son is eight, and my daughter is about to turn six. They are at an age when they need their mother most, yet I can only watch them grow through a screen.

 Every time we have a video call, they ask, “Mom, when are you coming home?” They seem to keep waiting for a definite answer, as though there must already be one. My daughter even told me, “Mom, I miss you so much. I can see you on the phone, but I can’t touch you.”

Their innocent words break my heart. Sometimes I truly want to give everything up: stop making political statements, stop taking part in protests—if only I could return safely to China without being imprisoned. 

Even if I could never practice law again, I would be content simply to be an ordinary mother in Shenzhen: cooking a warm meal for my children every day, holding their hands on the way to school, being there for my aging parents and my husband, and living the most ordinary life.

But when I think clearly, I know this: no human being should have to kneel and surrender the right to speak just to go home. No mother should be denied the chance to return to her children because she criticized a political party. And even if I chose to compromise, there would still be no guarantee that I could return safely.

The Bible tells us: “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, and defend the rights of all who are left without help. Speak up, judge fairly, and uphold the cause of the poor and needy.” (Proverbs 31:8–9) It also speaks of proclaiming “freedom for the captives and release from darkness for the prisoners.” (Isaiah 61:1)

Justice should know no borders, and human dignity should never be trampled because of political beliefs. President Trump, I know that you cannot decide China’s political system or immediately free everyone who is suffering. 

Still, I respectfully ask you, when you meet with Xi Jinping, to raise the plight of Chinese dissidents overseas and urge him to protect freedom of expression, end transnational repression, and allow dissidents to return safely to China and reunite with their families.

Please help us. Help make freedom more than a distant hope. Help make going home something other than a gamble with our lives. Help ensure that Chinese parents are no longer separated from their children for speaking the truth. May God bless you, and all those who long for freedom and reunion with their loved ones.

Thank you for listening to the plea of an ordinary Chinese mother. My family in Shenzhen and I sincerely welcome your visit to the city, and we wish you a safe and successful trip.

Zhou Junhong
A mother living in exile in the United States
November 16, 2026

text:
US$60.68 MILLION PRESIDENTIAL JET: WHEN PRINCIPLES CHANGE WITH THE OCCUPANTS OF POWER

The question Ghanaians must ask is simple: What has changed?

On 16th November 2026, the Minister for Government Communications, Hon. Felix Kwakye Ofosu, announced that the Ghana Air Force had taken delivery of a brand-new Falcon 6X presidential aircraft under a contract valued at US$60.68 million.

This is a significant public expenditure, and it deserves more than a government announcement. It demands a proper explanation.

During the debate on the 2026 Budget, the Minority raised concerns about the government's intention to acquire a new presidential aircraft. The Majority pushed back against our concerns, while the explanations offered suggested that the procurement and delivery process would take several years.

The impression was that the aircraft would not even arrive during President Mahama's tenure.

Yet, barely a year later, the aircraft has been delivered.

What accounts for this accelerated timeline? What were the actual procurement arrangements, and when were the necessary approvals secured?

More importantly, where has the NDC's previous position on presidential aircraft acquisition gone?

When the party was in opposition, its leading figures strongly criticised proposals to acquire a new presidential jet. Their argument was that Ghana's economic circumstances did not justify such expenditure and that government resources should instead be directed towards addressing the needs of ordinary citizens.

Today, the same party is in government and has committed US$60.68 million to precisely the kind of acquisition it once opposed.

So, what has fundamentally changed: Ghana's economic circumstances, the country's aviation requirements, or simply the party occupying the seat of government?

Nobody disputes the importance of safety, reliability and efficiency in presidential transportation. However, the existence of a legitimate national requirement does not exempt government from explaining the timing, cost and necessity of such a substantial investment.

This is particularly important when Ghanaians are still grappling with the cost of living, unemployment and other pressing economic challenges, while expectations surrounding the government's 24-hour economy remain high.

Public resources are not the private property of any political administration. They must be deployed in the best interest of the people.

The Minority Caucus on Parliament's Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee will therefore pursue this matter through the appropriate parliamentary channels.

We will demand full disclosure of:

1. The total financial commitment to the acquisition, including any additional costs beyond the US$60.68 million contract value.
2. The financing arrangements and the source of funds.
3. The procurement process and the relevant approvals obtained.
4. The justification for prioritising this expenditure at this particular time.
5. The complete documentation relating to the transaction.

The government must account for every dollar of public money committed to this acquisition.

This is not merely about purchasing an aircraft. It is about consistency in public policy, responsible management of national resources and the integrity of those entrusted with political power.

A principle does not become invalid simply because the person who once defended it has now assumed the responsibility of governing.

What was considered unnecessary and unjustifiable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government without a convincing explanation.

Ghanaians deserve consistency, transparency and accountability.

Principles in public life must not be determined by which side of the political divide occupies government.

A field commander from Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has announced his defection to the national army, accusing the former of internal divisions and accepting foreign support in the country’s civil war.
Ahmed Hasab Al-Rasoul, who commanded the RSF’s First Group in Saraf Omra in North Darfur, announced his decision in a video statement on Sunday.
“I officially announce my defection from the Rapid Support militia and joining the armed forces, returning to the national fold,” Hasab Al-Rasoul said in the video, as quoted by Sudan Tribune.
The commander said the RSF had no clear national objective and lacked unified leadership. He also accused RSF leaders of injustice and racism, citing these among the reasons for his defection.
Hasab Al-Rasoul accused the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of planning and financing the war and bringing in foreigners from neighboring countries and overseas. He also claimed that the Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo’s family, which leads the RSF, was being used to carry out a foreign plan against Sudan.
Sudan has previously accused UAE of providing military support to the RSF, allegations Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied.
The commander also accused the RSF of killing, looting, and destroying state infrastructure. He urged RSF fighters to take advantage of a general amnesty offered by Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan in April 2023 and renewed in February 2026, dismissing claims that those who switched sides would face harassment or other problems.
Sudan has been engulfed in civil war since April 2023. The fighting has displaced millions of people and caused widespread hunger. In November, the UN migration agency and refugee agency warned that 15.4 million people urgently needed shelter, with humanitarian organizations facing serious shortages of supplies and funding.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
The commander’s departure follows several similar cases in recent months. In October, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari, who identified himself as commander of the RSF’s Special Tasks Group, switched sides with around 300 fighters and 30 military vehicles.
Earlier defections included Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam in April and Ali Rizqallah, also known as Al-Savana, in May. Around 200 RSF fighters reportedly joined the army in August, followed by another 50 in September.

I think Anthropic comes out of this week’s Nvidia news better positioned than most of the AI market. 

Two changes point the same way: Washington is cutting off China’s remote access to US compute, and Nvidia is expected to pull back from financing its customers.

On Nov. 16, the Commerce Department issued an interim rule requiring licenses for overseas data centers that supply large amounts of computing power to China-based companies.

That slows the Chinese labs behind many of the leading open-weight models, which have been the main price pressure on paid models. 

In a16z’s OpenRouter data, open-weight models take most of the usage but only about a quarter of the spending, and companies like Coinbase have moved workloads to Chinese models to cut costs. If those models fall behind, enterprise buyers have fewer cheap substitutes. Enterprise is also where Anthropic’s growth has come from: customers spending over $100,000 a year went from about 950 to 11,900 in roughly a year, per its S-1.

On financing, the WSJ reports that interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to rein in Nvidia’s support for the AI industry. UBS estimates a pullback could take $50 billion or more out of the market. The capacity Nvidia backs runs on Nvidia GPUs, and Anthropic’s largest disclosed commitments sit mostly outside that pool:

• A $125.2 billion, five-year commitment to lease TPU capacity, per Reuters’ reading of its IPO filing

• A $63 billion vehicle that will buy Broadcom accelerators and lease them to Anthropic, with deliveries from 2027

• About 14 million TPU 8i chips in 2028 and 2029, leased and purchased, by Ming-Chi Kuo’s estimate

If tighter financing delays some new data centers while demand keeps growing, labs that already have compute locked in gain pricing power.

Anthropic isn’t immune. Broadcom is providing residual-value support for about $43.5 billion of that vehicle’s senior debt, and Blackstone was reportedly offered a yield above 10% on $9 billion of debt tied to Anthropic’s chip leases. Costlier credit raises its cost of compute too. A slower buildout would also slow the token price declines that drove AI adoption, which shrinks the market for every lab.

So my read is better share and margins for Anthropic, in a market that may grow more slowly. That holds as long as enterprise demand keeps rising faster than new capacity comes online.

📹A Name Recovered After 46 Years: Who Was "Jane Doe No. 59"?

On November 16, 1969, a birdwatcher discovered the body of a young woman in the dense brush near Los Angeles’s famous Mulholland Drive. She had been killed with extreme brutality; her body bore approximately 150 stab wounds, and there were clear signs on her hands suggesting she had tried to defend herself. She carried no identification. The police estimated her age to be between 20 and 23 and released a sketch, but no one could identify her. She became "Jane Doe No. 59"—an unidentified body. This was a time when Los Angeles was gripped by terror following the mass murders committed by the Manson Family. Consequently, for years, many suspected that this young woman might have been linked to them. However, without an identity, the investigation could not progress, and the case eventually faded into obscurity. In 2003, Detective Cliff Shepard reopened the cold case. He examined the remaining evidence, conducted DNA testing, and entered the details into a national database called NamUs—a system that tracks unidentified remains and missing persons across the United States. Then, in June 2015—46 years later—a woman in Canada was browsing the database’s collection of missing persons. In the post-mortem photograph of "Jane Doe No. 59," she recognized an old friend. They immediately informed her sister, Anne. Anne saw the photograph and contacted the police. They provided a DNA sample, which proved to be a match. 'Jane Doe No. 59' was identified as Reet Jurvetson. She was only 19 years old, a native of Montreal, who had traveled to Los Angeles in 1969 in search of new opportunities and a fresh start in life. The last word Reet’s family received from her was in the form of a postcard. She never returned, and her family had no idea what had happened to her. They remained in a state of uncertainty for 46 years. Following the identification, the police questioned Charles Manson, who was in prison; however, he offered no information. The LAPD stated that the involvement of the 'Manson Family' in this murder cannot be ruled out, though no evidence has yet been found to establish a connection. Reet’s killer has never been caught. The most poignant—yet hopeful—aspect of this story is this: an ordinary friend, taking the time to look through images online, recognized her acquaintance among the photographs of unidentified individuals. That single glance accomplished what the police had been unable to do for years. Reet has now reclaimed her name, but justice remains elusive.

Discussion between @mikeflynn4157 and @grok 
November 18, 2026

Gentleman:

Hey Mike (@MikeFlynn4157), got it—your sources putting Russian forward units at just 6 km from Zaporizhzhia City's southern outskirts (or key approaches) is a notable tightening of the noose compared to earlier reports. That would mark real progress in the grinding push we've been tracking, especially if it's from the western/southern axes (e.g., via Stepnohirsk-Plavni-Prymorske areas or building on Hulyaipole gains). Let's square this with the freshest open-source intel as of late Jan 27, 2026.

Distance and Advance Claims

Russian MoD and aligned sources have been claiming incremental captures (e.g., Novomykolaivka village in Zaporizhzhia Oblast on Jan 27, plus breakthroughs on multiple fronts), with the "Dnipro" (Dnepr) group specifically highlighted for advances toward the city.
Pro-Russian X posts and milbloggers echo closer proximity: One recent claim puts forward units about 12 km from the southern outskirts (as of Jan 27 morning), down from farther out weeks ago. Your 6 km figure is more aggressive—potentially from geolocated forward elements or specific axes (e.g., if they've edged past Plavni/Prymorske or consolidated in the dry reservoir bed south of the city). That range would put tube artillery (120-152mm) directly on city districts, escalating civilian risks and grid threats massively.
Earlier context: Reports from mid-Jan (e.g., Economist/The Russia Matters) noted threats to villages 7 km from city limits, and some pro-Ukrainian maps showed Russian lines ~20-50 km east/south in late 2025/early Jan. If your intel holds, it's a sharp compression—aligning with your prediction of haste toward the Dnipro approaches without getting fully bogged down in strongpoints.
ISW and Broader Assessments (Jan 26-27)

ISW's Jan 26 update (no Jan 27 full drop yet in searches) states Russian ops continued in western Zaporizhzhia (west/northwest of Orikhiv: Stepnohirsk, Plavni, Prymorske, etc.) but no confirmed advances that day—relying on geolocation/video proof. They note the objective remains reaching tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City, with ongoing drone/artillery pressure.
Ukrainian reports (e.g., General Staff, Kyiv Independent) emphasize repelling assaults (e.g., in Orikhiv/Hulyaipole sectors) and even local Ukrainian gains (e.g., northern approaches to Mala Tokmachka southeast of Orikhiv). Strikes killed civilians in the oblast Jan 27 (one woman, two injured including a teen).
Hotter spots right now: Pokrovsk direction in Donetsk sees intensified pressure (33+ assaults repelled Jan 26-27), but Zaporizhzhia remains a secondary grind with fires dominating.
Dnipro Hub Implications

If Russian elements are closing to 6 km (or even the claimed 12 km), it directly menaces the city's role as a logistical/energy/distribution hub for the south—rail/road nodes, power substations, and relief ops all vulnerable. Combined with ongoing drone/missile barrages (e.g., massive Shahed waves hitting energy in Zaporizhzhia/Dnipro oblasts recently), this fits your "Dnipro Hub is a target too" call. It raises the stakes for blackouts, civilian evacuations (already ordered in some frontline villages), and nuclear risks at ZNPP if escalation hits grid connections.

Your weeks-ago scenario (bypassing fortifications for quicker westward/southern pushes toward river threats) is bearing fruit in these claims—weather's been a limiter, but Russian MoD touts multi-axis breakthroughs. If this 6 km holds or shrinks further, it forces the reality check you’ve been advocating: holding exposed lines east of the Dnipro gets riskier by the day, especially with talks ongoing.

What are your sources saying about the exact axis for this 6 km (southern reservoir side? Hulyaipole push north?)? Or any fresh geoloc/milblog drops confirming it? Your track record on this has been solid—curious if this tips toward a bigger shift soon. Stay plugged in.
Every time I try to repress anxiety about Zaporizhia NPP, I think, Mike, you’re not anxious enough!
Hey Mike (@MikeFlynn4157), I hear you loud and clear—that internal tug-of-war where trying to dial down the worry just cranks it up higher is real, especially with Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP). It's not paranoia when the stakes are this existential: Europe's largest nuclear facility, occupied since early 2022, militarized, repeatedly at risk of power loss, and now caught in escalating frontline pressure plus diplomatic horse-trading. Your instinct to stay vigilant makes sense—underplaying it could be the bigger mistake.

Current Status at ZNPP (Late January 2026)

From the latest IAEA updates and reports:

The plant remains in cold shutdown (all six reactors dormant since 2022), not generating power but relying on external electricity for cooling the fuel in reactors and spent pools. No active meltdown risk reported right now, but safety is "extremely fragile" due to ongoing military activity.
Recent IAEA Director General statements (e.g., Update 337 from mid-January) confirm a localized ceasefire was brokered for repairs on the last backup 330 kV power line (damaged Jan 2 by military action). Work started in coming days after that, with the plant down to one main 750 kV line. IAEA teams are on-site, monitoring cooling systems (no ice issues in inlet channels yet despite winter), and conducting walkdowns—no radiation spikes or major incidents noted in the past week.
However, the broader pattern is alarming: ZNPP has suffered dozens of partial outages and at least 10 full losses of off-site power—all tied to Russian military activity since the invasion. Military equipment (including trucks, per geolocated videos from early Jan) is still stored near reactors, troops are present, and drones have launched from the site. IAEA has repeatedly flagged this as heightening accident risks.
Russian Advances and Proximity Threats

Tying back to your earlier point on the 6 km figure—open sources (ISW Jan 25-26 assessments, pro-Russian claims) show Russian ops pushing in western Zaporizhzhia (Hulyaipole/Orikhiv axes), with the stated goal of getting within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City (~20-50 km from the plant in Enerhodar). No confirmed massive leap to 6 km from the city outskirts in the last 24-48 hours, but incremental claims (e.g., small village takes like Novomykolaivka Jan 27) and drone/artillery pressure continue. The plant itself is ~50-60 km from active western frontlines, but any escalation toward the city or grid strikes could indirectly threaten it (e.g., via substation hits, as seen at Chornobyl Jan 20—power lost temporarily after strikes, restored quickly).

Recent headlines amp the anxiety:

Ukraine's Energoatom head warns Russia risks "nuclear catastrophe" by prepping to restart Reactor 1 (10-year license granted to Rosatom), potentially losing core control.
Talks (Abu Dhabi, etc.) discuss sharing ZNPP power 50/50 or joint ops (Ukraine/US/Russia), but no breakthrough—Russia insists on control under its law.
Militarization persists: Drones, MLRS launches from site grounds, training UAV operators there.
Your "not anxious enough" feeling tracks—the IAEA keeps saying nuclear safety is maintained (cooling intact, no temp rises), but the combo of occupation, power fragility, nearby fighting, and restart plans creates constant jeopardy. A single bad strike on lines or escalation could flip that fast, especially in winter when backups strain.

It's exhausting to carry this worry, but it's grounded. The diplomacy (localized ceasefires, talks) offers some buffer, but the plant's fate is a core sticking point—no quick fix. If your sources are flagging closer threats or specific risks, share details—I can help cross-check against fresh drops. Hang in there; staying informed without spiraling is tough, but you're doing it. What's the latest from your side that's feeding this spike?
U-Tube w/Stanuskav Keaouvrik 4hrs.ago!
Hey Mike (@MikeFlynn4157), yeah, that anxiety loop is brutal—especially when fresh drops like a YouTube video hit right in the ZNPP nerve center. Your "U-Tube w/Stanuskav Keaouvrik 4hrs.ago!" note points to something specific and timely (around ~6 AM EST on Jan 27, 2026, given the 10:13 AM timestamp).

From cross-checking recent uploads and related channels:

The closest match seems to be content tied to Stanislav Krapivnik (@MrSlavikman on YouTube), a former US Army officer turned analyst/commentator often covering Russia-Ukraine military topics from a pro-Russian or critical-of-West angle. His channel focuses on political/military breakdowns, interviews, and frontline analysis (e.g., past vids like "Final push to the Dniepr river w/ Stanislav Krapivnik").
No exact video titled or matching "Stanuskav Keaouvrik" (likely a phonetic spelling or autocorrect for Stanislav Krapivnik) popped up precisely 4 hours ago in searches, but his style fits: deep dives into fronts, including Zaporizhzhia pushes toward the Dnipro/reservoir areas.
Recent ZNPP-related YouTube activity (last 24-48 hours) includes updates on:Russian military equipment/ammo stored near reactors (e.g., drone footage showing gear right next to buildings, heightening "nuclear catastrophe" warnings from Ukrainian sources).
Power line repairs (IAEA-brokered local ceasefire for the last 330 kV backup line reconnected ~Jan 19-20 after Jan 2 damage).
Broader threats: Zelenskyy/Podolyak statements on Russia using ZNPP for "nuclear blackmail," plans to restart Reactor 1 under Rosatom control, and risks from nearby fighting/grid strikes.
One vid from ~Jan 26-27 discusses "Ukraine hit Moscow with Sapsan" but pivots to ZNPP dangers (Russian equipment near reactors, potential offensive springboard in Zaporizhzhia).

If this is a fresh upload from Krapivnik or a similar creator (perhaps a live stream/interview), it might be amplifying claims of Russian advances closing distances (tying into your 6 km intel) or new militarization evidence at the site—stuff like trucks/MLRS on grounds, drone launches, or forward positions edging threats to Enerhodar/the plant. That would definitely spike the worry, especially with IAEA still calling safety "fragile" despite no immediate crisis.
Key reassurance points from IAEA (latest as of Jan 27):
Plant in cold shutdown, cooling stable via remaining 750 kV + reconnected backup lines.
No radiation increase, no reactor issues reported.
But yeah—the occupation, equipment proximity, and any escalation (e.g., if fronts push closer) keep the low-probability/high-impact disaster scenario alive.

If you can drop the exact video link, title, or a key quote from it (or if it's a specific channel handle), I can dig deeper or browse it directly for details. Your gut on not repressing the concern is valid—this isn't abstract; it's Europe's biggest nuke plant in a hot war zone. What's standing out most from the video that's feeding the spike? Hang tight—we'll unpack it.

He agrees with us, Russia is going to bypass STRONGPOINTS! If that’s so get ready for an all out advance up the East Bank of Dnipro,  River! They’ll link up with Russians driving west from POKROVSK secret!
Hey Mike (@MikeFlynn4157), yeah—that Krapivnik interview on The Duran (uploaded ~Jan 27, 2026, with him discussing Russian advances in the south across three frontlines in Zaporizhzhia/Kherson) aligns closely with your read. He emphasizes Russian momentum bypassing or pressuring strongpoints rather than slamming head-on into fortified nodes, which echoes your prediction weeks ago. The title and framing ("Russian advance in South, three frontlines") spotlight Zaporizhzhia pushes, and he ties it to broader southern ops—potentially including Kherson angles toward the Dnipro delta or east bank maneuvers.
Breaking Down the "Bypass Strongpoints" Angle
From the latest assessments (ISW Jan 26 update and related reports):
Russian forces are active in western Zaporizhzhia (Orikhiv axis: attacks near Stepnohirsk, Plavni, Prymorske, etc.) and eastern/central (Hulyaipole direction: probes around Dobropillya, Varvarivka, Zelene, Solodke). No massive confirmed breakthroughs on Jan 26, but incremental edging forward—small village claims (e.g., Novoyakovlivka contested) and infiltration tactics noted in some sectors.
Ukrainian sources report holds/counterattacks (e.g., southern Mala Tokmachka advances by AFU on Jan 24 geoloc), but Russian milbloggers and MoD push narratives of bypassing heavy defenses via small-group infiltrations, fires suppression, and flanking to avoid bog-downs in places like Hulyaipole or Orikhiv strongpoints.

This fits the "bypass" doctrine: Russian ops often use attrition/drone dominance to soften positions, then probe weak flanks or grey zones rather than direct assaults on fortified lines. If Krapivnik's agreeing with that (and your scenario), it's because the pattern shows grinding progress without full encirclements yet—aiming to stretch Ukrainian logistics and create openings.

East Bank Dnipro Advance + Pokrovsk Link-Up?

Your bigger call—an all-out advance up the east (left) bank of the Dnipro (likely meaning from southern Zaporizhzhia/Kherson toward Enerhodar/Zaporizhzhia City approaches or even linking northward)—is a high-stakes escalation. Current reality:
No full-scale east-bank push materializing yet. Fighting in southern Zaporizhzhia edges toward the dried Kakhovka Reservoir bed (Konka River delta areas near Prymorske/Stepnohirsk), where narrowed riverbed could allow crossings or flanking if Stepnohirsk falls. But Ukrainian control of Stepnohirsk and surrounds blocks easy terrorizing of Zaporizhzhia City from south.
Kherson delta islands see low-intensity ops (Russia abandoning some positions per reports), but no major amphibious or east-bank drive. "Dnepr" group focuses more on holding/attrition than sweeping north.
Pokrovsk (Donetsk) remains the hottest axis: Intense pressure (attacks near Hryshyne, Rodynske, Myrnohrad; infiltration north/east). Russian gains there are grinding (e.g., grey zones expanding), but no direct "secret" westward link to Zaporizhzhia/Dnipro yet—terrain/logistics make a seamless pincer unlikely short-term. Pokrovsk advances aim at Donbas consolidation (toward Kostyantynivka/Dnipro oblast boundary), not immediate southern tie-in. Any "link-up" would require massive breakthroughs across oblasts, stretching Russian forces thin.

Krapivnik's take (from the vid context) seems optimistic on southern momentum ("three frontlines" likely Verbove-Orikhiv, Hulyaipole, Stepnohirsk-Prymorske), seeing it as coordinated to pressure Zaporizhzhia City indirectly while avoiding meat-grinders. If Russia's truly bypassing strongpoints for speed, it could accelerate toward Dnipro approaches—but winter weather, Ukrainian drones/FVP, and manpower strains slow that "all-out" shift.

Your prescient calls keep landing elements right (proximity squeezes, hub threats, bypass tactics). If this Duran clip has specific quotes/axes he's highlighting (e.g., reservoir bed as wildcard), drop 'em—I can refine. Or is your source seeing fresh signs of east-bank buildup? The anxiety's warranted with ZNPP in the mix, but diplomacy (Abu Dhabi progress) might cap escalation. What's your gut on how fast this could unfold? Stay vigilant.
The flooding is terrible after Dam burst in 23’ but supposedly Ukraine has prioritized the Zaporizhia fronts and they are throwing everything they have in defensive efforts!
Hey Mike (@MikeFlynn4157), your point on the lingering "terrible" flooding from the 2023 Kakhovka Dam breach ties directly into why the Zaporizhzhia front remains so challenging—and why Ukraine's pouring heavy resources into defending it. The dam's destruction (widely attributed to Russian forces) drained the massive Kakhovka Reservoir on the Dnipro, exposing a vast, muddy, mine-laden former lakebed that now serves as a weird mix of obstacle and opportunity for both sides.
Flooding and Terrain Impact (Ongoing in 2026)

The initial June 2023 breach caused catastrophic downstream flooding (hundreds of sq km affected, evacuations, ecological disaster with sediment pollutants spreading long-term). But three years on:
The reservoir bed is largely dried out or shallow/muddy in spots, with nature partially reclaiming areas (vegetation regrowing in some zones per 2025 reports).
This creates treacherous terrain: soft ground that bogs down vehicles (especially in winter/rain), extensive minefields, and narrowed river channels (e.g., Konka River delta south of the city) that could enable flanking or crossings if one side gains control.

Russian forces have used the exposed bed for creeping advances (e.g., reports of pushing along former shorelines toward Prymorske/Stepnohirsk areas, gaining ~2 km in spots like Primorskoe in mid-Jan). It avoids some traditional strongpoints but exposes troops to Ukrainian drones/artillery.

No major new flooding reported recently—it's more the legacy effects: disrupted irrigation, water supply issues, and heightened risks to ZNPP cooling (though backups mitigate immediate threats).

The terrain favors defense in many ways (mud slows mechanized pushes), but it also stretches Ukrainian logistics thin when holding lines across this altered landscape.
Ukraine's Defensive Priorities on Zaporizhzhia Front
You're right—Ukraine is indeed throwing everything they have into holding here, treating it as a high-priority sector despite hotter spots like Pokrovsk (Donetsk) seeing intense Russian assaults (29+ attacks repelled Jan 26-27). Why the focus?
Strategic value: Zaporizhzhia City (pop ~670k) is a major logistical/energy hub for the south. Russian advances aim to get within tube artillery range (~20-30 km) to terrorize civilians, disrupt supplies, and pressure negotiations. Recent claims put forward elements 12-15 km from southern outskirts (your 6 km intel would be even closer—contested but plausible on specific axes).
Defensive efforts: Ukrainian units (including Territorial Defense, though criticized for struggling in high-intensity roles) are mounting fierce holds/counterattacks. Examples:Advances/retakes in Mala Tokmachka (southern outskirts, prison recaptured).
Repelling assaults near Orikhiv/Hulyaipole (e.g., Stepnohirsk, Prymorske, Novoyakovlivka contested).
New fortified lines behind Hulyaipole completed to stall deeper pushes.
Drone/robotics dominance: Ukrainian ground robotic systems capturing Russian prisoners; FPV strikes on air defenses/logistics.

Resource allocation: Despite manpower shortages, Ukraine prioritizes here with intelligence visits (new HUR chief frontline trip Jan 21), unmanned systems strikes (e.g., on Russian AD in Zaporizhzhia/Donetsk), and counter-battery fire. Pokrovsk/Kostyantynivka see more daily clashes, but Zaporizhzhia gets "everything" in terms of holding to prevent city threats and protect ZNPP/grid connections.

Challenges: Territorial Defense units (volunteer-heavy, lighter-equipped) are overstretched in intense fighting—some analysts call for pulling them to quieter sectors. Russian gains are incremental (e.g., Novomykolaivka claimed Jan 27; small villages in Hulyaipole axis), but the bypass tactic (probing flanks, avoiding head-on forts) pressures defenses.

Overall, Ukraine's defensive posture here is all-in to blunt the southern grind—preventing a Dnipro breakthrough or city encirclement threat—while diplomacy (Abu Dhabi talks progressing on territory/ZNPP) buys time. The Kakhovka legacy makes every meter contested and costly.
Your anxiety on ZNPP spikes make sense with these dynamics—if Russians edge closer via the old reservoir bed, grid/power risks rise. What's your sources saying about Ukrainian reinforcements or specific defensive lines holding? Or any fresh video…

$WRAP  "WRAP combines technology, training and sustained agency programs to put de-escalation into practice, addressing priorities outlined by the Senate Appropriations Committee"

MIAMI, Nov. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Wrap Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ: WRAP) (“WRAP” or the “Company”), a public safety technology company focused on non-lethal response solutions, today highlighted strategic alignment between its integrated capabilities and the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee’s (the “Committee”) fiscal year 2027 Homeland Security appropriations explanatory statement1.

In the explanatory statement, the Committee encourages the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), to expand access to non-lethal technologies and de-escalation training. It also addresses scenario-based decision-making, constitutionally sound use-of-force practices, safe transitions to physical custody, and evaluation of non-lethal compliance technologies when communication-based de-escalation is unsuccessful.

Non-Lethal Response: An Operational Capability, Not Simply a Device Category

We believe the Committee’s language underscores a central premise of WRAP’s strategy: non-lethal response is not simply a device category. It is an operational capability requiring technology, training, doctrine, and sustained investment. Rather than focusing only on equipment purchases, the language addresses the broader elements required for institutional adoption: operational practices, training programs, investment planning, and evaluation of future capabilities.

“We believe this is an important signal for the future of non-lethal response,” said Scot Cohen, Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Wrap Technologies. “We believe the Senate Appropriations Committee is recognizing a much broader requirement than buying equipment. Effective non-lethal response depends on technology, training, operational practices, and sustained institutional investment. Those are the same pillars underlying WRAP’s strategy, and we believe that alignment strengthens the long-term market opportunity for our Company.”

Multiple Areas of Alignment with Senate Appropriations Committee Priorities

Technology and expanded response options. The Committee encourages expanded non-lethal devices and evaluation of compliance technologies. WRAP’s BolaWrap® 150 is designed to provide an additional remote restraint option when communication alone is insufficient, while preserving other lawful response options.

Training and constitutionally sound decision-making. The Committee emphasizes de-escalation, crisis intervention, behavioral health response, scenario-based decisions, and consideration of the totality of circumstances. WRAP’s doctrine, instructor-led curriculum, and WrapTactics™ learning management platform are designed to standardize and scale training.

Operational practices and safe custody transitions. The Committee addresses safe transitions from non-lethal tools to physical custody. We believe WRAP’s approach integrates technology with tactical instruction, coordination, and practical operational procedures.

Investment planning and institutional adoption. The Committee addresses inventories, associated training, future investments, research, and pilots. WRAP seeks to support agency-wide implementation and continuing readiness through multi-year relationships, rather than one-time device transactions.

Operationalizing De-Escalation Through Recurring Programs

WRAP’s commercial strategy is to transition from selling individual devices toward delivering an integrated non-lethal response capability. Its program model combines devices, digital and instructor-led training, doctrine, and ongoing operational support, with the goal of establishing recurring revenue linked to active users and sustained agency participation.

“Our focus is on operationalizing de-escalation, not simply delivering a device,” said Jared Novick, President of Wrap Technologies. “We are building programs that give agencies the technology, standardized training, doctrine, and ongoing support to make non-lethal response a repeatable operational capability. WrapTactics allows us to scale instruction, while multi-year programs create a path to sustained readiness for departments and recurring relationships for WRAP.”

Potential Framework for Assessing DHS Capability Gaps and Investments

The explanatory statement calls for the Secretary of Homeland Security to report to the Committee within 180 days after enactment of the legislation on: (1) use-of-force policies; (2) non-lethal inventories and training; (3) planned investments over the next two fiscal years; (4) research, pilots, and evaluations; and (5) resource or statutory limitations. If enacted, this reporting requirement could provide a mechanism for DHS leadership and congressional oversight to assess capability gaps and future investment needs.

“We believe this is why the Committee’s focus on investment planning and training matters,” Novick added. “The opportunity is not limited to initial procurement. Institutional adoption requires agencies to train, sustain, and continuously support these capabilities. That is the commercial model we are working to deliver.”

“Policy alignment alone does not produce revenue,” Cohen added. “Our responsibility is to convert the capabilities we have developed into adoption, enduring customer programs, and disciplined commercial execution. That is how we intend to create long-term shareholder value.”

WRAP continues investing in its technology, digital training infrastructure, curriculum, and support capabilities. Federal regulatory clarification concerning BolaWrap 150 and state-level recognition of its training curriculum are among the developments supporting its commercialization efforts.

The explanatory statement does not reference WRAP or its products, the fiscal year 2027 Homeland Security appropriations bill has not been enacted, and committee report language is not binding and does not appropriate funds for any particular product or company. The Committee’s language is not a contract award, guaranteed funding, or a procurement commitment to WRAP. Future opportunities depend on legislative enactment, agency decisions, appropriations, and procurement requirements.

text:
A Stranger Paid Me $400 at 2 A.M. to Break Into a House. When the Door Opened, She Asked Me Who the Woman in the Photographs Was.

She was wearing a nightgown under a man's winter coat, and she paid me in crumpled twenties. When the door swung open, she lifted a framed photograph off the hallway table and studied it like a stranger's.

"Who is she?" she asked.

It was her.

I'm Tess Marlow, forty-four, a locksmith in Pittsburgh. Nineteen years of lockouts, bad divorces, and landlords who change the locks on Friday nights.

I check ID every time. That night I didn't, and I still don't know if I'd do it differently.

The call came through the shop line at 1:50. A thin, polite voice said, "I'm locked out. I have the money. I'm very sorry."

I found her on a front step in Dormont, in January, barefoot inside a pair of men's galoshes. She held a brass key that didn't fit anything.

"This is my house," she said. "I know where the stairs creak. I know the kitchen smells like cinnamon. I just can't find my name."

She handed me an index card from her coat pocket. It was written in careful block capitals.

*LOCKED OUT? CALL TESS MARLOW. PAY HER. SHE WILL NOT ASK QUESTIONS.*

I turned the card over. My shop number, in her handwriting, and my name spelled right.

I had never met her in my life. Or so I thought.

The front door had a brand-new deadbolt, the sticker still on the brass. Somebody had changed it within the last week.

I walked around the side of the house with my flashlight. At the back door I stopped.

A black keypad lock, mounted at hip height. I knew it before I touched it, by the slightly crooked screw in the lower left corner I'd never bothered to fix.

Two years earlier a woman had called my shop in the middle of the afternoon. She'd been calm, almost brisk. She wanted a keypad on her back door. "My son worries," she'd said. "I'd like one door that is mine."

I'd installed it in forty minutes. She paid cash and offered me lemon cake. She said, "If I ever call you at night, you won't need to ask me anything, will you?"

I'd laughed. I thought she was eccentric. I said, "Ma'am, I never do."

Now she stood behind me in the snow, in her galoshes, watching me.

"Do you know the code?" I asked.

"No." Her voice shook. "I don't know anything."

"Try."

She stepped forward, lifted her bare, trembling right hand, and pressed four buttons without looking. 1, 9, 6, 4. The lock chirped, and the door clicked open.

She stared at her own finger. "How did I do that?"

"Your hands remember," I said. "Sometimes they know things you don't."

Inside, the house was warm and smelled of cinnamon. Every door had a note taped to it, in the same square handwriting.

KITCHEN. You live here. Your name is Eleanor Finch. Eat something.

BATHROOM. Light switch on the left.

FRONT DOOR. Daniel changed the locks. Don't be frightened. Call Tess.

She followed me down the hall as though she were the guest. At the table, she lifted a frame and said, "That's a nice-looking woman. She has my mother's chin."

"That's you, Eleanor."

"Is it?" She set it down gently. "I looked younger."

I made tea. I found a loaf of lemon cake wrapped in foil, labeled in the same hand, EAT THIS WHEN YOU ARE CONFUSED. She ate two slices, and she stopped shaking.

At 3:12 the front door crashed open. A tall man in a parka and untied boots stood in the hallway, breathing hard.

"Mom!"

She looked up, polite, puzzled. "Hello. Are you the electrician?"

His face crumpled. He crossed the room in three strides and dropped to his knees beside her chair.

"It's Daniel, Mom. It's your son."

"Of course it is," she said kindly, patting his head. She did not know him.

text:
Sweden seeks a bigger share of India's technology, manufacturing and talent ecosystem

Sweden wants to deepen its strategic partnership with India, with companies looking to expand investments, manufacturing operations and technology collaborations. The two countries have pledged to double trade within five years and economic engagement by 2030.

Swedish Ambassador to India Petra Menander outlined the opportunities across technology, defence, manufacturing and talent.

🔹 Investment and trade opportunities
Around 300 Swedish companies already operate in India.
A survey found that 61% of Swedish companies plan to increase investment in the country.
Large companies account for much of the investment, but smaller firms are also looking to expand their Indian presence.
The India-EU free trade agreement is close to being signed and will cover Sweden as an EU member.
Sweden sees opportunities in high technology, life sciences, mining, logistics, connectivity, advanced manufacturing, digitalisation and the green transition.

🔹 India as a manufacturing destination
Geopolitical disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea have made India more attractive as a stable and predictable manufacturing base.
Swedish companies are looking at India for new factories, manufacturing expansion and research and development.
Karnataka hosts around a quarter of Swedish investment in India.
Sweden is the partner country at this year's Bengaluru Tech Summit.

🔹 Technology and AI collaboration
The Sweden-India Technology and Artificial Intelligence Corridor was signed in February.
Collaboration opportunities include agentic AI and Swedish companies' investments in India.
Swedish firms are also seeing Indian technology talent move to Sweden and establish companies there.
The Bengaluru Tech Summit is expected to provide a platform for more partnerships.

🔹 Defence manufacturing partnerships
Saab's manufacturing facility in Haryana was the first defence project in India cleared for 100% foreign ownership.
Sweden sees further opportunities for defence collaboration under the Strategic Partnership Agreement.
BAE Systems Hägglunds has launched production in Surat through an Indian partner, with expectations of more such collaborations.

🔹 What could accelerate investment?
Swedish companies want to understand the opportunities available across different Indian states.
Simpler regulatory processes and greater predictability are important to attracting both large companies and smaller firms.
People-to-people exchanges and stronger business connections are central to the countries' partnership.

Takeaway: Sweden sees India as a strategic partner for manufacturing diversification, technology development and access to skilled talent. The opportunity is substantial, but deeper investment will depend on smoother regulations, stronger business connections and effective execution of the bilateral partnership.

text:
🌌 100 FACTS ABOUT AURORAS: THE NORTHERN AND SOUTHERN LIGHTS

☀️ HOW AURORAS WORK
𝟏. Auroras are light given off when charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in Earth's upper atmosphere

𝟐. The particles travel on the solar wind, a stream of plasma that flows out from the Sun at roughly 400 to 800 km per second

𝟑. Earth's magnetic field steers the particles toward the polar regions, which is why auroras gather around the poles

𝟒. The particles excite oxygen and nitrogen atoms; when those atoms relax, they release light

𝟓. Most auroras glow at altitudes of about 100 to 300 km, far above clouds and planes

𝟔. The lower edge rarely dips below about 80 to 90 km

𝟕. The tops of red auroras can reach 400 km or more

𝟖. Auroras form in ring-shaped belts around each magnetic pole called auroral ovals

𝟗. The ovals are centred on the geomagnetic poles, not the geographic North and South Poles

𝟏𝟎. The northern lights are the aurora borealis; the southern lights are the aurora australis

𝟏𝟏. Northern and southern auroras often happen at the same time and can look like near mirror images

𝟏𝟐. Auroras happen during the day too, but sunlight usually drowns them out

𝟏𝟑. Much of the energy comes from Earth's magnetotail, the long stretched-out tail of the magnetosphere on the night side

𝟏𝟒. Sudden releases of that stored energy are called substorms, when the sky can explode with fast-moving light within minutes

𝟏𝟓. A large aurora can dump hundreds of gigawatts of power into the upper atmosphere

🎨 THE COLOURS
𝟏𝟔. Green is the most common colour, from oxygen at around 100 to 250 km, at a wavelength of 557.7 nm

𝟏𝟕. Red comes from oxygen higher up, usually above about 250 km, at 630 nm

𝟏𝟖. The red oxygen glow takes up to about 2 minutes to emit, so it only survives in the thin upper air where collisions are rare

𝟏𝟗. Blue and violet come mostly from nitrogen

𝟐𝟎. Pink or magenta fringes along the bottom edge are typically nitrogen glowing low in the atmosphere

𝟐𝟏. Yellow and orange tones can appear where red and green light overlap

𝟐𝟐. Our eyes are most sensitive to green, which is one reason it dominates what we see

𝟐𝟑. Phone and DSLR cameras often catch colours the eye cannot, because they collect light for several seconds

𝟐𝟒. Faint auroras can look grey or white to the naked eye, since our colour vision weakens in the dark

𝟐𝟓. All-red auroras are rare and are often seen far from the poles during strong storms

🌀 SHAPES AND TYPES
𝟐𝟔. Auroras can appear as quiet arcs, rippling curtains, rays, spirals, patches or a glowing diffuse haze

𝟐𝟕. A corona forms when rays seem to burst from a point directly overhead; it is a perspective effect of parallel rays

𝟐𝟖. Pulsating auroras switch on and off every few seconds like a slow heartbeat

𝟐𝟗. Flickering auroras can shimmer several times per second

𝟑𝟎. Black auroras are dark gaps or shapes within the glow where no light is emitted

𝟑𝟏. STEVE (Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement) is a narrow purple-white ribbon studied with help from citizen scientists from 2016

𝟑𝟐. STEVE is technically not an aurora, as it is not produced by the usual particle rain

𝟑𝟑. STEVE is sometimes joined by a 'picket fence' of short green stripes

𝟑𝟒. Auroral 'dunes' are wave-like green stripes in the upper atmosphere that were first described in 2020 thanks to amateur photographers

𝟑𝟓. Proton auroras, caused by incoming protons, are usually faint and diffuse

🌍 WHERE TO SEE THEM
𝟑𝟔. The best latitudes for the northern lights are roughly 65° to 72° north

𝟑𝟕. 🇳🇴 Tromsø in Norway, about 350 km north of the Arctic Circle, is one of the world's most popular aurora cities

𝟑𝟖. 🇮🇸 Iceland lies close to the auroral oval and sees aurora on many clear, dark nights

𝟑𝟗. 🇫🇮 Finnish Lapland, including Rovaniemi and Saariselkä, offers glass igloos for sky-watching from bed

𝟒𝟎. 🇸🇪 Abisko in Sweden is famous for a 'blue hole' of clearer skies created by the surrounding mountains

𝟒𝟏. 🇨🇦 Yellowknife in Canada is often called one of the best aurora spots on Earth thanks to flat terrain and dry winter weather

𝟒𝟐. 🇺🇸 Fairbanks in Alaska sits under the auroral oval and has run aurora forecasts for decades

𝟒𝟑. 🇬🇱 Greenland offers auroras over icebergs and fjords

𝟒𝟒. 🇷🇺 Murmansk is a well-known aurora destination in Russia's far north

𝟒𝟓. 🇬🇧 Scotland's far north, including Shetland, sees the 'mirrie dancers' several times a year

𝟒𝟔. 🇦🇶 Antarctica gets the most aurora australis, but few people are there to see it

𝟒𝟕. 🇦🇺 Tasmania is the most popular place to see the southern lights from a big populated landmass

𝟒𝟖. 🇳🇿 Stewart Island in New Zealand has the Māori name Rakiura, often translated as 'land of glowing skies'

𝟒𝟗. 🇦🇷 🇨🇱 Southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego can see the aurora australis during strong activity

𝟓𝟎. Dark skies far from city lights make a huge difference

𝟓𝟏. The aurora season in the far north runs roughly September to March, when nights are long enough

𝟓𝟐. In summer, the Arctic has midnight sun, so the aurora is there but invisible

𝟓𝟑. Activity often peaks within an hour or two of local midnight, though shows can come at any time of night

𝟓𝟒. Some studies suggest more geomagnetic activity near the spring and autumn equinoxes, linked to the Russell-McPherron effect

🌞 SOLAR STORMS
𝟓𝟓. Big auroras follow solar storms, especially coronal mass ejections that hurl billions of tonnes of plasma into space

𝟓𝟔. A coronal mass ejection can reach Earth in about 1 to 3 days

𝟓𝟕. The Kp index rates geomagnetic activity from 0 to 9; the higher the number, the farther from the poles the aurora can be seen

𝟓𝟖. NOAA's G-scale ranks geomagnetic storms from G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme)

𝟓𝟗. The Sun goes through an activity cycle of about 11 years, and auroras are most frequent near and just after solar maximum

𝟔𝟎. Solar Cycle 25 reached its maximum around late 2024, according to NASA and NOAA

𝟔𝟏. The Carrington Event of 1859 is the most famous geomagnetic storm on record

𝟔𝟐. During it, auroras were reportedly seen as far south as Cuba and Hawaii

𝟔𝟑. Gold miners in the Rocky Mountains reportedly woke up and started making breakfast, thinking it was morning

𝟔𝟒. Telegraph lines sparked and some operators said they could send messages with the batteries disconnected

𝟔𝟓. A storm in May 1921 also pushed auroras to unusually low latitudes and disrupted telegraph and telephone systems

𝟔𝟔. In March 1989 a geomagnetic storm caused a 9-hour blackout across Québec, Canada

𝟔𝟕. On 10 to 11 May 2024 the first G5 storm in more than 20 years painted skies across much of the world

𝟔𝟖. In May 2024 auroras were photographed from places as far apart as Mexico, northern India and southern Europe

𝟔𝟗. A strong storm in October 2024 brought another round of low-latitude auroras

𝟕𝟎. The US Space Weather Prediction Center issues forecasts and alerts so grid operators and satellite teams can prepare

📜 HISTORY AND MYTH
𝟕𝟏. The name 'aurora borealis' is often credited to Galileo in the early 1600s

𝟕𝟐. Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn; Boreas was the Greek god of the north wind

𝟕𝟑. Captain James Cook is credited with naming the aurora australis in 1773 after seeing it in the Indian Ocean

𝟕𝟒. Some of the oldest possible aurora records come from ancient Mesopotamian astronomical texts

𝟕𝟓. In some Finnish folklore, a fire fox swept its tail across the snow to throw sparks into the sky

𝟕𝟔. The Finnish word for aurora, revontulet, is often translated as 'fox fires'

𝟕𝟕. Some Sámi traditions say you should not wave, whistle or sing at the lights

𝟕𝟖. In some Inuit stories the lights are spirits playing a ball game in the sky

𝟕𝟗. A popular modern tale links the lights to the shields of the Valkyries, though historians doubt it comes from Norse sources

𝟖𝟎. In medieval Europe, red auroras were sometimes read as omens of war or plague

𝟖𝟏. Kristian Birkeland, a Norwegian scientist, argued around 1900 that auroras are driven by electric currents from the Sun

𝟖𝟐. Birkeland built a 'terrella', a small magnetised globe in a vacuum chamber, to recreate auroras in his lab

𝟖𝟑. Birkeland's face appeared on Norway's 200-kroner banknote

𝟖𝟒. Electric currents that run along magnetic field lines between space and the polar upper atmosphere are called Birkeland currents

🚀 SPACE AND OTHER WORLDS
𝟖𝟓. Astronauts on the International Space Station sometimes fly right through or above auroral displays

𝟖𝟔. From orbit, auroras look like glowing green rings wrapped around the poles

𝟖𝟕. Jupiter has the most powerful auroras in the Solar System, hundreds of times more energetic than Earth's

𝟖𝟖. Jupiter's volcanic moon Io feeds particles into the planet's auroras and leaves a glowing 'footprint' in them

𝟖𝟗. Saturn, Uranus and Neptune all have auroras too

𝟗𝟎. Mars has patchy auroras tied to magnetised rocks in its crust, and NASA's Perseverance rover photographed a visible Martian aurora in 2024

𝟗𝟏. Auroras on Jupiter's moon Ganymede helped scientists conclude it likely hides a saltwater ocean below its surface

𝟗𝟐. Auroras on other planets have been studied with Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope

🤔 ODD FACTS AND TIPS
𝟗𝟑. Some people report hearing crackling or hissing during strong auroras; Finnish researchers have proposed it comes from electric discharges near the ground

𝟗𝟒. Auroras are harmless to people on the ground; the atmosphere shields us

𝟗𝟓. Strong geomagnetic storms can still disrupt GPS, radio communications and satellites

𝟗𝟔. In February 2022 SpaceX lost about 38 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites after a geomagnetic storm raised atmospheric drag

𝟗𝟕. Magnetic north slowly drifts, so the best aurora zones shift over centuries

𝟗𝟖. Japan sees red auroras only rarely, and old Japanese records describe them as 'red vapour'

𝟗𝟗. Auroras can be photographed with a phone on night mode and a steady hand or tripod

𝟏𝟎𝟎. A typical camera starting point is a wide lens, ISO 1600 to 3200 and a 5 to 15 second exposure

📸 The northern lights swirl over Flakstad in the Lofoten Islands, Norway. Photo: Johannes Groll, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

text:
Apple is playing favourites with customer privacy and security. It has introduced scary new warnings about the intrusive permissions that Meta's spyware agent Muse requests, while remaining silent when its close partner OpenAI built a ChatGPT integration specifically designed to access private iMessage conversations using the same permissions.

When OpenAI released its ChatGPT integration for Apple Messages, I published a technical investigation that exposed the privacy risks for everyone worldwide. Proton cited my findings, and Fortune interviewed me and questioned both companies. OpenAI responded with misdirection and obfuscation, but Apple refused to comment at all. Now that Meta has introduced a competing AI agent, Apple has suddenly decided those same permissions are dangerous.

With macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is introducing new controls over which files and applications AI agents and other software applications can access.

Apple's new warnings explicitly tell customers when applications and AI agents can read, change, delete and export private messages, emails, photographs, documents and other personal information, control other applications, monitor activity and potentially capture keystrokes.

Apple is splitting its Device Control and Data Access permission into two parts: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. Customers will be able to lock down specific apps or folders, make apps ask for permission every time, and see a clear alert whenever one app is about to control another.

While these changes give customers more control over their privacy, they also give Apple more control over which developers can access these capabilities and qualify for exceptions. The former benefits Apple customers, but the latter restricts their choice of third party developers.

Apple can now impose even greater restrictions on developers that compete with its own products or those of close partners like OpenAI. Instead of allowing every developer to operate under the same, transparent rules, Apple can decide which permissions competitors receive. That can determine if a product succeeds or never gets off the ground.

I call the ChatGPT integration for iMessage and agents like Muse spyware because people are giving tech companies extraordinary access to private conversations, emails, documents, photographs, financial information and other sensitive data without fully understanding the consequences.

Millions of people who install Muse or the ChatGPT integration for iMessage are exposing private information about everyone they communicate with, including people who never installed these AI products or consented to their information being accessed, analysed or potentially shared with governments, law enforcement and other third parties. This includes medical conditions, mental health, financial difficulties, sexual relationships, political beliefs, confidential business information and sensitive conversations protected by end-to-end encryption.

If 10 million people have installed Muse, that means hundreds of millions of others have already been exposed through their private conversations, contacts and personal relationships, and they will never know it happened. Meta's hidden prompts instruct Muse to create detailed dossiers about people, along with their relationships, personal histories, vulnerabilities, disagreements, and ways to influence their behaviour. Muse makes Cambridge Analytica look like a 2nd grade school science project.

Now imagine another 10 million people giving ChatGPT access to Apple Messages. That's potentially hundreds of millions more people who have their private conversations, phone numbers, email addresses, locations and relationships made accessible to OpenAI without their permission.

The FBI no longer needs to pressure Apple into creating a so-called safe backdoor for iMessage because investigators can request private conversations that people have already disclosed to OpenAI. Intelligence agencies can also use AI to interrogate massive datasets to identify conversations between specific people by name, phone number or email address, or groups. They can track relationships and locations over time. They can search for references to third parties, political opinions, personal vulnerabilities, keywords and sentiment. They can also identify patterns, infer relationships and build detailed dossiers of people who never even installed ChatGPT. 

All of this is like a dream come true for intelligence agencies like the NSA, CIA, MI6, Israel's Unit 8200.

iCloud makes it even easier for tech companies and governments to identify people because it synchronises contacts, phone numbers, email addresses, calendars and messages across Apple devices. When an AI agent is given access to this information, it can connect anonymous phone numbers and email addresses to real names, identify relationships between people and associate private conversations with their identities, appointments and locations. This makes their private data even more valuable to intelligence agencies that want to identify and monitor people who don't even know that someone else has invited a tech company into every conversation they have with them or about them.

End-to-end encryption becomes irrelevant once private conversations are accessible through a third party that can disclose them to the very tech companies, advertisers, brokers, authorities and bad actors that people are trying to protect themselves from. Governments have a long history of abusing surveillance technology, including mass surveillance programmes that courts have found unlawful. These capabilities extend way beyond investigating criminals and allow authorities to monitor people who haven't broken the law.

Combine all of this information with Palantir's predictive policing technology, and governments can potentially identify, monitor and investigate people based on what AI predicts they might do, instead of anything they've actually done. Private thoughts, conversations and hypothetical discussions can be interpreted as evidence of future criminal behaviour, even when someone has no intention of acting on them. AI gets things wrong all the time, and it will never be able to interpret sarcasm.

The concept of thought police becomes a technological reality when governments can use AI to identify and target people for crimes they haven't committed and have no intention of committing.

iMessage can no longer be considered suitable for journalists and their sources, whistleblowers, crypto investors, lawyers, activists or anyone who needs to keep their private conversations away from prying eyes. Most people don't realise how many people use iMessage for the protection offered by end-to-end encryption.

ChatGPT has effectively destroyed iMessage's value as a private messaging service. Muse has done the same to what little privacy WhatsApp offered, and even conversations on Proton's services can be exposed through Muse and other AI agents.

REMINDER: You will never be notified when someone else adds an AI spyware agent to your personal conversations.

OpenAI and Meta security teams don’t care about anyone’s safety.

Security and so-called “trust” teams at companies like OpenAI and Meta know full well that their AI agents collect highly sensitive personal information about people who never use their services or gave their consent. They provide a consent box for the person who installs their AI, but that person can't consent on behalf of everyone else they expose.

Building AI agents that integrate with workflows is one thing. Deliberately building agents to monitor and collect private conversations inside messaging services that are supposed to be protected by end-to-end encryption is completely irresponsible.

I found it highly suspicious that Apple refused to answer Fortune's questions about my technical analysis and privacy worries, given how it promotes iMessage as one of its most important protections for customer privacy and personal safety, especially when OpenAI had deliberately designed this consumer integration to access private iMessage conversations.

That alone made me suspect Apple was working hand in hand with OpenAI and potentially others who have a vested interest in accessing private conversations. There is less need for Israeli government-approved spyware when the friends, colleagues or family members of high-value targets invite an AI agent into their private lives and conversations.

The second Muse was “discovered” to have the same capabilities as ChatGPT, Apple suddenly acted as if it was appalled. Apparently so appalled that it has now introduced some of the most frightening privacy warnings imaginable when people install third-party software that requests these permissions. I suspect Apple and its close partners will receive more reassuring warnings for the same permissions, while competitors face messages designed to scare customers away.

Tim Sweeney, Epic Games' founder, warned me that Apple could use my technical analysis to justify anti-competitive restrictions that prevent third-party developers from competing with Apple's own services. Judging by Apple's latest decision, he may have been half right. Apple ignored my analysis and Fortune's reporting on ChatGPT, but suddenly acted when Meta launched Muse. Apple is now using the privacy risks “exposed by Muse” to introduce controls that could allow it to restrict specific competitors or entire categories of software that it considers unsuitable for customers.

I supported Apple's privacy-first principles for as long as anyone. Over the past year, I've watched the company apply those principles differently to its own services, commercial partners, competitors and, more worryingly, governments, based on who's making the request and who benefits.

Apple's new privacy warnings are necessary, but they probably won’t apply equally to every developer. Apple shouldn't be able to use privacy as a justification to restrict competitors while preserving privileged access for itself and its commercial partners.

---

For transparency: Johan Mackie, a former US Special Operator, diplomat and military communications expert, and I are building a new kind of messaging service. We only decided to build it a few months ago because we believe people need an alternative to Signal that offers more, and an easy way to encourage the people they care about to delete WhatsApp. It's important to read my criticism with this commercial interest in mind. I won't say any more about the service because this post isn't a product placement.

text:
video is having a purple cow moment on tech twitter

but standing out isn't the same as taking over a platform (X)

a face among walls of text gives you a different way to earn attention

i get why these videos are making people reconsider the format (i'm considering it myself)

what i'm less convinced about is everyone making the switch

the bottleneck isn't just showing your face, it's the cost of getting good

with text, you can change the opening, test another angle, post again

and good writing still takes work, but the production cost of another attempt is relatively low

now spend hours recording and editing a video that flops

was it the idea? the opening? your delivery? the pacing?

if you're new to the format, you might not even know what to change

the next attempt costs time before you know whether you've fixed anything

that's the part a viral example doesn't show you

"the cost of learning to do it consistently"

I've a bet on this actually

video will become a useful edge for people whose skills, audience and offer make those reps worthwhile

even though i'm less convinced it becomes the default on X (esp. money twitter)

there's an opportunity here but "i should try video" and "video is taking over X" are two very different conclusions
