🇹🇷🤝🇶🇦🛡️✍️ 🇹🇷 Turkey and 🇶🇦 Qatar sign five agreements in Istanbul, led by a new Mutual Defense Agreement

On Friday, Nov 13, 2026, 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 💡 President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani signed five documents at the Presidential Dolmabahçe Working Office in Istanbul. The signing closed the 12th session of the 🇹🇷-🇶🇦 Supreme Strategic Committee. The headline item is a Mutual Defense Agreement that the two leaders signed personally. The other four cover consumer protection and market surveillance, education, peace and conflict resolution, and the session's joint communiqué.

Both governments say the defense pact commits them to "a unified stance in confronting any external armed attack targeting either party or both of them." Its full text has not been published. Nothing public says an attack on one counts as an attack on both, or that either side must send forces. It was signed amid the fallout of the 🇺🇸-🇮🇱 war on 🇮🇷 Iran, 🇮🇷 Iranian strikes on 🇶🇦 Qatar this year, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, and 🇮🇱 Israel's September 2025 strike on Hamas officials in Doha.

📍 The setting:

🗓️ - Thursday, Nov 12, 2026: Senior officials held a preparatory meeting.

🗓️ - Friday, Nov 13, 2026: The two foreign ministers held their preparatory committee meeting. 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 💡 Erdoğan then welcomed 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Emir Tamim with an official ceremony at Dolmabahçe, followed by one-on-one talks, delegation talks and the signing ceremony in the evening. The 🇶🇦 Emir came to Istanbul after attending the UN COP31 climate summit in southern 🇹🇷 Turkey.

👥 Also in the room: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and 🇹🇷 MİT intelligence chief İbrahim Kalın sat in on the leaders' talks. On the 🇶🇦 Qatari side, the Amiri Diwan lists 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defense Affairs Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Amiri Diwan chief Abdullah bin Mohammed Al Khulaifi, 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Finance Minister Ali bin Ahmed Al Kuwari and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Commerce Minister Sheikh Faisal bin Thani Al Thani.

📍 The five agreements:

1️⃣ - 🛡️ Mutual Defense Agreement (Karşılıklı Savunma Anlaşması)
✍️ Signed by: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 💡 Erdoğan and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Emir Tamim.
📄 What's known: Per the joint communiqué, it aims to strengthen collective defense, promote regional security and set "a unified stance in confronting any external armed attack targeting either party or both of them." Both sides will consult on threats, regional and global security and defense policy, and expand joint military exercises, defense-industry cooperation and personnel training exchanges.
⚠️ Not public: the full text, what triggers it, what form a joint response would take, and whether 🇹🇷 Turkey's parliament must ratify it.

2️⃣ - 🛒 Memorandum of Understanding on Cooperation in Consumer Protection, Market Surveillance and Inspection
✍️ Signed by: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 Trade Minister Ömer Bolat and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Commerce and Industry Minister Sheikh Faisal bin Thani bin Faisal Al Thani.
📄 What's known: The communiqué says it will deepen economic cooperation and institutional ties. No further details have been released.

3️⃣ - 🎓 Agreement on Cooperation in the Field of Education
✍️ Signed by: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 National Education Minister Yusuf Tekin and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Minister of State Dr. Mohammed bin Abdulaziz Al-Khulaifi.
📄 What's known: The communiqué ties it to cooperation on setting up and running schools, teacher training, Turkish and Arabic language teaching, and student and teacher exchanges. It also floats a possible joint scholarship program between 🇹🇷 YTB and the 🇶🇦 Qatar Fund for Development for students from conflict-hit countries, which would need a separate written agreement.

4️⃣ - 🕊️ Memorandum of Understanding on Cooperation in Peace, Reconciliation and Conflict Resolution
✍️ Signed by: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 Hakan Fidan and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, between the two foreign ministries.
📄 What's known: The communiqué says it institutionalizes their mediation work through regular consultations, exchange of expertise and joint efforts on mediation, facilitation and preventive diplomacy.

5️⃣ - 📜 Joint Communiqué of the 12th Session of the Supreme Strategic Committee
✍️ Signed by: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 Fidan and 🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.
📄 What's known: The full text is public on 🇶🇦 Qatar's foreign ministry site. It covers trade, energy, defense, security, technology, culture and regional files (details below).

⚠️ On the count: Five is the official figure from 🇹🇷 Turkey's presidency, its Directorate of Communications and Anadolu, and 🇶🇦 QNA and the Amiri Diwan list the same documents. Only four are cooperation agreements, though. The fifth is the session's joint communiqué. Some outlets, including Israel Defense, described the other four as "memorandums," which isn't accurate: the defense and education texts are agreements, not MOUs.

📍 What was said:

🇹🇷 - Turkey side:

🇹🇷 👨‍💼 💡 Erdoğan, per the 🇹🇷 Turkish presidency's post on X: "President Erdogan stated that we would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the Gulf region and establish a basis for dialogue and achieve peace."

Per the 🇹🇷 Directorate of Communications, he said the Mutual Defense Agreement will add "another dimension" to the two countries' brotherhood, and that the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, in force since last year, brings them closer to their trade target. He said 🇹🇷 Turkey is working to develop and diversify its 🛢️ energy partnership with 🇶🇦 Qatar, and that defense-industry cooperation will keep growing. He also said it is important to persuade the parties to settle disputes through diplomacy. The talks also covered 🇮🇱 Israel's attacks on Gaza and the humanitarian situation, 🇸🇾 Syria's normalization steps, and the latest in 🇱🇾 Libya.

🇶🇦 - Qatar side:

🇶🇦 👨‍💼 Emir Tamim on X (English per Ynet's translation): "The strategic partnership between Qatar and Turkey continues to develop across various fields. This was reflected in the meeting of the Supreme Strategic Committee between our two countries, which I chaired in Istanbul alongside Erdoğan. During the meeting, we discussed ways to build on our achievements and set priorities for joint action in the coming period."

📍 Inside the joint communiqué:

🇹🇷🇶🇦 - Trade and 🛢️ energy: They restated a goal of 🇺🇸 $5 billion in trade "in near future." Turkish contractors have carried out 206 projects in 🇶🇦 Qatar worth 🇺🇸 $20.8 billion. They welcomed the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), signed in 2018 and in force since Aug 1, 2025. They declared readiness for "concrete energy collaborations, particularly in LNG trade." They also agreed to hold the 2nd JETCO trade committee and the 7th Joint Economic Commission in Doha.

🛡️ - Defense industry: They welcomed the Badr Memorandum signed by 🇶🇦 Qatar, 🇹🇷 Turkey, 🇵🇰 Pakistan and 🇮🇩 Indonesia, which covers joint production, technology development, information sharing and defense supply chains. Ynet and Alhurra date its signing to Oct 21, 2026, in Doha.

🛰️ - Space and tech: They welcomed the May 19, 2026, Türksat–Es'hailSat strategic partnership and the Es'hail-3/Türksat-Biruni satellite project. They also agreed on joint work in AI, quantum technology and cybersecurity, and noted a planned data-protection MOU between 🇹🇷 KVKK and 🇶🇦 Qatar's National Cyber Security Agency. That MOU is "to be signed" and is not one of the five.

👮 - Security: They pledged to keep fighting "all terrorist organizations including PKK/PYD/YPG, DAESH, FETO, and their affiliates." Hamas is not mentioned.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - US–Iran war: The conflict "must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy." They backed the 🇺🇸-🇮🇷 Memorandum of Understanding "or a new agreement," said "no country should be exposed to threats or attacks as a consequence of wider regional tensions," and called for "the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz."

☪️ - palestine and Gaza: Writing "as mediating countries, in close cooperation with" 🇪🇬 Egypt, they expressed "deep concern" that 🇮🇱 Israeli violations in Gaza undermine the UN-endorsed Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict (UNSC Resolution 2803), including its second phase, which palestinian factions have accepted. They agreed to coordinate Gaza's early recovery, reconstruction and aid. They also condemned settlement activity and settler violence in the West Bank, backed a ☪️ palestine state on the June 4, 1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital, and defended UNRWA.

🇸🇾 - Syria: They backed the 🇸🇾 Syrian government's push to stabilize the country and its reconstruction. They called for a "firm stance" to halt 🇮🇱 Israel's violations of 🇸🇾 Syrian sovereignty, respect for the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, and an 🇮🇱 Israeli withdrawal.

🇱🇧 - Lebanon: They condemned 🇮🇱 Israel's violations and called for implementing UNSC Resolution 1701. They warned against a security vacuum when UNIFIL withdraws in 2027.

🇾🇪 - Yemen: They condemned Houthi attacks on 🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia and on Red Sea shipping.

🌍 - Also covered: 🇸🇩 Sudan, 🇸🇴 Somalia and the Horn of Africa, 🇱🇾 Libya, 🇮🇶 Iraq and 🇨🇾 Cyprus.

🗓️ - Next: The 13th session will be held in 🇶🇦 Qatar in 2027.

📍 The defense angle:

🪖 - The base: Turkish troops began deploying to 🇶🇦 Qatar in 2015 under a December 2014 defense cooperation agreement, and 🇹🇷 Turkey has a military presence at the Tariq bin Ziyad base near Doha (per The New Arab). During the 2017 blockade by 🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia, 🇦🇪 UAE, 🇧🇭 Bahrain and 🇪🇬 Egypt, 🇹🇷 Ankara sped up its deployment and refused demands to close the base.

✈️ - Hardware: 🇶🇦 Qatar operates 🇹🇷 Baykar's Bayraktar TB2 armed drones (per The New Arab). A Qatari partner holds a 49.9% stake in 🇹🇷 BMC, maker of the Altay main battle tank (per Alhurra and QNA). Qatari writer Khalid bin Daham told Alhurra that 🇶🇦 Qatar bought a short-range 🇹🇷 Tolga air defense system this year and is weighing an offer for 🇹🇷 Turkey's Steel Dome air defense. That's his account, not an official one.

🔮 - What could come next: Anadolu analyst Özcan Tikit expects the cooperation to grow into missile defense, drones and armored vehicles, possibly with 🇶🇦 Qatar joining 🇹🇷 Turkish air defense projects. He stressed these are possibilities, not announced projects.

📍 The 🇺🇸 US angle:

🇺🇸 Al Udeid Air Base in 🇶🇦 Qatar remains one of the most important 🇺🇸 US military installations in the region. Analyst Nayef Al-Nabet of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs told Alhurra that 🇹🇷 Turkey would not replace 🇶🇦 Qatar's existing partners. He said the pact "expands Qatar's defense options within its existing network of partnerships."

⚖️ - The US guarantee: On Sept 29, 2025, 🇺🇸 👨‍💼 Trump signed Executive Order 14353, which treats an armed attack on 🇶🇦 Qatar as a threat to 🇺🇸 US peace and security. It is an executive order, not a ratified treaty, and it does not require an automatic 🇺🇸 deployment (per The Deep Dive).

🔍 - The test case: The Deep Dive reports that in March 2026, 🇮🇷 Iranian 🚀 missiles hit 🇶🇦 Qatar's Ras Laffan gas complex. It cites QatarEnergy as saying the strikes damaged two of its 14 LNG trains, taking out 17% of export capacity, at an estimated cost of about 🇺🇸 $20 billion a year.

📍 The 🇮🇷 Iran angle:

🇮🇷 Iran is not named in the agreement or the communiqué. Al-Nabet told Alhurra the pact "carries deterrent messages" but is "not a declaration of a new alignment against Iran." Qatar University's Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi told Al Jazeera the aim is to raise the cost of any aggression, not to form an alliance against any particular country.

Two days after the signing, 🇮🇷 IRGC claimed a six-drone attack on a 🇺🇸 air defense radar at 🇧🇭 Bahrain's Al-Riffa base (per Ynet). Damage was not independently confirmed.

📍 The 🇮🇱 Israel angle:

Israeli analysts were critical.

🇮🇱 - Dr. Yoel Guzansky (INSS, ex-National Security Council), speaking to Ynet: "Both Israel and Iran have struck Qatar. The Iranians have attacked repeatedly since February, and there has not exactly been a Turkish response." He also asked: "Why didn't they provide the Qataris with missile defense?"

🇮🇱 - Writer Yoav Stern, speaking to Alhurra, called the pact "a theoretical threat to Israel," limited by 🇶🇦 Qatar's small military. He said the flashpoint would be 🇸🇾 Syria joining a similar pact: "This is something Israel will never allow."

🇯🇴 - Retired Jordanian Maj. Gen. Mohammed Falah Al-Abadi, speaking to Alhurra, said the pact is aimed primarily "against Israel, and then Iran," and framed it as 🇶🇦 Qatari money for 🇹🇷 Turkish protection.

📍 Pattern analysis:

🔁 A growing web of pacts with 🇹🇷 Turkey at the center: the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with 🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia and 🇵🇰 Pakistan (Aug 7, 2026; an attack on one is an attack on all; ratified by 🇹🇷 Turkey's parliament in early November), the Badr defense-industry MOU (Oct 21), and now this bilateral pact. Unlike Mecca, the 🇹🇷-🇶🇦 text published so far stops short of an automatic "attack on one" clause.

🔁 Last year's session: At the 11th session in Doha on Oct 22, 2025, the two sides signed four documents: a joint declaration, a strategic development planning MOU, a joint trade ministerial statement, and a defense-industry MOU signed by 🇹🇷 SSB chief Haluk Görgün and 🇶🇦 Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. This year's session moves from defense-industry cooperation to a mutual defense commitment.

🔁 The track record: Since the first session in 2015, the two countries have signed more than 120 agreements (per QNA via ILoveQatar). The committee meets every year and alternates between the two countries.

🔁 Trade lags the politics: 🇹🇷 👨‍💼 Bolat puts 2025 bilateral trade at 🇺🇸 $1.3 billion (per QNA via ILoveQatar), while a 🇹🇷 Turkish Trade Ministry country brief says 🇺🇸 $1.1 billion. Either way it's far below the 🇺🇸 $5 billion target, and below the roughly 🇺🇸 $2.5 billion peak around the 2022 World Cup. About 250 Qatari companies operate in 🇹🇷 Turkey with 🇺🇸 $7.8 billion invested, and about 1,116 Turkish companies are active in 🇶🇦 Qatar.

📍 What it means:

🇹🇷 - For Turkey: 💡 Ankara gets a formal security role in the 🌍 Gulf on top of its troops in Doha, a deep-pocketed partner for its defense industry, and another node in a network it anchors (Mecca, Badr, Qatar). It also takes on a new commitment to a state that 🇮🇷 Iran has already struck this year.

🇶🇦 - For Qatar: 🇶🇦 Doha hedges. It keeps the 🇺🇸 umbrella and Al Udeid, but after being hit by both 🇮🇱 Israel (2025) and 🇮🇷 Iran (2026), it adds a second named defender that is also a NATO member. Because 🇶🇦 Qatar isn't in NATO, an attack on it would not trigger NATO's Article 5.

🎯 - The open question: Until the text is published, the pact is mainly a deterrence signal. Whether 🇹🇷 Turkey would actually fight for 🇶🇦 Qatar, and how that would fit with 🇺🇸 CENTCOM's plans for Al Udeid, is unanswered.

🗓️ - Watch for: publication of the defense agreement's text, whether it goes to 🇹🇷 Turkey's parliament for ratification, any 🇶🇦 Qatari order for Steel Dome or other air defense, joint exercises, and reactions from 🇺🇸 Washington, 🇮🇷 Tehran and 🇮🇱 Jerusalem.

QESHM BLASTS REPORTED, KERCH BRIDGE TRAFFIC HALTED, HORMUZ TANKER CREW UNACCOUNTED FOR

World Conflict Live 24/7 | Morning situation report | Tuesday, November 17, 2026
Good morning. This report covers Monday’s developments and the updates received through 10:43 a.m. Eastern today.
IRAN | QESHM AND MISSILE ACTIVITY

@hey_itsmyturn reported 6 explosions on Qeshm Island in southern Iran’s Hormozgan Province. A separate report said U.S. forces struck an air defense site in Nariman. Iranian media later reported a U.S. strike on an Iranian air defense missile launcher in the Nariman area.

@hey_itsmyturn subsequently reported 5 powerful explosions in Qeshm city and said the blasts may have occurred at the Nariman air defense site.
The same account reported a ballistic missile launch from Urmia, in West Azerbaijan Province, at 12:25 UTC (7:25 a.m. Eastern). It also reported 5 missiles launched from Omidiyeh and a ballistic missile launch from Kouye Ramezan in Ahvaz, both in Khuzestan Province.

In another Omidiyeh report, @hey_itsmyturn said a missile launched at 15:21 UTC (10:21 a.m. Eastern) headed south.

Earlier Tuesday, @hey_itsmyturn reported a column of smoke in western Tehran at 06:09 UTC and 2 missiles launched from the 15 Khordad Garrison in Isfahan at 07:16 UTC. It also reported jets heard in Ahvaz and intense anti-aircraft activity in Ramhormoz.

On Monday, the same account reported 2 missile launches from Haftkal, at 8:01 a.m. and 3:18 p.m. Eastern. The first missile’s destination remained unclear. The account also reported anti-aircraft fire along the Andimeshk-to-Ahvaz road, intense air defense activity in Ramhormoz and jet activity over western Tehran. What prompted the Ramhormoz activity was unclear, as were the aircraft’s identity and the reason for the Tehran activity.

A report attributed to Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency said air defenses were activated in Isfahan on Monday.

Iran International reported that bread rationing took effect Tuesday in parts of Iran. Separately, i24NEWS said Israel’s security cabinet was told Sunday that gas shortages could leave Iranian families struggling to heat their homes this winter. Reuters cited Iran’s national gas company as saying wartime damage to 4 processing plants had worsened the shortage. Whether the shortage will trigger protests remains unclear.

STRAIT OF HORMUZ | TANKER ATTACKS AND TALKS

In Update 001 to Warning 208-26, UK Maritime Trade Operations said a maritime security agency reported that a tanker was struck a second time, starting a fire on board. The crew is now unaccounted for, and the extent of the damage is unknown.

UKMTO listed 2 p.m. Eastern as the time of Monday’s third-party report from about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. It described a disabled tanker and an engine-room fire. The crew was reported safe at the time. Damage and any environmental impact were unknown. UKMTO advised caution while authorities investigated.

@Osint613 reported a large plume of smoke rising from a tanker hit Monday, about 13 kilometers north of Khasab. The account attributed that strike to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.
In Warning 207-26, UKMTO said an unidentified projectile hit a tanker leaving the strait at 12:58 a.m. Eastern Monday, sparking an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, and no casualties were reported. Damage and any environmental impact were unclear. UKMTO urged caution and asked vessels to report suspicious activity.

Warning 209-26 concerns a November 13 strike. UKMTO said it received a delayed, verified report that an unidentified projectile hit a tanker heading east through the Arabian Gulf before it entered the strait. All crew members are safe and accounted for. Damage and any environmental impact remain unknown.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed Monday that 2 more oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines on the southern route through the strait. It put the number of tanker fires since Sunday at 6. Its statement gave no vessel names or crew details.

Iran’s regular navy made a separate claim Monday, relayed by @Osint613. It described a fourth tanker fire in 24 hours and said the ship was badly damaged after hitting a mine east of the strait. It claimed the vessel had switched off its navigation systems in waters Iran calls restricted.

On Tuesday, Iran’s navy claimed another tanker caught fire and sustained severe damage after hitting a mine east of the strait. It said the ship had switched off its navigation systems and violated Iran’s maritime restrictions. The report described video of an intense fire and called the vessel a total loss.

Fars News separately reported that Iran’s navy described a third tanker fire on Tuesday after a mine strike east of the strait. The navy claimed that vessel had also violated Iran’s maritime restrictions.

@hey_itsmyturn also reported a blast in the strait on Monday. Its exact location and cause remained unclear.

Iranian Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia said the strait would remain closed until Washington accepts Iran’s terms. He warned of a stronger response to renewed attacks and previously claimed Iran controls the strait and could retaliate beyond the region.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi left Islamabad for Muscat on Monday evening after talks with Pakistani officials. They said they were awaiting Washington’s response to Iran’s reopening proposal. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that a planned meeting will focus on existing proposals and ways to narrow the differences between Tehran and Washington.

UKRAINE AND RUSSIA | KERCH BRIDGE, STRIKES AND AIR DEFENSE

Tuesday’s reports say part of the Kerch Bridge, which links Russia to occupied Crimea, fell into the strait after a second attack in 24 hours damaged the road arch. Both road and rail traffic have been halted.

The Kremlin’s initial Monday account described minor damage after a Ukrainian drone strike and said road traffic briefly stopped while trains kept running. No injuries were reported. Russian occupation authorities in Crimea later confirmed another overnight strike. Other reports said a span was gone and more than 15 strikes had been observed.

A report received at 9:55 p.m. Eastern Monday described a large-scale Ukrainian missile and drone attack still underway. It said at least 10 cruise missiles and 25 drones had struck the bridge.

Late Monday, reports described a major ballistic missile attack on Ukraine. Kyiv Mayor Klitschko said Russian strikes hit the city’s Northern and Southern bridges. A separate report named Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Zircon hypersonic missiles in a strike on a Kyiv bridge.
Ukraine’s defense forces said Tuesday that Russia launched ballistic, cruise and guided aircraft missiles in an overnight attack, along with 306 attack drones and decoys, including 92 jet-powered Shaheds.

Ukraine said it shot down or suppressed 211 targets, including 205 drones, 3 Kh-59 or Kh-69 missiles and 3 Banderol or Dan-T targets. Hits were recorded at 44 locations. The status of cruise missiles and 60 more drones was still being checked.

In Dnipro, a Russian drone hit a roadway Monday morning and set cars on fire, according to regional officials. 1 person was killed. Officials first reported 10 injuries, with all 10 hospitalized. 2 men, ages 26 and 47, were in serious condition. The reported injury count later rose to 13. Apartment buildings and vehicles were also damaged.

DTEK said Russian strikes on energy facilities cut power across Dnipro. Crews prioritized electricity for water and heating systems and essential public facilities. A separate strike set fire to the Oleina sunflower oil plant. Its U.S. owner, Bunge, confirmed the strike, said no employees were injured and temporarily suspended operations at the plant.

In Komyshuvakha, Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, crews ended a two-week search after the November 2 Russian airstrike on a school where residents had gathered for humanitarian aid. The confirmed death toll stands at 72. Those killed included rescue workers, police, medical staff, utility workers and school staff, including a teacher who gave online lessons from the shelter to children who had evacuated.

4 people remain missing and 4 are still hospitalized. Ukraine’s Interior Ministry said Russian forces struck the search site 9 times during the operation, injuring 3 police officers and 4 rescuers.

Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down a record 2,049 Ukrainian drones over 24 hours and intercepted 4 long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 7 guided bombs. Early reports put the size of a later Ukrainian drone wave at more than 400, an unverified figure. Moscow Mayor Sobyanin said 142 drones were shot down during a heavy attack on the capital. All Moscow airports were reported closed at the time.

In Russia’s Rostov region, the governor said an overnight Ukrainian drone attack set fires at 4 industrial sites in Azov. 3 men were hospitalized. ASTRA reviewed footage and located one fire near 2 oil depots. A separate report said Ukrainian forces hit the Ilsky refinery’s AT-4, AT-5 and AT-6 oil processing units and its gasoline production complex. Ilsky can process about 6.6 million tons of oil a year.

Salavat residents reported an attack and a fire late Monday at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan. A report Tuesday attributed a strike there to Ukrainian forces and placed the facility about 1,500 kilometers from the border. The complex can process about 10 million tons of oil a year and makes gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, lubricants and other products used by Russia’s economy and military.

Another report said Ukrainian strikes have disabled more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity and hit 15 refineries in 19 days, including 7 of the largest. It said Russia is shifting refining to more distant plants, whose capacity and transport limits leave them unable to meet demand, and using reserves to cover part of the shortfall.

Russian media now report 17 deaths after a military An-12 crashed near Kemerovo while flying from Novosibirsk to Kansk. Earlier local reports put the death toll at 13.

BLACK SEA | GAS HUSKY CREW RESCUED

All 19 Filipino crew members of the motor tanker GAS HUSKY (IMO 9507764) were rescued off Bulgaria. The crew was reported in generally good condition, with 2 minor injuries. The captain said 4 drones struck shortly after midnight, hitting the engine room and the ship’s bridge.

The first report said the tanker sank after a drone strike in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The latest report describes it as lying overturned about 50 nautical miles east of Byala. The ship was carrying 3,403 metric tons of propane from Egypt to the Romanian port of Midia.

Bulgarian military aircraft, a Cougar helicopter and rescue teams were sent to search for the crew. The initial report described this as the sixth vessel hit in the region in 48 hours.

A separate rescue operation was reported Monday after the crew of BETUL 8 said their ship was sinking about 40 nautical miles southeast of Bulgaria’s Cape Kaliakra. Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry said the Somali-flagged ship was taking wheat from Romania to Egypt and had 12 crew members aboard.

Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey sent 4 ships, and Bulgarian aircraft joined the search. Bulgarian broadcaster bTV reported that the crew took to life rafts. Their condition and the cause of the emergency remained unclear.
Romania advised ships to avoid an area off the Danube Delta after drones struck 3 commercial vessels near the Sulina Canal late Saturday. Officials said 2 were hit in Romanian territorial waters. No casualties were reported. Maritime advisory 172/2026 took effect November 15 and remains in force. Transit is permitted, and the Defense Ministry recommends routing around the area because of airborne and floating objects approaching from the north.

A French Navy Atlantique 2 patrol aircraft spotted 2 drones drifting off Romania’s coast on November 15 during a NATO deterrence mission. Romania sent 2 Navy bomb disposal teams. One was checking for explosives from a Coast Guard vessel about 45 nautical miles east of Mangalia. The second was on a minesweeper heading toward Sfântu Gheorghe. That drone was first seen about 53 nautical miles east of Chituc. The drones’ origin remains unclear.

ELSEWHERE IN EUROPE

Near Belgrade, a Serbian Air Force MiG-29 crashed in a field between Nova Pazova and Stara Pazova around 8:45 a.m. local time. Serbia’s Defense Ministry identified the pilot who died as Maj. Goran Bulajić. The cause is under investigation.

In Prague, 2 passenger trains collided at low speed near the city’s main railway station Tuesday morning. 4 people were seriously injured, and about 42 others suffered minor injuries.

AFP reported that North Macedonia says it thwarted what it described as an Iran-linked terror plot in Greece.

U.S.–IRAN MILITARY AND SECURITY DEVELOPMENTS

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claims its drones struck a U.S. military radar system at Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain early Tuesday. It described the strike as retaliation for alleged U.S. drone incursions into Iranian airspace. In a separate claim, it says its air defenses shot down a U.S. LUCAS one-way attack drone near the Strait of Hormuz.

On Monday, the Guard’s navy claimed it captured a U.S. MQM-170 intact south of Qeshm Island. It said an electronic warfare unit took over the guidance system and landed it. The Guard said the drone had been monitoring air defense and electronic warfare systems and called it the unit’s fourth capture of that model and its forces’ eighth intact capture near the strait.

The Guard separately claimed it shot down a U.S. Army MQ-1C Gray Eagle over Qeshm Island. Iranian state broadcaster IRIB aired footage it said showed the interception.

U.S. Central Command confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) is operating in its area of responsibility. i24NEWS reported that the carrier’s arrival brings the U.S. aircraft carrier count in the Middle East to 3 and put the number of U.S. troops in the region at about 53,000.

The U.S. Army is seeking 17 reinforced concrete bunkers to replace converted shipping containers used as troop shelters. It plans 10 for Israel, 5 for Saudi Arabia and 2 for Lebanon. The shelters are intended to offer better protection against indirect fire, including blasts from nearby missile and drone strikes.

The Army wants each order completed within 45 calendar days of award and expects contractors to have 3 days to quote once a formal request is issued. The Pentagon has recorded 23 U.S. service member deaths in operations tied to the Iran war, attributing 11 to enemy fire and classifying 12 as nonhostile.

CNN cited 7 U.S. officials on Monday as saying intelligence suggested Iran was exploring ways to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C., with options including a dirty bomb or chemical weapon. CNN said the intelligence identified possible locations and targets and prompted U.S. contingency planning. Officials were divided over Iran’s ability or intent to act.

The White House said it was monitoring potential threats and that there were no credible threats to the homeland at the time. Iran’s U.N. mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations. On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the CNN report a “fabricated media narrative.” He also rejected a separate New York Times report suggesting some Iranian dams could help supply underground missile bases.

Separately, @Osint613 reported that a news channel affiliated with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard published a threat against Hoover Dam in the United States.

YEMEN, SAUDI ARABIA, LEBANON, GAZA AND IRAQ

Local sources told Al Arabiya English they heard 3 blasts near al-Hafa military camp in Sanaa and another on Mount Nuqum. They also reported explosions at Houthi barracks in Bani Jarmuz, in the Bani al-Harith district. At Beit Dahrah camp, sources said they heard explosions after airstrikes targeted fortifications, tunnels and weapons depots.

The Saudi-led coalition says air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi-launched drone in the Riyadh area Tuesday. A statement attributed to the coalition on Monday said air defenses intercepted and destroyed 2 Houthi drones in the Makkah and Riyadh regions.

Israel’s military said its air force hit a weapons shipment bound for Hezbollah overnight near Janta, in eastern Lebanon’s Beqaa Valley. It said the shipment crossed from Syria through an area previously used to move weapons to Hezbollah. Lebanese media described it as the first Israeli strike there in several months. Lebanon’s National News Agency reported no injuries. In southern Lebanon, @Osint613 cited Lebanese reports of a strike on Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh area.

U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz urged Hezbollah to hand over its weapons voluntarily during a Monday visit to Beirut. “No country can have two armies,” he said. Waltz met Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to discuss what follows the U.N. peacekeeping operation. Its mandate expires December 31, and withdrawal is scheduled through 2027.

Waltz said Washington expects U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which helped end the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, to stay in force with some amendments.

In Gaza, Israel’s military said it demolished a 300-meter tunnel in an area it controls near the Yellow Line. It said its Harel Brigade found the tunnel during an operation to dismantle Hamas tunnels and other infrastructure.

An explosion was reported in Erbil Governorate in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region on Monday morning. Separately, Reuters cited 2 security sources as saying sirens sounded at the Khor Mor gas field after a drone flew over the facility. Iraq and Jordan also banned Telegram on Monday, citing national security, extremist content, cybercrime and other illegal activity.

UNITED STATES | NSA NET OUTAGE, TRAVEL AND LOCAL UPDATES

CNN, citing 6 sources familiar with the matter, reported an outage on the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network, NSA Net. The agency uses it to exchange classified information. CNN reported that there was no evidence of a cyberattack at that point and that the NSA staggered staff arrivals while investigating.

By about 8 a.m. Eastern Monday, FlightAware counted 18,531 flight cancellations and 28,560 delays since Friday, a total of 47,091 disruptions from multiple causes. Reuters later said U.S. air travel had largely returned to normal after Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, with more than 18,000 cancellations and nearly 28,000 delays over 3 days.

United Airlines experienced a separate systemwide IT and operational problem that held up departures Monday. The airline later said it had resolved the issue.

In the Bronx, 2 police officers and a civilian were reportedly shot. Initial reports described the suspect as barricaded and the victims’ conditions as unclear. A later update said the suspect had died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound and all 3 victims were expected to survive.

New York City announced it was disbanding the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced a civilian Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division. Its members will be unarmed, have no arrest powers, speak with demonstrators and coordinate with police.

While the civilian division is being set up, 30 uniformed officers will handle dialogue and de-escalation. A separate patrol unit will support crowd management and make arrests when needed. The reforms ban tear gas, long guns and kettling, a tactic that confines protesters to a limited area.
In Columbia, Missouri, a bomb threat around 5:30 p.m. Central Sunday led to the evacuation of about 40 to 50 workers at the Kraft Heinz plant on Waco Road. Police and bomb-detection dogs searched the building and found no explosives. Workers returned around 10 p.m. Central.

No injuries were reported. The investigation remained open Monday, with no suspects in custody. Local station 93.9 The Eagle reported that the plant is the only facility in North America that makes Oscar Mayer hot dogs.

Downdetector logged more than 2,000 reports about Chase by 11:04 a.m. Eastern Monday. Customers reported problems signing in and viewing balances or transactions. Plaid confirmed disruptions to its Chase connections.

Trackers also logged issues involving Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One and TD Bank. One tracker showed 59 reports about U.S. Bank and 113 about Capital One in separate hourly snapshots. TD Bank users reported trouble signing in and using the app. The extent of the problems at the other 5 banks remained unclear.

In Michigan, a report described boycott calls by veterans and gun owners over comments by Fenix Ammunition owner Justin Nazaroff. It said he questioned veterans’ benefits and tax breaks, compared military service risks with logging, fishing and roofing, and accused troops of fighting for defense contractors. The report described derogatory remarks about veterans and Gold Star widows and inflammatory comments about U.S. troops, race and Jewish people.

The report said Nazaroff also posted what it described as a Nazi salute and threatened to shoot military recruiters if they came to his home to force him into a war involving Israel. Critics pointed to pandemic loans received by his company, some of which were forgiven. Fenix sells to customers who include veterans and has sought business from police departments.

Thanks for following along this morning. Have a good Tuesday, and we’ll see what the day brings.

— World Conflict Live 24/7 | @WCLNews247

text:
The American Identity We Share
NooGenesis 2028
Live Together or Die Alone

We should never have to apologize for who we are. But neither should we define ourselves primarily by who we are not.

America has always been a nation of different people, cultures, religions, and traditions. Our diversity is part of our history, but it is not the whole of our identity.

What makes us Americans is something greater than our differences: a shared commitment to liberty, individual dignity, equal rights, and the constitutional principles that allow us to live together as one nation.

Our history has never been perfect. Slavery, segregation, and discrimination are undeniable chapters of the American story. But so are emancipation, civil rights, integration, and generations of Americans who worked to bring our country closer to its founding ideals.

We should remember both.

We inherit our history. We do not inherit its conclusions.

Today, too much of our political culture encourages us to see one another through competing identities: race, gender, religion, ancestry, and political allegiance.

We are encouraged to remember what divides us while too often forgetting what unites us.

But no American should inherit guilt because of their race, nor should anyone's opportunities or dignity be limited by the circumstances of their birth.

We can be proud of our heritage without making it a barrier between ourselves and our fellow Americans.

We can acknowledge historical injustice without surrendering our belief in progress.

We can celebrate our differences without allowing those differences to define our future.

Unity does not require uniformity. It requires a shared commitment to the freedom of others as well as ourselves.

This is the unfinished promise of the American experiment.

Our Constitution provides the framework. Individual liberty provides the foundation. And our willingness to recognize mistakes, learn from reality, and take responsibility for what comes next determines whether that promise continues to grow.

We are not destined to repeat the divisions of the past.

We have the freedom to choose something better.

Different backgrounds. Shared principles. One American future.

Live Together or Die Alone.

Liberty • Responsibility • Reality

text:
Trump – Xi and Putin at APEC: Nuclear Restraint and the Limits of Summit Diplomacy 
The most defensible positive outcome from Shenzhen is a mandate for sustained nuclear-risk negotiations; a comprehensive trilateral treaty would require substantial changes in publicly documented negotiating positions.

China has acknowledged the three-leader meeting, but its official account does not establish a detailed agreed agenda or negotiated deliverables. https://t.co/OAGgO7EP8d

New START expired on 5 February 2026. Its replacement requires a new agreement; its existing extension provision had already been exhausted. https://t.co/OvoUlyDV9h

Beijing reiterated in October that participation in trilateral nuclear-disarmament negotiations was unacceptable at the present stage. https://t.co/j0UuhSbnCW

Ukraine presents a separate implementation problem: three leaders cannot supply Ukrainian consent, European commitments or NATO accession by agreement among themselves.

European governments should assess any outcome against published mandates, verification provisions, participating authorities and implementation milestones.

The decisive uncertainty is whether political contact produces an authorised negotiating process with identifiable technical work and follow-up dates.

Shenzhen’s Real Test Is Whether Governments Can Deliver What Leaders Promise
The meeting involving US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin around the Shenzhen APEC summit should be judged by the commitments their governments can execute, not the breadth of their declarations. As of 17 November 2026, nuclear restraint, a Ukrainian settlement and European security guarantees depend on different authorities, resources and negotiating conditions. Treating them as one bargain risks exchanging immediate concessions for obligations that remain unfunded, legally unresolved or outside the negotiator’s control. Europe’s response should connect diplomatic participation to industrial delivery, national authorisation and sustained support for Ukraine. Otherwise, a summit announcement could reduce political pressure to act before it reduces the security risks that governments, manufacturers and public budgets must continue to carry.

A mandate would matter more than a promise of disarmament
New START’s expiration on 5 February 2026 removed a contractual framework for interpreting strategic forces as well as limiting them. Its ceilings depended on agreed definitions, declarations and verification procedures. Reintroducing a familiar number without its accounting rules would create the appearance of continuity while potentially regulating something different. Each deployed nuclear-capable heavy bomber counted as one warhead under New START, whereas deployed ballistic missiles were counted according to their actual warheads. That distinction makes counting rules a substantive negotiating issue, not technical housekeeping. The US Senate’s examination of New START shows why a political endorsement of restraint cannot substitute for an agreement about what restraint means.

China’s statement of 16 October 2026 rejected trilateral nuclear-disarmament negotiations at the present stage. Attendance at a leaders’ meeting would therefore not establish acceptance of arsenal reductions. A useful initial outcome would identify authorised delegations, defined subjects and subsequent meetings, allowing practical risk-reduction measures to develop without pretending that a comprehensive limitation framework already exists. The governing test is whether the process generates usable information or changes conduct. A meeting that merely schedules another meeting leaves the underlying planning uncertainty intact. China’s official negotiating position makes that distinction unavoidable.

The financial figures expose different obligations, not a common European war chest
France’s amended military programming provides a funding trajectory, while Germany’s parliamentary budget account describes proposed expenditure and Britain’s nuclear-enterprise figures cover a specialised national system. France’s updated mission Défense programming rises from €57.1 billion in 2026 to €75.7 billion in 2030, in current euros, excluding pensions and on a constant perimeter. Germany’s September first-reading account of the 2027 budget describes €109.7 billion in the regular defence budget and €29.9 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund, totalling €139.6 billion. These figures establish different financial decisions and stages; neither demonstrates completed capability. France’s amended programming law and the Bundestag’s budget account cannot be turned into a readiness ranking by placing their totals side by side.

Britain’s Defence Investment Plan provides £63.6 billion for the Defence Nuclear Enterprise over financial years 2026–27 to 2029–30. The enterprise reports more than 47,000 personnel and workforce demand expected to reach approximately 65,000 by 2030. At EU level, SAFE’s €150 billion loan envelope contained a €21.3 billion second call announced on 29 October 2026; almost €13.5 billion had been disbursed as prefinancing across 11 member states. The second call is part of the envelope, and prefinancing is not equipment delivery. These distinctions expose the real constraint: money must pass through national decisions, contracts, production, acceptance and sustainment before it can support an operational undertaking. The British investment answer and the Commission’s SAFE implementation record describe commitments whose practical effects arrive on different schedules.

Procurement decides whether European influence becomes usable power
The additional French SAMP/T NG order announced by OCCAR on 21 October 2026 illustrates the transmission mechanism. The programme links France and Italy through cooperative procurement, with EUROSAM responsible for the contracted systems. An order establishes demand and contractual responsibility; it does not establish the availability of the additional systems for an immediate security mission. Governments must still connect equipment to trained personnel, maintenance, interceptors and replenishment. If diplomatic commitments assume that these elements arrive together, procurement delay becomes a security exposure rather than merely a programme-management problem. OCCAR’s contract announcement supports an industrial commitment, not a claim of additional operational readiness.

Italy’s presidency of the Tallinn Mechanism offers a different contribution to the same problem of sustained implementation. The Rome declaration published on 30 October 2026 emphasised civilian cyber resilience, local infrastructure and cooperation with implementing partners. Such projects can preserve essential functions through negotiation and reconstruction, but installation without maintenance ownership creates another form of incomplete capability. Rome’s influence will depend on projects that remain effective after its rotating presidency ends, just as Berlin’s financial expansion must produce accepted equipment and London’s nuclear programmes must secure qualified personnel. The Tallinn Mechanism’s Rome declaration places continuity of delivery alongside the allocation of resources.

Consent prevents a three-leader bargain from becoming a European settlement
Ukraine’s Constitution makes territorial commitments more demanding than an exchange of presidential assurances. Article 73 assigns questions concerning changes to Ukrainian territory exclusively to an all-Ukrainian referendum, while Article 157 restricts constitutional amendments directed against territorial integrity and prohibits constitutional amendment under martial law or a state of emergency. These provisions do not make every operational ceasefire equivalent to a territorial transfer. They require the proposed instrument to distinguish where forces stop from what happens to sovereignty. A referendum provision is not a general licence for any concession, and a foreign government’s endorsement cannot resolve the constitutional requirements of the affected state. Ukraine’s referendum provision and its amendment restrictions therefore constrain the content and sequence of a settlement.

The Paris Declaration of 6 January 2026 also distinguishes ceasefire monitoring, continued support for Ukraine’s armed forces and a multinational contribution to regeneration and deterrence. These functions cannot be merged into a generic guarantee. Monitoring may document a breach without providing the authority or capability to stop it; a reassurance force may have a military task without adjudicating compliance. The declaration’s reference to national legal and constitutional arrangements reinforces the implementation constraint: collective language requires decisions by the governments expected to act. The Paris Declaration is consequently a framework for responsibilities that must be made executable, rather than proof that protection is already operational.

Europe’s leverage lies in decisions the summit participants cannot make for it
The European Council’s proposed negotiating team, outlined on 13 November 2026, comprises EU institutions alongside France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. Its importance lies in connecting negotiations to the authorities expected to provide resources and accept obligations. The proposal does not establish that every other negotiating participant has accepted that format, nor does a smaller European team eliminate the need for wider national decisions. Representation becomes consequential when it prevents promises being made about European contributions before their providers have agreed to them. The European Council’s account describes coordination intended to bridge that gap.

European sanctions demonstrate the same boundary of authority. The Council adopted additional listings on 16 November 2026 while diplomatic efforts continued; those measures did not disappear because another government might prefer a wider political exchange. Any proposed relief must identify the restrictions concerned, the competent decision-maker and the conduct expected in return. Linking sanctions, territorial terms and nuclear restraint can widen bargaining space, but it also increases the number of decisions that can fail to align. Europe should resist an arrangement in which it is expected to deliver a legal or financial concession against a reciprocal promise that remains outside the other negotiator’s control. The Council’s sanctions decision shows that economic pressure remains a separate policy instrument.

The next two years will reveal who has mistaken commitments for capacity
Over the 12–24 months following November 2026, the decisive evidence will come from implemented measures: working crisis procedures, accepted security responsibilities, sustained Ukrainian support and procurement milestones that produce maintainable capability. SAFE prefinancing, French military programming, Germany’s budget proposals and Britain’s Defence Nuclear Enterprise plans must each be assessed against their own intended outputs. A useful summit process would survive disagreement and produce corrections when implementation fails. An ineffective one would allow broad declarations to coexist with unresolved obligations while governments continue to credit themselves with progress.

The cost of inaction would fall first on Ukraine if protection and assistance remain conditional while its exposure persists. European armed forces would carry the operational cost where commitments exceed available capacity; public budgets would carry the cost of programmes that require correction, prolonged support or replenishment; manufacturers and specialist suppliers would face procurement schedules that do not match the political promises built upon them. For the Paris Declaration and Europe’s procurement instruments, the choice is whether to establish accountable, sustained implementation now or leave those costs to accumulate behind an announcement. Shenzhen can initiate a more predictable security relationship. It cannot supply Ukrainian consent, European authorisation or industrial delivery by declaration.

Of all the times and dates a baby could choose to arrive, J'Aime Brown seemed determined to make one number impossible to forget: 7-Eleven. 😂👶

The Missouri baby was born on July 11, 2019 — 7/11 — at exactly 7:11 p.m.

Then nurses put her on the scale.

She weighed 7 pounds, 11 ounces.

Her mother, Rachel Langford, told reporters that she had already noticed the numbers 7 and 11 repeatedly appearing during her pregnancy. She would sometimes look at the clock and see 7:11, but she never imagined the coincidence would continue all the way into the delivery room.

Once the story spread, it inevitably reached .

The company initially celebrated J'Aime's remarkably on-brand arrival with gifts for the family.

Then it took the coincidence one step further.

7-Eleven pledged $7,111 toward J'Aime's future college education. The company also provided diapers and other baby supplies, turning an already unforgettable birth story into something that could benefit her years later.

And there was another sweet detail: July 11 is already a special day for the convenience-store chain. In the United States, 7/11 is traditionally "7-Eleven Day," when participating stores celebrate the brand's birthday and have historically offered customers free Slurpees.

So J'Aime managed an almost absurd numerical hat trick:

Born on 7/11.
At 7:11 p.m.
Weighing 7 lbs., 11 oz.
Then receiving $7,111 for college. 🎉

Some babies arrive with a good story.

J'Aime arrived with what looks like a sponsorship deal written into the universe. 😂❤️

Sources: CNN; BBC News; USA Today; 7-Eleven; contemporary reporting from Missouri.

Subject: Building Diplomatic Relations and Strategic Partnerships with the Republic of Balochistan: An Invitation to International Recognition and Cooperation

Your Excellency,
Filipinos launched the 1896 revolution against Spanish rule, with figures like José Rizal and Andrés Bonifacio, and declared independence in 1898. They resisted American rule, endured Japanese occupation, and achieved full independence in 1946, then ended dictatorship through the 1986 People Power Revolution.
We admire the Philippines' People Power Revolution and the resilience of its people. Balochistan extends its warm friendship.
Southeast Asia’s great trading tradition and Balochistan’s Arabian Sea coast are natural partners on the Indian Ocean’s maritime routes.

The history of Balochistan
Balochistan is not a newcomer to sovereignty. The Khanate of Kalat held a distinct treaty relationship with the British Crown (1876) and was never part of British India’s princely states. On 4 August 1947, at a round-table meeting in Delhi attended by Lord Mountbatten, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and the Khan of Kalat, Mir Ahmad Yar Khan, it was agreed that Kalat (Balochistan) would become an independent sovereign state with a status different from that of the Indian princely states.
On 11 August 1947, three days before Pakistan came into being, Balochistan declared its independence from British rule. The announcement was published in the New York Times and broadcast by All India Radio on 12 August 1947. A standstill agreement with the new Dominion of Pakistan followed.
Kalat’s bicameral parliament, the Dar-ul-Awam (House of commons) and the Dar-ul-Umara (House of lords), unanimously rejected accession to Pakistan when it met in December 1947 and February 1948. On 27 March 1948 Pakistan illegally invaded and annexed Balochistan. The Baloch have never regarded this as a free act: the Khan and Jinnah were photographed together on other occasions, yet not a single photograph of the signing of the accession instrument has been published, which is consistent with our position that it was never a mutual agreement.

Since 1948 the Baloch people have continued to assert their right to independence and sovereignty, through political action, diplomatic manners and, at times, defensive armed resistance (1948, 1958, 1962, 1973–77 and since the early 2000s). Millions of Baloch, scattered across the globe but united in purpose, are raising one voice under the leadership of Hyrbyair Marri, President of the Free Balochistan Movement. They call on the nations of the world to recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state, a recognition it has earned and rightfully deserves.
The Baloch nation has long suffered the plunder of its resources, enforced disappearances, ethnic cleansing, and relentless repression by Pakistan. Across the western part of Balochistan, the Baloch people face the same fate under Iranian rule: fabricated encounters, mass executions, expulsion from their own land, and the denial of birth certificates and legal identity, a deliberate effort to erase their existence.

The significance of Balochistan
Balochistan sits where South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East meet, on the Arabian Sea coast just outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil passes. It is a natural gateway for global trade. Two globally important deep-sea ports lie on the Baloch coast: Chabahar, which is under Iran’s illegal rule, and Gwadar, which is under Pakistan’s unlawful rule. Beneath the land lie Balochistan’s mineral resources include copper, gold, chromite, coal, natural gas, lead, zinc, barite, iron ore, limestone, gypsum, marble, granite, onyx, magnesite, sulphur, fluorite, antimony, manganese, bauxite, celestite, rock salt, silica sand, fuller’s earth, lapis lazuli, agate, and reported traces of uranium and rare earth elements of strategic value, including the Reko Diq and Saindak deposits and the Sui gas field.
Because the Republic of Balochistan declared independence on 11 August 1947, we, the Baloch, consider ourselves independent. A free, Secular, democratic and stable Balochistan is vital for regional and global peace and for connectivity between the Indian Ocean and the heartland of Eurasia.

Balochistan offers: Building Partnerships for Peace, Security, and Sustainable Development

The Philippines faces maritime pressure in the South China Sea, typhoons and floods, and insurgent and extremist groups in the south. A free, stable Balochistan, as an Indian Ocean coastal state committed to freedom of navigation and the rule of law at sea, proposes cooperation in maritime security and coast-guard training, disaster-response and early-warning experience, and the sharing of lessons in counter-extremism and community reconciliation. We hope in this way to contribute to peace, security and connectivity in the region.

The Republic of Balochistan offers your country:
•Maritime security: training and information-sharing between two archipelagic and coastal peoples, and Mindanao–Balochistan peace-building exchange.
•Maritime security: cooperation on anti-piracy, anti-smuggling and coast-guard training along the Arabian Sea and the wider Indian Ocean.
•Climate resilience: cooperation on drought, flood and water management, and on renewable energy.
•Countering extremism: as a Secular state with deep Secular and tribal traditions of tolerance, Balochistan offers intelligence-sharing, joint training and a model for countering radicalisation. 

Our request
On behalf of the Republic of Balochistan, we respectfully ask your Government to:
1.Recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state and establish diplomatic relations;
https://t.co/HiRWcoQDnP appropriate observer-level engagement for Balochistan at the United Nations and, in line with each Organization’s own procedures, at the European Union, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the African Union.
3.Stand with the Baloch in nation-building: education, health, infrastructure, technology, defense and security.
The commitments in this letter are those of the Republic of Balochistan as it takes up the effective exercise of sovereignty over its territory and resources; we make them in good faith so that your Government can plan with us from the outset.
Partnership with Balochistan is of real benefit to your country and to the world. We would welcome the opportunity to meet your representatives at the earliest convenience.

With our highest consideration,
THE REPUBLIC OF BALOCHISTAN

Mir Yar Baloch
Representative for the Republic of Balochistan

text:
The passengers of an American airliner, Delta Flight 15, tried to pay the small Canadian town that fed and sheltered them after 9/11. The town refused every dollar.

So on the flight home they passed pledge sheets through the cabin, and by the time the jet landed in Atlanta they had promised about $15,000 to the town's children.

Flight 15 left Frankfurt, Germany, for Atlanta on September 11, 2001, with 218 passengers. When the United States closed its airspace, the jet became one of 38 airliners sent down to Gander, Newfoundland.

Nobody could get off at first. The passengers sat inside the parked plane for about 27 hours.

Then buses carried them 45 kilometers north to Lewisporte, a town of about 4,000 people that suddenly had 773 stranded strangers to look after.

The travelers had no rooms, so the town opened its schools, churches and community halls. One passenger, Shirley Brooks-Jones of Columbus, Ohio, slept on an army cot at the Lions Club.

Some had left their medicine on the plane. Residents delivered prescriptions and drove the sick to local doctors.

The town bakery worked overtime to keep up with the bread. People handed out laundry tokens, donated towels, blankets, baby food and toys, and local fishermen offered boat rides.

When the passengers tried to pay, nobody would take the money. "They wouldn't take anything in payment," Brooks-Jones said.

The answer came in the air. A doctor on board suggested a scholarship for the town's young people.

Brooks-Jones, a longtime fundraiser at Ohio State University, drew up makeshift pledge sheets. Capt. Michael Sweeney let her make the pitch over the plane's PA system, and then he made the first donation himself.

In 2002 she set up the fund at The Columbus Foundation in Ohio. It has since passed $1 million, and by 2021 it had paid scholarships to 341 students of Lewisporte Collegiate.

She kept flying back to hand out the awards, 27 trips by 2017.

In 2005 the high school made her its first honorary graduate.

Hung Cao: Senator Sheehy, I began my questioning concerning the frigate program and so I appreciate you circling back to the importance of that type of vessel also.

Wicker: And I believe, Senator Rosen, you are next.

Rosen: Well, thank you. Thank you, Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, for holding this hearing. I'd like to thank Secretary Cao for testifying today for your service to our country and for meeting with me, I guess, a month ago, maybe a month and a half ago now. Of course, I want to talk about continuing to implement Fallon modernization as we discussed in my office. And so I do want to thank you for sending Assistant Secretary Rogers to Fallon last month to meet with me and Churchill County and the impacted ranchers so that we can finally work together to implement the FY23 NDAA in line with congressional intent and make things right for my constituents. It was a very productive meeting, I'm sure that you heard. However, as you and I discussed and we met a few months ago, we're nearly four years into the modernization effort of the Fallon Range Training Complex, and in that time, the divide between the Navy and local community has only grown larger. I've made it clear each time that Navy leadership has come before this committee that as part of the deal struck in 2022, the Navy must fully and completely compensate the grazing permit holders for their lifetime loss of ranching operations due to the necessary range expansion. Yet the payments offered to the ranchers in the B-16 range completely missed the mark. The Navy is not utilizing existing USDA metrics and formulas to evaluate the ranching operations, which would be the appropriate way to do this. And so we've had two years with no progress addressing the gap between the Navy's offers and what existing U.S. government data says they should be. That's why our teams, this committee, other committees in Congress working on that language to include an FY27 NDAA to address these issues, clarify our congressional intent of the 2020, excuse me, 2022 agreement under which multigenerational ranchers agreed to give up their livelihood in service to this country. If you heard a readout of the meeting, they are patriots. They love living next to Fallon. They are out there on their ranch every morning. They hear that national anthem in the morning. They hear the taps at night and they said there is nothing that feels more American to them. And so it is really important. So if confirmed, when you make those fair valuations and standardized payment offers, would you commit to utilizing existing data from the Department of Agriculture from qualified USDA appraisers who understand ranching operations, as was the congressional intent to ensure that every single permit is made whole?

Hung Cao: Senator, thank you for that question.

Rosen: Thank you again for the time in your office where we're able to discuss this. And thank you also for receiving Secretary Rogers. He's one of the brilliant men that have been able to negotiate so many things for us and as well as to help get the good, clean, safe, comfortable housing for our sailors and Marines. But right now, to be able to finally come to, I think we're almost at the finish line on this, where we're able to work with the ranchers. Because one of the issues we had was we didn't know how they got to that. Well, their estimate is like 10 times off of ours. I don't want to pay them too low. But then we're seeing-- I think that's where we had agreement using the USDA, those standard metrics. I know we can meet with this offline. I have a couple other things.

Hung Cao: Absolutely, Senator. It was a terrific meeting, but we do-- time is of the essence in order to get this in this year's NDAA. And so I want to just bring up the other portion, which are the roads, moving the roads. The Navy's agreed to take on maintenance and liability requirements on the relocated Sand Canyon Road. Churchill and Pershing Counties are still concerned about underlying maintenance and liability requirements falling to them for Sand Canyon and Pole Line Roads in particular. During the meeting last month with Assistant Secretary Rogers, all parties were happy with the Navy's commitments related to maintenance and liability for the relocated Sand Canyon Road, working collaboratively to address ongoing certainty related to Pole Line Road. The Navy offered to coordinate with Department of Interior to see if there's that opportunity to seek a waiver for maintenance and liability requirements when granting a Bureau of Land Management right of way.

Rosen: So will you commit to working with my office? I think we're about there, but to meaningfully address the issue of the roads as we move them and take care of them with the Department of Interior and get their authority to grant this important waiver.

Hung Cao: Absolutely, Senator. I mean, we've discussed in your office where, you know, I want to make sure we're not closing off roads with our gates and stuff like that. And where does our-- where do we end? You know, does it start where-- This is more the maintenance and liability of these types of roads. Absolutely, Senator. Counties have never had to do before and in Pershing County I think it's 4 million acres and 8,000 people. We'll absolutely continue working with your office, Senator.

Rosen: Thank you, appreciate it. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Wicker: Thank you very much, Senator Rosen.

Moody: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Good to see you. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on your nomination. I want to raise Naval Support Activity Orlando. It's an installation that matters to Florida and to the entire Joint Force. Naval Support Activity Orlando anchors the Central Florida Research Park and that's the nation's premier hub for modeling, simulation, and training, an ecosystem worth over 7 billion a year to Central Florida. Every soldier, sailor, airman, marine, and guardian trains on systems touched by this ecosystem. Its security detachment provides the armed response that classified facilities across the park need to keep their skiffs within the five to 15 minute window intelligence community standards require and it's not just a Navy issue. The Navy may be able to protect its own spaces but the partners cannot. Army, Air Force, and Marine Corps commands in the park have told us they would lose their skiffs without this detachment. So with the Navy Space Force and UCF Warming Gaming Center set to stand up in fiscal year 2027, Florida has invested over 150 million to build space for these missions. If they lose their classified capability, those missions and the high skilled jobs that come with them will face real pressure to leave the state. In July, my senior senator Scott and myself, we wrote to ask about the consolidation of NSA Orlando under NAS Jacksonville and asked to be brief before any decision. My office specifically reached out and wanted to be kept in the loop and briefed. This was the letter we got back about that from Scott Gray and it said that I could expect a detailed response by November 13th, 2026. We have not gotten that response. It's not just my office that has reached out and expressed concerns. Last week, the National Center for Simulation and its more than 300 industry members, UCF, Orange and Seminole Counties, the City of Orlando, and our regional economic partners wrote to you warning this consolidation would disrupt a $7 billion industry with no tangible gains. That we know of because we haven't been briefed. So will you commit to keeping that security detachment in place until the impact on every tenant's SCIF has been assessed and until our offices have been totally briefed?
