text:
Twenty-Fifth Sunday after Pentecost (taken from the Sixth Sunday after Epiphany) ON THE DEATH OF THE JUST by St Alphonsus Liguori.
.
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal until the whole was leavened.” MATT. xiii. 33.
.
IN this days gospel we find that a woman, after putting leaven in the dough, waits till the entire is fermented. Here the Lord gives us to understand that the kingdom of heaven that is, the attainment of eternal beatitude is like the leaven. By the leaven is understood the divine grace, which makes the soul acquire merits for eternal life. But this eternal life is obtained only when”the whole is leavened ;” that is, when the soul has arrived at the end of the present life and the completion of her merits. We shall, then, speak Today of the death of the just, which we should not fear, but should desire with our whole souls. For, says St. Bonaventure, “Triplex in morte congratulatio, hominem ab omni labore, peccato, et periculo liberari.” Man should rejoice at death, for three reasons First, because death delivers him from labour that is, from suffering the miseries of this life and the assault of his enemies. Secondly, because it delivers him from actual sins. Thirdly, because it delivers him from the danger of falling into hell, and opens Paradise to him.
.
First Point. Death delivers us from the miseries of this life, and from the assaults of our enemies.
.
 1  What is death? St. Eucherius answers, that “death is the end of miseries.” Job said that our life, however short it may be, is full of miseries, of infirmities, of crosses, of persecutions, and fears. “Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” (Job xiv. 1.) What, says St. Augustine, do men who wish for a prolongation of life on this earth desire but a prolongation of suffering ?” “Quid est diu vivere nisi diu tor queri.” (Serm. xviL de Serb. Dom.) Yes; for, as St. Ambrose remarks, the present life was given to us not for repose or enjoyment, but for labour and suffering, that by toils and pains we may merit Paradise. ”Hæc vita homini non ad quitem data est, sed ad laborem.” (Serm. xliii.) Hence the same holy doctor says, that, though death is the punishment of sin, still the miseries of this life are so great, that death appears to be a relief rather than a chastisement: ”Ut mors remediuni videatur esse, non pœna. ”
.
2   To those who love God, the severest of all the crosses of this life are the assaults of hell to rob them of the divine grace. Hence St. Denis the Areopagite says, that they joyfully meet death, as the end of their combats, and embrace it with gladness, because they hope to die a good death, and to be thus freed from all fear of ever again falling into sin. ”Divino gaudio et mortis terminum tanquam ad finem certaminum tendunt, non amplius metuentus pervertii.” (De Hier. Eccl., cap. vii.) The greatest consolation which a soul that loves God experiences at the approach of death, arises from the thought of being delivered from so many temptations, from so many remorses of conscience, and from so many dangers of offending God. Ah! says St. Ambrose, as long as we live, “we walk among snares.” We walk continually in the midst of the snares of our enemies, who lie in wait to deprive us of the life of grace. It was the fear of falling into sin that made St. Peter of Alcantara, in his last moments, say to a lay brother who, in attending the saint, accidently touched him: ”Brother, remove, remove from me, for I am still alive and in danger of being lost.” The thought of being freed from the danger of sin by death consoled St. Teresa, and made her rejoice as often as she heard the clock strike, that an hour of the combat was past. Hence she used to say: ”In each moment of life we may sin and lose God.” Hence the news of approaching death filled the saints not with sorrow or regret, but with sentiments of joy; because they knew that their struggles and the dangers of losing the divine grace were soon to have an end.
.
3  ”But the just man, if he be prevented with death, shall be in rest.” (Wis. iv. 7.) He who is prepared to die, regards death as a relief. If, says St. Cyprian, you lived in a house whose roof and walls were tottering and threatening destruction, would you not fly from, it as soon as possible? In this life everything menaces ruin to the poor soul the world, the devils, the flesh, the passions, all draw her to sin and to eternal death. It was this that made St. Paul exclaim: ”Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. vii. 24.) Who shall deliver me from this body of mine, which lives continually in a dying state, on account of the assaults of my enemies? Hence he esteemed death as a great gain, because it brought to him the possession of Jesus Christ, his true life. Happy then are they who die in the Lord: because they escape from pains and toils, and go to rest. ”Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth now, saith the spirit, that they may rest from their labours.” (Apoc. xiv. 13.) It is related in the lives of the ancient fathers, that one of them who was very old, when dying, smiled, while the others wept. Being asked why he smiled, he said: “Why do you weep at seeing me go to rest? Ex labore ad requiem vado, et vos ploratis ?” At the hour of death, St. Catherine of Sienna said to her sisters in religion: Rejoice with me: for I leave this land of suffering, and am going to the kingdom of peace. The death of the saints is called a sleep that is, the repose which God gives to his servants as the reward of their toil”When he shall give sleep to his beloved, behold the inheritance of the Lord.” (Ps. cxxvi. 2.) Hence the soul that loves God neither weeps nor is troubled at the approach of death, but, embracing the crucifix, and burning with love, she says: ”In peace in the self same I will sleep and I will rest.” (Ps. iv. 9.)
.
4  That “Proficiscere de hoc mundo,” (” Depart, Christian soul, from this world,”) which is so appalling to sinners at the hour of death, does not alarm the saints. ”But the souls of the just are in the hands of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them.” (Wis. iii. 1.) The saint is not afflicted, like worldlings, at the thought of being obliged to leave the goods of this earth, because he has kept the soul detached from them. During life, he always regarded God as the Lord of his heart and as the sole riches which he desired: ”What have I in heaven? and, besides thee, what do I desire upon earth? Thou art the God of my heart and the God that is my portion for ever.” (Ps. Ixxxii. 25, 26.) He is not afflicted at leaving honours, because the only honour which he sought was, to love and to be loved by God. All the honours of this world he has justly esteemed as smoke and vanity. He is not afflicted at leaving his relatives, because he loved them only in God. In his last moments he recommends them to his heavenly Father, who loves them more than he does. And having a secure confidence of salvation, he hopes to be better able to assist his relatives from Paradise, than on this earth. In a word, what he frequently said during life, he continues to repeat with greater fervour at the hour of death”My God and my all.”
.
5 Besides, his peace is not disturbed by the pains of death; but, seeing that he is now at the end of his life, and that he has no more time to suffer for God, or to offer him other proofs of love, he accepts those pains with joy, and offers them to God as the last remains of life; and uniting his death with the death of Jesus Christ, he offers it to the Divine Majesty.
.
6 And although the remembrance of the sins which he has committed will afflict, it will not disturb him; for, since he is convinced that the Lord will forget the sins of all true penitents, the very sorrow which he feels for his sins, gives him an assurance of pardon. ”If the wicked do penance. … I will not remember all his iniquities that he hath done.” (Ezec. xviii. 21 and 22.) “How,” asks St. Basil, “can anyone be certain that God has pardoned his sins? He may be certain of pardon if he say: I have hated and abhorred iniquity.” (In Reg. inter. 12.) He who detests his sins, and offers to God his death in atonement for them, may rest secure that God has pardoned them. ”Mors,” says St. Augustine, ”quæ in lege naturæ erat poona peccati in lege gratiæ est hostia pro peccato.” (Lib. iv. de Trin. c. xxii.) Death, which was a chastisement of sin under the law of nature, has become, in the law of grace, a victim of penance, by which the pardon of sin is obtained.
.
7 The very love which a soul bears to God, assures her of his grace, and delivers her from the fear of being lost. ”Charity casteth out fear.” (1 John iv. 18.) If, at the hour of death, you are unwilling to pardon an enemy, or to restore what is not your own, or if you wish to keep up an improper friendship, then tremble for your eternal salvation; for you have great reason to be afraid of death; but if you seek to avoid sin, and to preserve in your heart a testimony that you love God, be assured that he is with you: and if the Lord is with you, what do you fear? And if you wish to be assured that you have within you the divine love, embrace death with peace, and offer it from your heart to God. He that offers to God his death, makes an act of love the most perfect that is possible for him to perform; because, by cheerfully embracing death to please God, at the time and in the manner which God ordains, he becomes like the martyrs, the entire merit of whose martyrdom consisted in suffering and dying to please God.
.
Second Point. Death frees us from actual sins.
.
8 It is impossible to live in this world without committing at least some slight faults. ”A just man shall fall seven times: ” (Prov. xxiv. 16.) He who ceases to live, ceases to offend God. Hence St. Ambrose called death the burial of vices: by death they are buried, and never appear again. ”Quid est mors nisi sepultura vitorum?” (De Bono Mort. cap. iv.) The venerable Vincent Caraffa consoled himself at the hour of death by saying: now that I cease to live, I cease for ever to offend my God. He who dies in the grace of God, goes into that happy state in which he shall love God for ever, and shall never more offend him. ”Mortuus,” says the same holy doctor, ”nescit peccare. Quid tanto pere vita mistam desideramus, in qua quanto diutius quis fuerit, tanto majori oneratur sarcina peccatorum.” How can we desire this life, in which the longer we live, the greater shall be the load of our sins?
.
9 Hence the Lord praises the dead more than any man living: ”I praised the dead rather than the living.” (Eccl. iv. 2.) Because no man on this earth, however holy he may be, is exempt from sins. A spiritual soul gave directions that the person who should bring to her the news of death, should say: ”Console yourself, for the time has arrived when you shall no longer offend God.”
.
10 St. Ambrose adds, that God permitted death to enter into the world, that, by dying, men should cease to sin: “Passus est Dominus subintrare mortem ut culpa cessaret.” (Loco cit.) It is, then, a great error to imagine that death is a chastisement for those who love God. It is a mark of the love which God bears to them , because he shortens their life to put an end to sin, from which they cannot be exempt as long as they remain on this earth. ”For his soul pleased God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities.” (Wis. iv. 14.)
.
Third Point. Death delivers us from the danger of falling into hell, and opens Paradise to us.
.
11 ”Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of the saints.” (Ps. cxv. 16.) Considered according to the senses, death excites fear and terror; but, viewed with the eye of faith, it is consoling and desirable. To the saints it is as amiable and as precious, as it appears terrible to sinners. ”It is precious,” says St. Bernard, ”as the end of labours, the consummation of victory, the gate of life.” The joy of the cup-bearer of Pharaoh, at hearing from Joseph that he should soon be released from prison, bears no comparison to that which a soul that loves God feels on hearing that she is to be liberated from the exile of this earth, and to be transported to the enjoyment of God in her true country. The Apostle says, that, as long as we remain in the body, we wander at a distance from our country in a strange land, and far removed from the life of God: ”While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord.” (2 Cor. v. 6.) Hence, St. Bruno teaches, that our death should not be called death, but the beginning of life. ”Mors dicenda non est, sed vitæ principium.” And St. Athanasius says: ”Non est justis mors sed translatio.” To the just, death is but a passage from the miseries of this earth to the eternal delights of Paradise. O desirable death! exclaimed St. Augustine; who is there that does not desire thee? For thou art the term of evils, the end of toils, and the beginning of everlasting repose!”O mors desirabilis, malorum finis, laboris clausula, quietis principium.”
.
12 No one can enter into heaven to see God without passing through the gate of death. ”This is the gate of the Lord the just shall enter into it.” (Ps. cxvii. 20.) Hence, addressing death, St. Jerome said: ”Aperi mini soror mea.” Death, my sister, if you do not open the gate to me, I cannot enter to enjoy my God. And St. Charles Borromeo, seeing in his house a picture of death with a knife in the hand, sent for a painter to cancel the knife, and substitute for it a key of gold; because, said the saint, it is death that opens Paradise. Were a queen confined in a dark prison, how great would be her joy at hearing that the gates of the prison are open, and that she is to return from the dungeon to her palace! It was to be liberated by death from the prison of this life that David asked, when he said: ”Bring my soul out of prison.” (Ps. cxli. 8.) This, too, was the favour which the venerable Simeon asked of the infant Jesus, when he held him in his arms: ”Now thou dost dismiss thy servant.” (Luke ii. 29.)”As if detained by force,” says St. Ambrose, ”he asked to be dismissed.” Simeon sought to be delivered by death, as if he had been compelled by force to live on this earth.
.
13 St. Cyprian says, that the sinner who shall pass from temporal to eternal death, has just reason to be afraid of death. “Mori timeat, qui ad secundum mortem de hac morte transibit.” But he who is in the state of grace and hopes to pass from death to eternal life which is the true life tears not death. It is related that a certain rich man gave to St. John the Almoner a large sum of money to be dispensed in alms, for the purpose of obtaining from God a long life for his only son. The son died in a short time. The father complained of the death of his son; but, to console him, the Lord sent an angel to say to him: “You have sought a long life for your son, and the Lord has heard your prayer; for your son is in heaven, where he enjoys eternal life.” This is the grace which, according to the promise of the prophet Osee, the Redeemer obtained for us. ”death, I will be thy death.” (xiii. 14.) By His redemption, Jesus Christ destroyed death, and changed it into a source of life to us. When St. Pionius, martyr, was asked how he could go to death with so much joy, he answered: ”You err; I do not go to death but to life.”“Erratis non ad mortem, sed ad vitam contendo.” (Apud Eusub., lib. iv. cap. xiv ) Thus also St. Symphorosa exhorted her son, St. Symphorian, to martyrdom: ”My son,” said she, ”life is not taken away from you; it is only changed for a better one.”
.
14 St. Augustine says, that they who love God desire to see him speedily, and that, therefore, to them life is a cause of suffering, and death an occasion of joy. “Patienter vivit, delectabiliter moritur.” (Trac. ix. in Ep. Joan.) St. Teresa used to say, that to her life was death. Hence she composed the celebrated hymn, ”I die because I do not die.” To that great servant of God D. Sancia Carriglio a penitent of Father M. Avila it was one day revealed, that she had but a year to live; she answered: ”Alas! must I remain another year at a distance from God? O sorrowful year, which will appear to me longer than an age.” Such is the language of souls who love God from their heart. It is a mark of little love of God not to desire to see him speedily.
.
15 Some of you will say: I desire to go to God, but I fear death. I am afraid of the assaults which I shall then experience from hell. I find that the saints have trembled at the hour of death; how much more ought I to tremble! I answer: It is true that hell does not cease to assail even the saints at death, but it is also true that God does not cease to assist his servants at that moment; and when the dangers are increased, he multiplies his helps. ”Ibi plus auxilii,” says St. Ambrose, ”ubi plus periculi.” (ad Jos. cap. v.) The servant of Eliseus was struck with terror when he saw the city surrounded by enemies; but the saint inspired him with courage by showing to him a multitude of angels sent by God to defend it. Hence the prophet afterwards said: ”Fear not, for there are more with us than with them.” (4 Kings vi. 16.) The powers of hell will assail the dying Christian; but his angel guardian will come to console him. His patrons, and St. Michael, who has been appointed by God to defend his faithful servants in their last combat with the devils, will come to his aid. The mother of God will come to assist those who have been devoted to her. Jesus Christ shall come to defend from the assaults of hell the souls for which he died on a cross: he will give them confidence and strength to resist every attack. Hence, filled with courage, they will say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?” (Isa. xxvi. I.) Truly has Origen said, that the Lord is more desirous of our salvation than the devil is of our perdition, because God’s love for us far surpasses the devil’s hatred of our souls. ”Major ilia cura est, ut nos ad veram pertrahat salutem, quam diabolo, ut nos ad æternam damnationem impellat.” (Hom, xx.)
.
16 God is faithful, he will never permit us to be tempted above our strength: ”Fidelis Deus non patietur vos tentari supra id quod potestis.” (1 Cor. x. 13.) It is true that some saints have suffered great fear at the hour of death; but they have been few. The Lord, as Belluacensis says, has permitted this fear to cleanse them at death from some defect. ”Justi quandoque dure moriendo purgantur in hoc mundo.” But we know that, generally speaking, the saints have died with a joyful countenance. Father Joseph Scamacca, a man of a holy life, being asked if, in dying, he felt confidence in God, answered: Have I served Mahomet, that I should now doubt of the goodness of my God, or of his wish to save me? Ah! the Lord knows well how to console his servants in their last moments. Even in the midst of the agony of death, he infuses into their souls a certain sweetness and a certain foretaste of that happiness which he will soon bestow upon them. As they who die in sin begin to experience from the bed of death a certain foretaste of hell certain extraordinary terrors, remorses, and fits of despair; so, on the other hand, the saints, by the fervent acts of divine love which they then make, and by the confidence and the desire which they feel of soon seeing God, taste, before death, that peace which they shall afterwards fully enjoy in heaven.
.
17 Father Suarez died with so much peace, that in his last moments he said: ”I could not have imagined that death was so sweet.” Being advised by his physician not to fix his thoughts so constantly on death, Cardinal Baronius said: Is it lest the fear of death should shorten my life? I fear not; on the contrary, I love and desire death. Of the Cardinal Bishop of Rochester, Saunders relates, that, in preparing to die for the faith, he put on his best clothes, saying that ho was going to a nuptial feast. When he came within view of the place of execution, he threw away his staff, and said: O my feet, walk fast; for we are not far from Paradise. ”Ite pedes, parum a paradiso distamus.” Before death, he wished to recite the TE DEUM, in thanksgiving to God for permitting him to die for the holy faith; and, full of joy, he laid his head on the block. St. Francis of Assisium began to sing at the hour of death. Brother Elias said to him: Father, at the hour of death, we ought rather to weep than to sing. But, replied the saint, I cannot abstain from singing at the thought of soon going to enjoy God. A nun of the order of St. Teresa, in her last moments, said to her sisters in religion, who were in tears: O God! why do you weep? I am going to possess my Jesus; if you love me, weep not, but rejoice with me. (Dis. Parol. i. 6.)
.
18 Father Granada relates, that a certain sportsman found in a wood a solitary singing in his last agony. How, said the sportsman, can you sing in such a state? The hermit replied: Brother, between me and God there is nothing but the wall of this body. I now see that since my flesh is falling in pieces, the prison shall be destroyed, and I shall soon go to see God. It is for this reason I rejoice and sing. Through the desire of seeing God, St. Ignatius, martyr, said, that if the wild beasts should spare him, he would provoke them to devour him. “Ego vim faciam, ut devorer.” St. Catherine of Genoa was astonished that some persons regarded death as a misfortune, and said: ”O beloved death, in what a mistaken light do men view you! Why do you not come to me? I call on you day and night”(Vita, c. 7.)
.
19 Oh! how peculiarly happy is the death of the servants of Mary! Father Binetti relates, that a person whom he assisted in his last moments, and who was devoted to the Blessed Virgin, said to him: ”Father, you cannot conceive the consolation which arises at death from the remembrance of having served Mary. Ah! my father, if you knew what happiness I feel on account of having served this good mother! I cannot express it.” What joy shall the lovers of Jesus Christ experience at his coming to them in the most holy viaticum! Happy the soul that can then address her Saviour in the words which St. Philip Neri used when the viaticum was brought to him: ”Behold my love! behold my love! give me my love!” But, to entertain these sentiments at death, we must have ardently loved Jesus Christ during life.

text:
🇷🇺🇺🇦 RUSSIA'S MILITARY HAS A DESERTION PROBLEM THAT RECRUITING MORE SOLDIERS CANNOT SOLVE.

A captured Russian soldier has described something particularly disturbing about the conditions inside his own army: the punishment for trying to leave can allegedly be worse than the prospect of returning to the battlefield.

His testimony describes commanders beating soldiers accused of desertion, allegedly killing some of them and forcing other troops to dispose of their bodies. He also claims that executions were filmed and used as intimidation against anyone considering escape.

But his account reveals another problem: how Russia recruits and retains its soldiers.

He says he signed a military contract while serving a prison sentence after being promised rear-area duties, a one-year commitment and the possibility of clearing his criminal record.

Instead, he claims his contract was repeatedly extended, leaving him with no realistic way out.

Other Russian prisoners have described remarkably similar recruitment arrangements. In an investigation published by The Insider, former prison recruits explained how promises of one-year contracts, financial rewards and cleared criminal records contrasted with the conditions they encountered after joining the military.

This is not simply a collection of isolated battlefield complaints.

A UK government country assessment published in August 2026 also documented evidence of informal punishments against Russian soldiers accused of refusing orders or abandoning their units. These included torture, arbitrary detention, mock and actual executions, and forcing soldiers back into dangerous frontline assaults.

The assessment explicitly noted that the overall scale of these practices remains unclear.

That distinction matters. Individual testimonies do not establish that every Russian unit operates this way, but multiple investigations point to serious problems with coercion and discipline inside parts of the Russian military.

There is also a fundamental difference between recruiting soldiers and retaining them through fear.

Russia can offer money, recruit prisoners, pressure civilians into signing contracts and continually search for new manpower.

But none of those measures guarantees that the soldiers entering the army actually want to fight.

The captured soldier's decision to surrender alongside another serviceman, after hiding in a dugout and switching off their radio, brings this contradiction into focus.

He now says he fears being returned to the same military system through a prisoner exchange.

For Moscow, that creates an uncomfortable problem: even surrendering to the enemy can become preferable, in the eyes of some soldiers, to returning to their own commanders.

An army can force men to remain in uniform.

That does not mean it has earned their loyalty, trust or willingness to fight. https://t.co/tDG7JSlzqD

text:
12 TAKEAWAYS GEORGIA VS MISSOURI - Controlled Demolition

"Never waste a disaster"

Well run organizations live by this mantra in many sectors. In the case of the Georgia Bulldogs, they looked up during the bye week after the Auburn game and didn't like what they saw. 

On defense... 16 missed tackles and 217 rushing yards allowed after contact.

On offense, UGA had gone askew... 42 Passing Dropbacks/23 Designed Runs... Georgia RB’s vs Auburn — 19 ATT, 87 YDS, 4.5 YPC, 2.5 Yards After Contact per Rush Attempt

That's not what Georgia Football is supposed to look like. Let’s see how UGA has looked in those categories since the Auburn loss that came before its only bye week of the 2026 regular season…

Florida
- 7 missed tackles
- 52 rushing yards allowed after contact
- UGA Offense: 27 Dropbacks/38 Runs
- RB’s — 28 ATT, 161 YDS, 5.7 YPC, 2.85 YAC/rush

Ole Miss
- 4 missed tackles
- 65 rushing yards allowed after contact
- UGA Offense: 16 Dropbacks/47 Runs
- RB’s — 38 ATT, 233 YDS, 6.1 YPC, 4.0 YAC per Rush

Missouri
- 7 missed tackles (4 by starters)
- 87 rushing yards allowed after contact
- UGA Offense: 27 Dropbacks/33 Runs
- RB’s — 26 ATT, 146 YDS, 5.6 YPC, 3.3 YAC per Rush (3.7 for Frazier/Phillips)

This has been an all-time course correction by Georgia’s staff. In the theme of never wasting a disaster, to never waste a disaster you have to understand the anatomy of how that disaster occurred to begin with. In the case of UGA-Auburn, yes, there were some anomalous things (Frazier/Stockton injuries and no KJ Bolden), but I also think you had some legitimate issues that led to too much pressure being put on Gunner Stockton offensively and the Inside LB room defensively. That has flipped dramatically.

Georgia has flashed the most dominant form of any team in college football in recent weeks by making everything old new again. This game has always been won and lost up front, and no amount of sexy passing game trends is ever going to change that. If you take space from people at the line of scrimmage, you win football games. The game starts from the inside-out and it's often won there if one side is too good to be stalemated.

Easier said than done, so how did Georgia fix it? Georgia leaned into the mug front trend while putting their own twist on things to suit it to their personnel. The Dawgs are leaning into their strengths in the secondary, and using the reliability of their boundary corners to further blur the positional definitions in this defense. It has become a havoc engine of sorts. 

On offense, Georgia has recommitted to the ground game and found ways to lean on its biggest personnel advantages on the edges. They also got back a big weapon on Saturday, and now their most consistent wideout is back in the position he's supposed to be.  

Those are some of the themes. We explain the execution, dig into the details and put some tape on the screen in this week's 12 Takeaways on @DawgsCentral_

text:
I Give U My Allegiance: Howard Hewett’s Paisley Park Pledge Lands.

On November 17, 1992, former Shalamar frontman Howard Hewett released his fourth solo album Allegiance on Elektra Records, a sophisticated R&B set built around a title track written by Prince. 

Originally demoed by Prince in May 1988 and offered to Hewett’s then-wife Nia Peeples (who passed), the song was re-recorded early 1992 at Paisley Park Studios in Chanhassen, Minnesota. Produced by Tommy LiPuma and Ricky Peterson, the released version features the New Power Generation’s Michael B. on drums, Ricky Peterson on keyboards/synth bass/drum programming, and Paul Peterson on bass and acoustic guitar—though Prince himself does not appear on the track. The album also includes other Paisley Park sessions (Ronnie-O and a Bob Dylan cover of “Just Like a Woman”) alongside cuts from Narada Michael Walden, Nick Martinelli, and Barry Mann.

Allegiance peaked at No. 73 on the Billboard R&B chart and spawned two singles: the upbeat “Save Your Sex For Me” and the adult-contemporary ballad “How Fast Forever Goes” (lyrics by Sammy Cahn).

Formats (true to the 1992 release window, primarily US with European and Japanese pressings):
•  US CD album: Elektra 9 61393-2 (standard jewel case, club edition, and longbox retail variant catalogued with 61392-2)
•  Europe CD album: Elektra 7559-61393-2 (Made in Germany)
•  Japan CD album / promo: Elektra WMC5-564
•  US cassette album: Elektra 9 61393-4 / 61393-4 (SR pressing)

Packaging and artwork: The cover, photographed by Wayne Maser with art direction by Robin Lynch, is a clean, high-contrast portrait of Hewett in a black sleeveless vest, white T-shirt, and jeans, leaning against a stark white wall, head slightly bowed. Large gray “howard hewett” lettering dominates, with “allegiance” in maroon. Standard CD packaging used a jewel case with booklet/inlay notes listing producers, musicians, and Paisley Park credits; US longboxes offered extra retail display space. Cassettes came in conventional shells with printed J-cards.

The result is a polished, grown-up soul statement whose Prince-penned centerpiece still carries the lyric’s promise: “I give U my allegiance.”

text:
Here’s Why You Should Get a Landline—Yep, Even in 2025 https://t.co/4Np0rvmiNA
Going old school with a landline can be a smart call in certain situations
For better or worse, we’ve become increasingly reliant on technology, both in our personal and professional lives. This is especially true when it comes to phones, as a whopping 98% of Americans now own a mobile phone, according to Pew Research. And according to a 2022 survey by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, only about 29% of U.S. adults still own a landline, down steeply from 2004, when more than 90% of adults had one.

The massive swing over the past two decades is likely due to mobile phones’ ability to communicate from virtually anywhere instead of being limited to a home. Many Americans can’t justify paying a monthly fee for a service that seems, well, antiquated.

Problem is, cellphones are great … until they aren’t. Anyone who has been unable to charge their phone during a brief power outage from a thunderstorm or snowstorm or who was affected by a cell service outage knows that life can grind to a halt when we lose access to calls, texts and emails. Read on to learn about the advantages of a landline and how to get one.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, humor and fun facts all week long.
Why do you need a landline?

It may be time to rethink landlines after all. Also referred to as POTS, an easy-to-remember acronym that stands for “plain old telephone system,” this trusty ol’ tech may serve as a lifeline in the event of a mobile service disruption—including natural disasters, when you most definitely want to keep in touch.

FEATURED VIDEO
This Is the Nicest Place in America for 2026

“Actually, I still own a landline,” concedes Tony Anscombe, chief security evangelist for ESET, a leading cybersecurity company. “It’s mostly because I live in a house that’s remote, and so we still use copper for internet and phone service here.”

A landline can be a lifesaving backup if your mobile phone service goes down, which happens from time to time on all the major carriers, whether because of a random service outage or one caused by inclement weather.

AT&T customers, for example, experienced a wireless outage for several hours in February 2024, due to what was billed as a coding error during network expansion. In September 2024, Verizon suffered a major outage, and two months later, so did T-Mobile.

Hurricane Milton, a Category 4 hurricane that hit the United States in October 2024, caused 12.3% of cell sites to be down in areas of Florida impacted by the storm, according to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Disaster Information Reporting System report. AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon were all affected, as were other carriers.
How could a landline help in an emergency?

Landlines work better during power outages because they receive power directly through the phone line itself, which is separate from the household electricity grid. Therefore, the phone company’s backup generators can power the lines even when your home power is out.

Another advantage in an emergency situation: Landlines allow emergency services to locate a 911 caller‘s origin more easily than an enhanced 911 (also called “e911”) call on a cellphone or smartphone. That’s because mobile phones aren’t associated with one fixed location or address.

That said, enhanced 911 calls have improved over the years, thanks to advancements in carrier services, GPS tracking and dispatching equipment, which help emergency service pinpoint your location. “While it’s getting better, an e911 call [on a smartphone] doesn’t provide your location as accurately as a 911 call on a landline, when you’re right at the handset and they know your exact address, even if you can’t talk,” says Anscombe.
What is a landline?

Before we discuss why you might want a landline, it’s helpful to understand the technology.

POTS
A POTS phone system (aka traditional landline) was the standard form of telephone service from the 1880s to the fairly recent past. If you’re over 40 years old, you likely grew up with one of these in your home.

This technology (almost always) uses copper wires to transmit your voice, which is converted into analog electrical signals and then converted back into audible sound waves when it reaches its destination, allowing the person you’re calling to hear your voice.

While telephone users may think they’re calling someone else directly, behind the scenes, there is an extensive network of interconnected telephone lines, switches and infrastructure to enable communication between POTS lines. (As you may have seen in old movies, switchboard operators, usually female, played an important role in routing calls until the 1960s.)

Over the past couple of decades, digital and internet-based communication technologies took over, though landlines were still used in business environments until fairly recently.

The benefit of POTS
While POTS lines have declined in popularity since the rise of cellphones and smartphones, they are still common in regions with unreliable or limited internet access. They’re also ideal for critical services like emergency lines and home or business alarm systems that demand high reliability.

“In case of a power or cellular outage, I can see the appeal of a landline, as it should still work, unless you only have a cordless phone at home, which would also rely on power,” says Carolina Milanesi, president and principal analyst at Creative Strategies, a Silicon Valley–based market research firm. “Also, good luck in trying to remember anyone’s phone number if you lose power on your smartphone,” she adds with a laugh. “We’ve grown reliant on everything being stored on our smartphones.”

Landlines are also essential for connecting devices like fax machines, which are still heavily used in the health care and finance industries today, as they’re considered secure and dependable means of transmitting crucial and sensitive information.

Plus, compared with mobile phones, landlines are less likely to drop calls or have poor reception, often have better sound quality and are generally easier to operate for aging adults, especially among those with dexterity challenges. (An exception to the sound-quality benefit is the cordless phone, “which may sound worse than a mobile phone, especially older models that could have static and such,” Milanesi says.)

Anscombe says another consideration is that some fall detectors, like the Lifeline products—often worn on a lanyard or wrist of someone at risk of falling—may require a landline for the device to call someone in the event of a fall. This is something to keep in mind before considering the cancellation of landline service.

“I also think there’s a perceived security around owning a landline, especially for older folks,” adds Anscombe. “They could get rid of their landline, but many won’t, as they know they can pick up the handset, and it just works.” He adds that his mom falls into that category, “but if I asked her when the last time she actually used her landline was, it would probably be years ago.”

The disadvantages of POTS
Landlines can be difficult to find these days, as some telecommunications companies have ceased (or limited) their offerings. Because demand has subsided, the costs for a POTS line could be higher than a few years ago, even upwards of $50 per month. Additional charges may apply for features like long-distance calling, caller ID, voicemail and other add-ons.

“This isn’t always the case, though,” counters Milanesi, who says the only reason she still has a landline is because she gets the service for free from her mobile and internet company. “I don’t think I’ve ever used it, to be honest.”

Other downsides: You’re limited to using the landline at home. And it’s not a given that you’ll get service. Because fewer people now own a landline, the FCC is phasing out requirements for phone companies to provide landline services. In many new homes, builders aren’t even installing phone jacks.

With his cybersecurity expertise, Anscombe provides one more advantage to a smartphone compared with a landline: “Cordless phones are also less secure than smartphones, [as they’re] more susceptible to eavesdropping and open to other vulnerabilities.”

What’s the best alternative to a landline?

If your internet service provider or TV company doesn’t offer a landline service, you can research the companies in your area that can still provide one. A quick Google search may do the trick, or you can ask neighbors which service they use.
Still striking out? The following are alternatives to a traditional landline.

Consider a VoIP line

If you’re having trouble finding a POTS provider, an alternative would be a VoIP phone, which uses the internet to make phone calls. VoIP services are often more cost effective than landlines (especially for long-distance calls), and you often get free features and add-ons, such as voicemail, three-way calling, call forwarding and caller ID.
Use messaging apps, websites and smart speakers

Another option is to leverage messaging apps and websites to make free phone calls to others. But the caveat is the person you’re calling must be on the same service as you. Popular options include WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, Skype, FaceTime, Zoom, Google Meet, Signal and Microsoft Teams. These services support video calls and file transfers, and they offer other benefits.
If you have power and internet connectivity, remember that you can place free audio calls using a smart speaker, such as an Amazon Echo or Google Nest device. Simply say the wake word, like “Alexa” (on Amazon devices) or “Hey Google” or “OK Google” (on Google Nest speakers), followed by “dial [10-digit number].” No smartphone is required.

Consider backup power

Both a VoIP phone and messaging apps require power and internet access. While there’s little you can do if your Wi-Fi or wired (Ethernet) connection fails, such as if your internet service provider experiences an outage, you can invest in a backup solution for your devices should you be without power.
Similar to small and portable chargers (“power banks”) that juice up a smartphone and other gear, larger battery-based power generators can keep appliances, computers, medical devices and other equipment running for days. (A rechargeable battery-based generator may be better than a gas one since it can be used indoors, is quieter and doesn’t produce carbon monoxide.)

SOS satellite services

If your mobile phone can’t access cellular towers because your carrier’s network is down or you find yourself “off the grid” (such as in the woods), both Apple and Samsung support emergency satellite SOS services on the latest iPhones and Samsung Galaxy phones, respectively. Free for now, this feature first connects you to satellites via on-screen instructions. From there, you can type text-based messages to emergency services. You can also share location info and a description of what’s going on.
Mobile phone carriers, including AT&T and Verizon, are also offering emergency satellite support on certain devices.

Some satellite-based internet services, like Starlink, also support calls in emergencies. But be aware that the dish, router and other equipment will require power.

On the topic of satellite connectivity, Anscombe says the school his partner teaches at has satellite phones for use in case of earthquakes or other natural disasters that can knock out power or cellular service. When pressed about these phones still requiring power to use, Anscombe says they’re always charged up and ready to use in should an emergency occur.

There are many policy manifestations that provide irrefutable proof of Plato's assessment, particularly in America over the past half-century, but one grim bit of anecdotal evidence presently at hand is the accelerating collapse of even the most basic structures providing law and order. 

Traffic laws and civic codes governing public behavior are Exhibit A. 

Beginning in the summer of 2020, when a certain urban miscreant perished by his own bad decisions and the nation was plunged into a pre-loaded InstaRiot that produced the desired looting and arson on a staggering scale, law enforcement agencies and governments at the state, county and municipal levels across the country immediately suspended virtually all forms of traffic law enforcement, civic codes regulating public behavior (i.e. quality of life strictures such as prohibiting loud noise at certain hours, loitering, illegal parking, etc.) and anything else that could be seen as benchmark of a well-preserved high trust Western society. 

The rationale for the near-instantaneous jettisoning of civic standards and the demolition of the social pillars (few seemed to notice or question that the base charges had been carefully and methodically planted well before the alleged triggering event) was declared to be a reckoning with a social order that oppressed racial minorities as evidenced by 'disparate impacts.' 

Simply put, if more black drivers than white drivers were cited for reckless driving, then reckless driving prohibitions must be inherently oppressive and designed to target black drivers versus coercively prohibit dangerous driving. 

In Southern California — the birthplace and car culture capital of America — the California Highway Patrol disappeared from the regions freeways almost overnight and local police agencies suspended traffic law enforcement (including license, insurance and vehicle registration requirements) en masse. 

Now, more than six years down the road, all across Southern California and indeed throughout many other locales around the nation, wild-eyed savages terrorizing drivers and pedestrians alike can be seen everyday. In Los Angeles, so-called 'street takeovers' are a near nightly occurrence that see hundreds and sometimes thousands of bipedal primates packing metro intersections as muscle cars shriek and scream in smoking circles of burning rubber on the asphalt as the savage primates jump up and down, grabbing their crotches with one hand and holding their iPhones with the other as they livestream the chaos. 

LAPD units usually remain at a distance in observance of the policy that, on paper anyway, prioritizes concepts of deescalation and non-intrusive policing posture that is said to restore confidence in the community. 

In actual fact, the policy is clearly designed to facilitate, accelerate and propagate total social collapse into a permanent state of Third World chaos. Police protocols today are the real-world application of a governance committed to destroying the American construct and the Western world's imprint on the American homeland. 

Throughout the suburbs now, a dysfunctional rite that was forged in the tribal lands of Baltimore decades ago in what became known as the 12 O'clock Boys movement where hundreds of 'teens' (always the 'teens') raced through streets on dirt bikes and ATVs, taking over city blocks and riding like mad circus monkeys that were making a mass escape from the big top and their cruel captors at Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey garish exhibitions. A documentary that captured a granular look at the madness of the 12 O'clock Boys revealed that while most of them were descendants of people who have been in America for several centuries, their language skills were so limited that captions had to be used in an effort to interpret what they were apparently trying to say. Little understandable or coherent English was on offer from the 'teens' despite being born in the U.S. and having a bloodline that reached back to the 1700s in some cases. 

What was once confined to the urban jungles dotting eastern seaboard is now a feature of Southern California's streets (as well as Dallas and Miami, where I have witnessed it firsthand as well), as roving packs of savages fill the streets on E-bikes, motorcycles and bicycles where they intentionally harass and threaten other drivers and pedestrians alike for obvious sport. 

This past weekend, as many as 40 or so 'teens' took their circus monkey show into a large and somewhat upscale mall in the bedroom community of Montclair, about 40 miles east of LA. Inside the mall, the primates took to popping wheelies and peddling furiously at all manner of shoppers. Gas-powered minibikes also raced through the mall. 

If you are wondering what this very specific display of chaotic lunacy in a shopping mall has to do with Plato's observation that Chad has rightly highlighted, well, to bring it all back home: the rise of inferior cultures driven by the mass importation of foreign peoples — both historically and currently — from Third World tribal lands rooted in nihilistic and subsistence lifestyles is not a misunderstood or unanticipated byproduct of bad policy. 

It is the policy. 

The chaos unfolding on the streets in real time, right now even as you read this, is the desired result produced by a strange coalition of agents and operatives (sounds very cloak and dagger, but mostly its not) that seek to establish a new rule following the wholesale, top-to-bottom annihilation of America and its heritage population. 

In Montclair, a nice shopping mall that was already struggling in this economic climate may well have just received its death blow at the hands of the savage primates who raced across its polished floors. Word of that sort of experience spreads rapidly and consumers retreat, which triggers a hand off of sorts to the bipedal primates who consider such violent dysfunction to be something akin to a half-time show. They like it. Feels like home to them, or school when manage to attend. They call it 'Wildin' Out!' 

But it can be fatal for the businesses. 

So these are the stakes. Either we resolve to excise the tumors that are spreading or, and very soon, the cancer will be too far along and what remained left to us will be overwhelmed. 

A parting suggestion: Savages are as savages do. Never forget that. And never be afraid to call a savage a savage, a primate a primate, a spade a spade.

text:
Democrats Push Bill to Rescind Billions in Border Tech Funding, Including Tools to Detect Fentanyl!

H.R. 10974, introduced by Rep. Lauren Underwood and cosponsored by Nancy Pelosi, would claw back unspent money from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for non-intrusive inspection equipment and drug-trafficking efforts.

House Democrats have introduced legislation that would cancel remaining unobligated funding previously approved for U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including resources directed at detecting illicit narcotics and combating fentanyl trafficking. H.R. 10974, the DHS Funding Accountability Act, was introduced on November 10, 2026, by Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois. It targets specific sections of Public Law 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed earlier in 2025, by rescinding any unspent balances under those provisions and repealing the underlying sections.

Among the sections named in the bill is 90004, titled “Border security, technology, and screening.” That provision appropriated $6.168 billion to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, available through September 30, 2029. The money was designated for procurement and integration of new non-intrusive inspection equipment and related civil works, including artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” It also explicitly funded “enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals.” Additional uses covered air and marine platforms, border surveillance upgrades, biometric screening, and related mission support.

Nancy Pelosi is listed among the bill’s cosponsors, along with other Democratic members including Reps. Lateefah Simon, Bonnie Watson Coleman, Jan Schakowsky, Mike Quigley, and Stephen Lynch. The measure was referred to the House Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Homeland Security committees. As of mid-November 2026, it remains in committee with no further action reported. The bill affects only unobligated balances, funds not yet committed to specific contracts or expenditures, rather than money already spent or legally obligated.

Underwood has described the legislation as a response to the scale of additional ICE and CBP resources provided in the earlier reconciliation package, arguing that those funds have supported expanded enforcement activities. Critics of the new bill note that the targeted provisions include dual-use border technology long supported on a bipartisan basis for interdicting fentanyl and other drugs at ports of entry, where the majority of such seizures occur. Non-intrusive inspection systems (large-scale X-ray and related scanners) are a core tool CBP has cited for increasing vehicle scanning rates and reducing reliance on manual inspection. CBP has previously indicated that portions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act money were allocated toward expanding and modernizing these systems.

The proposal does not create new restrictions on existing baseline appropriations for drug interdiction; it seeks to reverse supplemental funding already enacted. Whether it advances will depend on committee action and broader congressional dynamics around border and immigration spending. The text of H.R. 10974 is public on https://t.co/gUCXEPenz9, as is the language of section 90004 in the underlying law.

text:
"The Mask Maker" - new 1/1 from the world of Luci

Acquired by The Alan Howard Collection

https://t.co/S24U3RRLir

In the spring of last year, @MrsRachelSpratt and I glanced at the baby monitor and saw our daughter, not even one at the time, throwing up what looked like half her body weight in her crib. We grabbed her, strapped her into the stroller, and sprinted through Manhattan to the nearest pediatric ER while she kept vomiting down the streets of New York.

A hard way to learn about an obscure allergy. They got the EpiPen in, and we held her on the crunch of hospital bed paper while her stomach quieted and her color slowly came back. An hour passed, stable. Another, and she was drinking water. Another and she was giggling like nothing had even happened and largely just amused by the red LED taped to her making her skin glow. And then my phone rang.

To explain that call, you have to spiral backward three months, and then three years.

Right after Masquerade released, I got a text from Benny.

I was spared from the ceremonially annoying "hey" which he waits until answered to get to the point, or something mangled in spelling beyond the english language. It was just: "Do you have any other 1 to 1 supply?"

I didn't.

“Nothing?”

What I had were studies and sketches of the figures inside Masquerade: built the same way I’d drawn character studies for The Monument Game. Stories about feelings had, memories of those feelings, and the people who rhymed with them along the way, all just dormant, waiting to be fleshed out with time.
Thanks to the people who participated in my last two works, Luci is now covered in stories—each a mark, a person who looked and left a piece of themselves on the surface. I love these marks. Beneath the metadata, IPFS pins, and talk of "networked art," though, there is still an artwork made from Millions of small decisions and brushstrokes, and every figure within has a story, and reason for being placed exactly where they are.

He said: “let me see.”

I sent one sketch over: "Who is asking?"

I didn't get an answer for three months.
Not until the ER.

@goldie_mceve  was on the line. Martina and I go back a ways now. Even before Venice, when I first exhibited The Monument Game. For months, it turned out, she had been quietly researching the work and larger body of Luci on behalf of and alongside Alan Howard and his advisory team. Martina, with her very cheery Italian accent that always sounds like she’s smiling says:
 “Hello, Sam, how is Rachel? Is now a good time? I have something I’d like to ask you.”

I looked at Rachel showing Syla the red light passing through the hole of the saltine crackers. 

“Now is great”

She was calling with an offer from Alan.

Out of every figure inside X. Masquerade, in the back-left corner, sitting in the mist of the Kingdom of the Included: there is a hooded man carrying a heavy pack covered in the Masks I had been making for each of you. The labor of performance and toil to imbue what we make with enough to keep the whole thing going.

Sitting in the hospital with my daughter was where this piece shifted out of idea-land, but for a figure to get off the corner of one painting and into a piece of its own was not a phone call and offer. This is not a “brokered by” situation, but rather a funny spiral of chance meetings happening from people creating moments for more, people pulling one moment to the next, and paths converging louder later from the collisions of connection years prior.

Years ago at a Bright Moments and Art Blocks event in Paris, (thank you to @seth and @ArtOnBlockchain  for building your own worlds to bring people together), I bumped into Alan. I didn't know him, but he told me his great love is Impressionism and that almost nothing in all of art since had held him until he fell back in love with art through digital and code-based work. Someone who devotes himself to collecting Monet, skips an entire century, and then waxes poetic on generative art is an oddity if nothing else. An eccentric within an eccentric night. Just a ripple.

Time went on.

In 2024, after the initial rush of the Venice Biennale opening had faded, I was standing at our dock door of the exhibition @kukulabanze  and @scrptdfntsy put on with me. Looking out across the canal, Alan and his wife Caroline pulled up by boat. It was a quiet day at the exhibition and I was able to walk them through all of Luci, Birth to The Muck, and then we sat for an hour in front of The Monument Game while we discussed the very old story that led to all of this. A Skull, a Player, and then some Masks entered his collection since, and that was already a wonderful chain of events. But I think what I’ve discovered is that people often mistake a moment as something able to just be “done”, rather than an opening of a relationship to another moment backwards and forwards in time. A flow.
That same weekend in Paris I had met Alan, I had also met @mickymalka of @Kanbas_ . Months later on that same dock, Micky brought @beckykleiner over. Both of them have become dear friends and nearly a year after led to Masquerade. Masquerade then led to the Toledo Museum of Art and the Infinite Images exhibition. Infinite Images filled with works from Alan’s collection, and suddenly loops were forming and bridges were being built. Benny keeping conversations alive, months of Martina's research, and years of all of you putting your own lives into the work came back around to a hospital room in Manhattan. I’m just staring at the best and only things that truly matter to me, the things I’m all in, my girl with her shining red light held by the rock of Rachel, and get to feel this chain reaction of relationships unfold to get there, all for her. Creation begetting creation.

In the background of making this piece, as well as the broader body of work still to come in the next chapter, I enjoy and will continue to enjoy the quiet time to create and experiment. When I poke my head up, it’s to share a story along the way, then duck back down to work. This poke, I see a newfound cannibalism: whispered and snake-like emerging - an eating of our own, blood-tainted water that is hungry to discard bodies. If you believe this is not the end of history, then it is odd to let a river be treated like it holds the stagnancy and scarcity of a pond. And if you believe it is the end, grace is the last thing to abandon at the gates. Everything still growing here came from movement. Big collisions flowing out into vast expanses. Currents combine, gather in force, carve through the land, and spread. To pathfind. Meandering, though the wander can be, I find it best to build on the bend and watch what floats downstream as nature clears the water with time.

The Mask Maker is the first 1/1 from this world I’m making with no Luci in the frame. The first without a numeral in the chronology. It has no “mechanics”.  But if you’re new here, it has all you need to know for now.

The next chapter from here, is a massive departure from anything I’ve done before. Creating The Mask Maker alongside it, dancing between a life as a painter, the hybridity of new tools slipping in and out of the old, developing my own software while drawing more than I ever have, sitting in the feeling of gathering, performing, dispersing, all has made the work “more”. Making art, especially for long periods of time for projects that will be shared over the course of the next several years, can be an isolating experience, there is no drip of daily connection from a well-fed algorithm.  As many components of what I do become ever-more complex, being rooted in the story of a single figure and feeling in time, the feeling of what it has been like to know each of you, interpret each of you, and open paths to know more than what is presented by each of us - the medium stays in relationships and the stories between us.

My deep thanks to Alan for his conviction and patronage in acquiring The Mask Maker, it means a tremendous amount to join the collection. There’s no room for aloofness in me with this, it’s a lot of trust to place, on a timescale that reaches back to Monument and commitment to a future far from now. 

Thank you to Martina for the friendship and scrutiny, and for passing the torch to Sebastian who has been an incredible voice in bringing it home, to Benny for always trying to stitch it all together, mess that you are, @musicalnetta for holding what I love up in the quiet with 613 days of vigilant ethnography, you live in the piece and I share it today in celebration of you as an opening to your close, and I hope this does not sound placating because I really do mean it: to everyone who has helped give me and The Mask Maker something to feel, even when it’s violent I greatly appreciate these collisions most of all.

For anyone who hasn’t yet added something of themselves, holds someone else’s contributions, or maybe feels what they presented in the past wasn’t quite what they are, my site has just undergone a massive change under the hood, and you may find a good place for the potential of what could be.

$IONQ Elisity joins a Texas water pilot

On 17 November 2026, Elisity announced it is an eligible Assessor in Project Watershed 250, a Texas Cyber Command pilot that connects water and wastewater utilities with no-cost cybersecurity help.

James Winebrenner, Chief Executive Officer of Elisity, said: "Water utilities need to keep essential operations running while they strengthen security. Zero Trust starts with understanding what is connected and limiting access to what each device needs to do its job. We're committing engineers and software to help utilities put those controls to work on the infrastructure they already own, at no cost during the pilot."

The offer includes assessments of utility networks and hands-on help implementing segmentation on compatible existing infrastructure, with plant operators controlling when policies take effect. Participating utilities receive an inventory of in-scope assets, a map of network communications and prioritized remediation recommendations. No purchase is required.

Texas Cyber Command listed Elisity, Inc among 63 industry partners in a release published the same day.

The Elisity release also describes prior work with the City of Waco, Texas. After deploying the pilot in less than a day, Waco deployed Elisity across three water and two wastewater treatment plants in 41 days, using existing network infrastructure.

IonQ completed its acquisition of Elisity earlier this month. Katrina Taylor, Sales Director at Elisity, wrote on LinkedIn: "We remain focused on delivering our best-in-class Zero Trust platform while helping organizations prepare for a post-quantum future."

text:
Bastrop ISD is paying for some of its own employees to become fully certified teachers.

The district's new Grow-Your-Own program officially launched Oct. 26 with an inaugural cohort of 10 educators. They will earn a bachelor's degree and Texas teacher certification with full financial support from the district, tuition-free, according to Community Impact.

How it works: Indiana Wesleyan University and Teachworthy, a teacher certification organization, built an accelerated path for employees who don't yet have a degree. Participants earn credits through Teachworthy courses, transferred college credits, IWU coursework and district professional development, then finish with a Teachworthy internship to receive their certification. The program takes one to three years, said Windy Burnett, Bastrop ISD's human resources special programs coordinator.

Who can apply: all full-time, uncertified Bastrop ISD employees. Applications were judged on commitment to the district, ability to finish the program, area of certification interest, readiness for the profession, and communication and professionalism.

Why now: new state rules require proper teacher certification, and the TEA gave Bastrop ISD until the 2029-30 school year to comply. In December 2025, 115 of the district's K-5 teachers did not have a full certification. Right now, 97 pre-K through fifth-grade teachers are working on theirs.

Burnett said the program is expected to continue and could expand in future cycles. "This program helps remove financial and time barriers for our employees who are already working in our district," she said.

Source: https://t.co/giPca8oMdk

text:
Anchor: We're now taking you to Capitol Hill where Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is taking questions after meeting with senators. It comes, of course, after the nationwide ground stop that left hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded over the weekend. Let's listen.

Sean Duffy: And it created instability. And we saw that we were having issues with communication between air traffic and our pilots and then we saw issues in our radar feeds. And it's because of that that we made the extraordinary step to shut down the airspace. And I just, on a side note, I was just out with the families of Flight 5342. And I think it's important to understand how serious we take aviation safety. My first full day on the job was with those families. And we want to make sure that we do everything we can, that the story is people were inconvenienced versus families are having a different conversation about the loss of a loved one. That's why we don't take any risk. So in regard to what we did after the airspace was reopened, we were able to take control of the router that was our issue. By the way, this was the 69th installation of that router. Sixty-eight times it worked well. This one, the router started to broadcast into our network and it started to overload the network. So we have it, or L3Harris who was the owner of our network and they monitor our network one, our network, they have it. We went to their facility with the router in Florida. So at that facility is L3Harris, HP is there, Cisco is there, the FAA is there. And I called Kash Patel and I said, you know, there's a lot of things happening right now that all of us don't know where it's coming from. And I've been told by our national security three-letter agencies that we weren't hacked. But I think it's important that we have all precautions. So I asked Kash to send me part of his FBI team to be part of the analyzing of this router. We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado, but the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet. And I promise all of you that when I know what happened with that router, injecting that overload into our system, I will most definitely share that with you. If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you as well. But all of my intelligence partners are telling me that wasn't the case. But again, we have the FBI there partnering with us as we work through this analysis. And I'll take your questions, I'm sure on that, that you have later. I want to talk about this $12.5 billion. Since I had this job, I've been pounding the drum about the need for investment in aviation. We've neglected it, our system is old, it's showing its age, we have to make the investments. And Congress gave me a historic down payment of $12.5 billion. I've heard some people say, "Well, you haven't spent the money, right? Where's all the money?" So let me just explain that to you all what's happening here. The Congress gave us very specific categories in which we had to spend the money. And so because our airspace is so big, we have so much equipment in the airspace, and I can't go to say a Best Buy and just take it off the shelf. We actually have to order the equipment, and then the companies that get the contracts, they actually have to build the equipment for us to then take possession. The senators in here would have been very annoyed had I prepaid for the equipment. So I only pay when they deliver. So we've had a lot of radios and voice switches and surface awareness systems that have been delivered, but not all of them. So I still hold some of that money. Good example is we haven't built radar in America for 30 years. And I thought that if we're going to have a historic buy for radar, we should build those radar in America with American workers. And so the companies that got the contract, they set up facilities in America, one Florida, one in Kansas, and they're building those radar. They have a contract with us to purchase the radar. Well, I haven't taken the delivery of those radar yet. In a few months, I'm going to. And when I do, when I receive them, I'll pay for them. So all of the money hasn't left our account and gone to those who won in the contract. I only am going to pay when they deliver. And I think the point here is all the money has been set aside for this mission of modernizing the airspace. It's all going to be done in two and a half, two years from now. This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky and we are switching out equipment. It's been a problem for decades. I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it. It's a little complicated, but we are doing great work and making great progress. So as part of this new ask to Congress, I want to talk about that. Then I'll take your questions. Part of it is I talked, we're switching this old network, this new, this old architecture from copper to fiber, right? From analog to digital. But it's an old architecture. We need a new mesh network that is, that it's state of the art, that's resilient. I've asked for money to build that new network and the Congress is very interested in that. The software that we use to manage the airspace was developed in the mid nineties. It works, it's functional, but the advancements in software, if we are able to go out, develop and buy it, it's going to give us far greater safety and far more efficiency in the airspace. And it's time, it's been 30 years, it's time that we make this investment. On top of that, the newest, so we have towers, tracons and centers, the centers that controls the upper altitude airplanes, we have 22 of them. Do you guys know the newest one was built when? The newest one that we have was built in 1969. That's how old this stuff is. We have old towers from the sixties, old TRACONs from the sixties. I'm asking the Congress to, as part of this historic investment, invest in that infrastructure. We have a country that's grown and expanded. Our people go to different places. We've seen growth in a lot of our cities. I want to invest in their infrastructure. Some of them need new runways. We need money for some of our airports. So this is, what I wanted to do is I wanted to put everything on the table. I wanted to show it, show it all to them. And I know that Congress will work its will. They'll pressure test it. They'll look at it and they'll make a determination and a decision on what they see as their priorities. But the current trajectory that we're on right now, if I stay on this course, I will replace every single tower in America in 300 years, in 300 years. So we have to do something different. I'm willing to take the heat, the pressure to dive in. Administrator Bryan Bedford, he's right here, has done a fantastic job in modernization. He's got a great team. We're all working together to make sure people stay safe and we have the right equipment and technology in our airspace. We're not going to let up. We're going to continue on that mission. And I hope that the Congress joins us at this really important time. One last point, then I'll take your questions. I don't want to start this work in six months, eight months, a year. The time is right now. And what I love about what's happening is I'm talking to Democrats and Republicans in both chambers and this is about America. This is about American airspace and they're all pretty engaged. What they're going to do, I can't tell you. I don't think anyone can tell you what the Congress will do, but they're all very interested in making sure we get the right investments here. And that's a great sign for all of us. Everyone who flies, everyone who's leading the project at DOT. With that, Bryan and I are willing to take your questions that you may have.

Reporter: I know you don't want to do this in a piecemeal fashion, you want $50 billion all at one time. However, if that's the only way Congress will get this through for you, are you willing to separate the most safety critical components of the system to get the funding from you?

Sean Duffy: I'm already in a piecemeal approach, the $12.5 billion was piecemeal, right? And so yeah, I'll take what I can get. And I will work with the Congress to make sure that we do the highest priorities first. And I would hope that they don't do that to me, but I'll take what I can get and I'm going to build with whatever they give me.

Reporter: There's millions of people that are planning to fly next week. What guarantees can you make that they won't face the same disruption that they faced last week?

Sean Duffy: So when we pulled this router out that was broadcasting into the network, it took longer than I would have liked to identify that router with L3Harris who monitors our network. Bryan and I are working through other procedures that we can have a belt and suspenders approach. But now we've isolated the problem. I think the airspace is going to operate like it has over the course of the last years and decades. But I will tell you that I'm not going to take a risk with anyone's life. I will not do that. And so if we see an issue, I want people to get safely to their destination. I don't want to see disruptions. We're working on delays and cancellations. But when the rubber meets the road, safety will always come first for the administrator and me.

Reporter: There are even some Republicans who say that someone in the administration should be held accountable for what happened on Friday. Will anybody be held accountable in the administration for the ground stop?

Sean Duffy: Well, to be held accountable, you have to look at, I mean, listen, this network dates back decades. It's decades old, right? It's what I inherited and Bryan inherited. And this is the first time that you've had, and many of you will cover this. I've been talking about it for two years. And so we are well on our way in transforming what we were given. If someone did something wrong, they should be held accountable. But Bryan and I do not apologize for shutting down the airspace. I'd rather have the disruption story versus the story and conversation I have with the families of Flight 5342. But I want to tell you how quickly we're moving and I don't want to throw darts at anybody. But the last administration was able to transition 19% of this old network from copper to fiber or analog to digital 19% of it in four years was transitioned. In one year, we've done over 50%. So we're moving at a different speed because we think the moment is now to actually fix the system. And we put a lot of effort and energy into making sure people are safe and our networks actually work. I've listened to all of you and some of you will say I'm moving too fast. Some of you say I'm moving too slow. Maybe I'm Goldilocks and I'm going just right here. We will not go faster than what the safety mission would allow. We are moving at the right pace. But I'll just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes. So we do have to charge forward. We do have to get this work done. Otherwise staying on the old system for longer is going to mean more risk as opposed to fix the system and you're going to reduce the risk. And by the way, build a new network, even less risk. That new network I mentioned, the new architecture, I've talked to AT&T, Lumen and Verizon. They have committed to make this a national priority, which is great on their part. We believe that with their counsel, we can do that in two years, which is for the FAA and the partnerships that we get is remarkable speed that American Telecom is going to offer us to deliver on behalf of the American people.

SOURCE: ABC News

Michigan LFP battery maker Our Next Energy (ONE) is going public through a merger with Wen Acquisition Corp, valuing the combined company at about $1 billion.

The combined company is set to trade on Nasdaq as ONEE once the deal closes, expected in the first half of 2027. The deal could raise up to $400 million in gross proceeds, including a $100 million PIPE, $30 million of which has been committed so far.

ONE makes LFP cells, packs and energy storage systems for defense, rail and grid customers at two Michigan factories. The company has booked about $40 million in cumulative revenue and holds more than $200 million in binding multi-year contracts.

The University of Michigan doesn't shrink from big things. We do them right, and we do them together.

text:
Spire | FY2026 results

Spire net income jumps 81.7% to $494M following major strategic utility repositioning

👉 Spire Inc. reported fiscal 2026 net income of $494M, an 81.7% increase over the previous year, as the company completed a massive structural overhaul. The utility successfully integrated Piedmont Natural Gas Tennessee while divesting its Gas Marketing and Storage segments. These strategic moves consolidated operations into a single Gas Utility reportable segment, focusing entirely on regulated natural gas distribution across its multi-state footprint.

👉 Revenue grew to $2.48B from $2.23B, supported by an expanded customer base and system modernization. Despite the headline profit surge, pre-tax income fell 15.9% to $199M, impacted by higher interest costs and the timing of regulatory recoveries. The company recently filed a general rate case in Missouri seeking a $228M revenue increase to support an $808M investment in system modernization and future rate base stability.

👉 Operating income rose 7.3% to $451M, though the operating margin edged lower to 18.2%. The result reflects the seasonal nature of the business and the transition to a fully regulated platform. To manage this capital-intensive shift, Spire Missouri issued $350M in mortgage bonds and extended its credit facilities through 2031, ensuring liquidity for ongoing infrastructure improvements and the pending sale of its Mississippi operations.

👉 Management has raised long-term EPS growth targets to a range of 6-8%, signaling confidence in the new simplified business model. Following the divestitures, the company's earnings are now primarily derived from its regulated utilities, which typically see peak performance during the November to April heating season. The company also demonstrated commitment to shareholders by raising its common stock dividend by 4.8% during the period.

👉 Growth catalyst: Management has established a long-term EPS growth target of 6-8% following the transition to a fully regulated utility platform.

👉 Road blocker: Spire faces near-term regulatory headwinds in Tennessee and Missouri as it seeks to resolve general rate cases and infrastructure surcharges.
